$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.1$ | $0.3$ | $0.4$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.1$ | $0.5$ | $0.6$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.2$ | $0.8$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a support ${S}_{X},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 0.4+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.6 \\  & =2.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =2.8-{1.6}^{2} \\  & =0.24.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a support ${S}_{Y},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.2+{1}^{2}\cdot 0.8 \\  & =0.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =0.8-{0.8}^{2} \\  & =0.16.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\text{E}[XY]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =(1)(0)f(1,0)+(2)(0)f(2,0)+(1)(1)f(1,1)+(2)(1)f(2,1) \\  & =0\cdot 0.1+0\cdot 0.1+1\cdot 0.3+2\cdot 0.5 \\  & =1.3.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =1.3-1.6\cdot 0.8 \\  & =0.02.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.24 & 0.02 \\ 0.02 & 0.16\end{aligned}].

$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{4}{5},$ $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{1}{4},$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=\frac{2}{3},$ find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y.$" :question/worked-solution "For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $Σ$ is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, we find $\text{Var}[X].$ Using the given results, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}-{(\frac{4}{5})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{75}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}48{y}^{3}(x-y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}(x{y}^{3}-{y}^{4})\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}x{y}^{4}-\frac{1}{5}{y}^{5}]}_{y=0}^{y=x/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{64}{x}^{5}-\frac{1}{160}{x}^{5})\text{d}x \\  & =48\cdot \frac{3}{320}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{5}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{9}{20}{[\frac{1}{6}{x}^{6}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{40}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{40}-{(\frac{1}{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{80}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\text{E}[XY]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}xy\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}48x{y}^{2}(x-y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}-x{y}^{3})\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{4}x{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=x/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{24}{x}^{5}-\frac{1}{64}{x}^{5})\text{d}x \\  & =48\cdot \frac{5}{192}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{5}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{[\frac{1}{6}{x}^{6}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{5}{24}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{5}{24}-(\frac{4}{5})\cdot (\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{120}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{75} & \frac{1}{120} \\ \frac{1}{120} & \frac{1}{80}\end{aligned}].

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}.
$$

We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{4}\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}]}_{-1}^{1}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{-1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}-{(0)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{y}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{4}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{4}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{-1}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{5}{y}^{5}]}_{-1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{33}{5} \\  & =\frac{11}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{11}{5}-{(\frac{5}{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{51}{80}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the covariance of $X$ and $Y.$ The joint support of $X$ and $Y$ is given by the rectangle

$$
S=[-1,1]\times [-1,2].
$$

Moreover, we can write

$$
f(x,y)=g(x)\cdot h(y),
$$

where $g(x)=\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}$ and $h(y)=\frac{{y}^{2}}{3}.$

Hence, $X$ and $Y$ are independent, and consequently $\text{Cov}[X,Y]=0.$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$

$$

$$

We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}x{y}^{3})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}]}_{0}^{1}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot 4 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{18}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}x{y}^{3})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{5}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{5}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {[\frac{1}{6}{y}^{6}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{32}{3} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}-{(\frac{8}{5})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{75}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the covariance of $X$ and $Y.$ The joint support of $X$ and $Y$ is given by the rectangle

$$
S=[0,1]\times [0,2].
$$

Moreover, we can write

$$
f(x,y)=g(x)\cdot h(y),
$$

where $g(x)=2x$ and $h(y)=\frac{{y}^{3}}{4}.$

Hence, $X$ and $Y$ are independent, and consequently $\text{Cov}[X,Y]=0.$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{18} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{8}{75}\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-294a6c0d-e8c4-539b-87eb-6c2be022c57a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "7039fb00-3d4a-54d6-a4b0-1bcf58d49ef2" :question/math-academy-id "q-159422" :question/problem "The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{16}({x}^{2}-y),\, & 0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le {x}^{2}, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{5}{3},$ $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{20}{21},$ and $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]=\frac{40}{27},$ find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y.$" :question/worked-solution "For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $Σ$ is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, we find $\text{Var}[X].$
We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\frac{5}{16}{x}^{2}({x}^{2}-y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}({x}^{4}-y{x}^{2})\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[y{x}^{4}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}{x}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y={x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{6})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{32}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{6}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{32}{[\frac{1}{7}{x}^{7}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{20}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{20}{7}-{(\frac{5}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{63}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{Var}[Y].$ Using the given results, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{40}{27}-{(\frac{20}{21})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{760}{1\,323}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\text{E}[XY]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}xy\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\frac{5}{16}xy({x}^{2}-y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}({x}^{3}y-x{y}^{2})\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}x]}_{y=0}^{y={x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{1}{6}{x}^{7})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{96}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{7}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{96}{[\frac{1}{8}{x}^{8}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{5}{3}-(\frac{5}{3})\cdot (\frac{20}{21}) \\  & =\frac{5}{63}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{63} & \frac{5}{63} \\ \frac{5}{63} & \frac{760}{1\,323}\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3850f8d6-6285-5466-abaf-4c01feeefec9"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id \frac{5}{63} & \frac{760}{1\,323}\end{aligned}]" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186188793 :question/problem "The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}x+y,\, & 0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\text{E}[Y]=\frac{7}{12},$ and $E[{X}^{2}]=\frac{5}{12},$ find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y.$" :question/worked-solution "For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $Σ$ is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, we find $\text{Var}[X].$ Using the given results, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{12}-{(\frac{7}{12})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{11}{144}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}(x+y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(x{y}^{2}+{y}^{3})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+x{y}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}+{y}^{3})\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{6}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{5}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{12}-{(\frac{7}{12})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{11}{144}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\text{E}[XY]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}xy\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}xy(x+y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}y+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{3}y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{6}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{6}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-(\frac{7}{12})\cdot (\frac{7}{12}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{144}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{11}{144} & -\frac{1}{144} \\ -\frac{1}{144} & \frac{11}{144}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}11 & -1 \\ -1 & 11\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186187038 :answer-field/correct "answer-0a71cefc-8de5-5de6-a1e7-e827ad772d4a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-0a71cefc-8de5-5de6-a1e7-e827ad772d4a" "answer-ef02e2b8-d181-5dc2-952d-5f459a779602" "answer-2529513a-9fa9-5a66-b66c-95b167283ef3" "answer-b1914b83-6794-52fe-91db-700c3ef7d55d" "answer-01df44a6-657a-5670-a985-4a87b7716922"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0a71cefc-8de5-5de6-a1e7-e827ad772d4a" :answer/id #uuid "0a71cefc-8de5-5de6-a1e7-e827ad772d4a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}11 & -1 \\ -1 & 11\end{aligned}]" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ef02e2b8-d181-5dc2-952d-5f459a779602" :answer/id #uuid "ef02e2b8-d181-5dc2-952d-5f459a779602" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}11 & -1 \\ -1 & 7\end{aligned}]" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2529513a-9fa9-5a66-b66c-95b167283ef3" :answer/id #uuid "2529513a-9fa9-5a66-b66c-95b167283ef3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}11 & 0 \\ 0 & 11\end{aligned}]" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b1914b83-6794-52fe-91db-700c3ef7d55d" :answer/id #uuid "b1914b83-6794-52fe-91db-700c3ef7d55d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}11 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}]" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-01df44a6-657a-5670-a985-4a87b7716922" :answer/id #uuid "01df44a6-657a-5670-a985-4a87b7716922" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}7 & -1 \\ -1 & 11\end{aligned}]" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186189409 :tutorial/content "For a set of random variables $X_1, \ldots, X_n,$ the **covariance matrix** $\Sigma$ is defined as

![](images/41/416ac73d7b76e9c62efead1278e7a2b47c00dd03a8af17df99f28aea99f3f7a0.svg)

Note the following:

- The $i$th diagonal element is $\Sigma_{ii} = \textrm{Var}[X_i].$

- The element in the $i$th row and $j$th column for $i \neq j$ is $\Sigma_{ij} = \textrm{Cov}[X_i, X_j].$

Now, since $\textrm{Cov}[X_i,X_j] = \textrm{Cov}[X_j,X_i]$ for any pair of random variables $X_i, X_j$, we have the following theorem:

*The covariance matrix is always symmetric. Moreover, it is a positive semi-definite matrix.*" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186188521 :activity/expected-seconds 900.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186217109 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-8dc89317-431f-536c-84f1-f80a52b02432" "question-0dbc8468-e68d-529c-9edc-f8593cda9fbb"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-8dc89317-431f-536c-84f1-f80a52b02432" :question/id #uuid "8dc89317-431f-536c-84f1-f80a52b02432" :question/math-academy-id "q-152279" :question/problem "The parabola $y={x}^{2}+2x+2$ and the line $y=2-2x$ intersect at the points $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})$ and $({x}_{2},{y}_{2}),$ where ${x}_{1}<{x}_{2}.$ What is the value of ${y}_{1}+{y}_{2}?$" :question/worked-solution "We need to solve the following system consisting of the equations of the curves:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y={x}^{2}+2x+2 \\ y=2-2x\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the equations equal to one another and solving, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2x+2 & =2-2x \\ {x}^{2}+4x & =0 \\ x(x+4) & =0 \\ x & =-4,0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${x}_{1}<{x}_{2},$ the $x$-coordinates of the intersection points are ${x}_{1}=-4$ and ${x}_{2}=0.$ 

To find the $y$-coordinates of the intersection points, we plug these values into either curve. Let's choose the line since it's simpler.

- Substituting ${x}_{1}=-4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & =2-2{x}_{1} \\  & =2-2(-4) \\  & =10,\end{aligned}
$$

so one point of intersection is $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(-4,10).$

- Substituting ${x}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2} & =2-2{x}_{2} \\  & =2-2(0) \\  & =2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the other point of intersection is $({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(0,2).$

Therefore, ${y}_{1}=10,\,{y}_{2}=2,$ and

$$
{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}=10+2=12.
$$

possible values of $k?$" :question/worked-solution "To determine whether the line $y=x+k$ intersects the parabola $y={x}^{2}+1,$ we need to solve the following system of equations for the two curves:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y={x}^{2}+1 \\ y=x+k\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the equations equal to one another and writing in standard form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+1 & =x+k \\ {x}^{2}-x+1-k & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve this equation using the quadratic formula with $a=1,\,b=-1,$ and $c=1-k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{-(-1)\pm \sqrt{(-1)^{2}-4(1)(1-k)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{1\pm \sqrt{1-4+4k}}{2} \\  & =\frac{1\pm \sqrt{4k-3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the line and parabola do not intersect, our quadratic equation must have no real solutions; hence, the expression inside the square root must be negative.
Setting up and solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4k-3 & <0 \\ 4k & <3 \\ k & <\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the range of possible values of $k$ is $k<\frac{3}{4}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-83300691-a442-5ef8-b2cc-b11ca96f7be8"] $$
\{\begin{aligned}y={x}^{2}+5x-1 \\ y=-2x-13\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the equations equal to one another and solving, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+5x-1 & =-2x-13 \\ {x}^{2}+7x+12 & =0 \\ (x+4)(x+3) & =0 \\ x & =-4,-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${x}_{1}<{x}_{2},$ the $x$-coordinates of the intersection points are ${x}_{1}=-4$ and ${x}_{2}=-3.$

To find the $y$-coordinates of the intersection points, we plug these values into either curve. Let's choose the line since it's simpler.

- Substituting ${x}_{1}=-4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & =-2{x}_{1}-13 \\  & =-2(-4)-13 \\  & =-5,\end{aligned}
$$

so one point of intersection is $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(-4,-5).$

- Substituting ${x}_{2}=-3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2} & =-2{x}_{2}-13 \\  & =-2(-3)-13 \\  & =-7,\end{aligned}
$$

so the other point of intersection is $({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(-3,-7).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+x+4 & =5x \\ {x}^{2}-4x+4 & =0 \\ (x-2)(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =5x \\  & =5(2) \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only point of intersection is $(2,10).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}) \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =2x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}+\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x) \\  & =2x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}\cdot 2 \\  & =-\frac{2xy}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given expression for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ into the above and simplify the resulting expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =-\frac{2xy}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\cdot 2x\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}+2\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =-4{x}^{2}y+2\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the point $(0,0)$ lies on $f,$ we substitute the coordinates of our point into the above expression for the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}|}_{(0,0)} & =-4\cdot {0}^{2}\cdot 0+2\sqrt{1-{0}^{2}}=2\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, note that we are given $y(0)$ and asked to find $y(0.2).$ The distance from $x=0$ to $x=0.2$ is $0.2,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be 

$$
Δx=\frac{0.2-0}{2}=0.1.
$$

Now, let's proceed with Euler's method. We'll start by creating a table that includes the initial condition data $y(0)=0.$

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ | $$ | $$ |

**Step 1.** We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy$ (using the values of $x$ and $y$ in the first row) and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}}$ and ${y}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2x\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}=2\cdot 0\cdot \sqrt{1-{0}^{2}}=0 \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=0\cdot 0.1=0 \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=0+0.1=0.1 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=0+0=0\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| $0.1$ | $0$ | $$ | $$ |

**Step 2.** We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy$ (using the values of $x$ and $y$ in the second row) and new values of ${x}_{\text{new}}$ and ${y}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2x\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}=2\cdot 0.1\cdot \sqrt{1-{0}^{2}}=0.2 \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=0.2\cdot 0.1=0.02 \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=0.1+0.1=0.2 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=0+0.02=0.02\end{aligned}
$$

 

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |

$$

:question/problem "Using the first two non-zero terms of the Maclaurin expansion of $f(x),$ approximate ${\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x.$ Write your answer as a fraction in its lowest terms.

${\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x\,\,≈\,\,$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We have that

$$
f(x)≈{x}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{6}}{6}.
$$

We can approximate $\int f(x)\,\text{d}x$ by integrating the above series term-by-term, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ≈{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{6}}{6})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{42}{x}^{6})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{42}]-0 \\  & =\frac{13}{42}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-96f0fd95-c9b0-5cbe-abcc-ca8956c4e2ea"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-96f0fd95-c9b0-5cbe-abcc-ca8956c4e2ea" :answer-field/id #uuid "96f0fd95-c9b0-5cbe-abcc-ca8956c4e2ea" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-2c6372b2-3f3a-5d2d-9b9b-d69b71a08c40" :answer-field/choices ["answer-2c6372b2-3f3a-5d2d-9b9b-d69b71a08c40"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2c6372b2-3f3a-5d2d-9b9b-d69b71a08c40" :answer/id #uuid "2c6372b2-3f3a-5d2d-9b9b-d69b71a08c40" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{13}{42}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092269 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-8679792d-1ee6-50ba-bf59-17896dc979de"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-8679792d-1ee6-50ba-bf59-17896dc979de" :question/id #uuid "8679792d-1ee6-50ba-bf59-17896dc979de" :question/math-academy-id "q-126769" :question/problem "Given that the Maclaurin expansion of $f(x)$ can be represented as

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}{x}^{4n+2}}{(2n+1)!},
$$

calculate the radius of convergence $R$ of this power series.

$R\,\,=\,\,$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "To find the radius of convergence, we apply the ratio test.

So, let's denote ${a}_{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n}{x}^{4n+2}}{(2n+1)!}.$ Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(-1)^{n+1}{x}^{4n+6}}{(2n+3)!}\cdot \frac{(2n+1)!}{(-1)^{n}{x}^{4n+2}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|-\frac{{x}^{4}}{(2n+2)(2n+3)}| \\  & ={x}^{4}{lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{1}{(2n+2)(2n+3)}| \\  & ={x}^{4}\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if $L<1.$ In this case, the convergence condition is satisfied for all $-\infty <x<\infty .$ Therefore, we conclude that the radius of convergence is $R=\infty .$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ee13cf7b-506a-556c-9c39-4af06c9d75a9"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-ee13cf7b-506a-556c-9c39-4af06c9d75a9" :answer-field/id #uuid "ee13cf7b-506a-556c-9c39-4af06c9d75a9" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-c0ee0055-9260-50e8-82d0-59ef2f03f218" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c0ee0055-9260-50e8-82d0-59ef2f03f218"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c0ee0055-9260-50e8-82d0-59ef2f03f218" :answer/id #uuid "c0ee0055-9260-50e8-82d0-59ef2f03f218" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\infty" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054682 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-1f6c3d65-e721-5449-9ddc-958a81a54048"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-1f6c3d65-e721-5449-9ddc-958a81a54048" :question/id #uuid "1f6c3d65-e721-5449-9ddc-958a81a54048" :question/math-academy-id "q-126770" :question/problem "Calculate the first three non-zero terms of the Maclaurin expansion of ${f}^{′}(x).$

"Since we want to find the projection onto the $xz$-plane, we need to eliminate the variable $y.$ First, we solve the equation of the plane for $y,$ as follows:

$$
2x-y=0\,⟹\,y=2x
$$

Substituting the expression for $y$ into the equation of the elliptic cone, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(2x-1)^{2} & ={z}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+4{x}^{2}-4x+1 & ={z}^{2} \\ {z}^{2}-5{x}^{2}+4x & =1 \\ {z}^{2}-5({x}^{2}-\frac{4}{5}x+\frac{4}{25})+\frac{4}{5} & =1 \\ {z}^{2}-5{({x}^{2}-\frac{2}{5})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{5} \\ 5{z}^{2}-25{(x-\frac{2}{5})}^{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is the equation of a hyperbola centered at $(\frac{2}{5},0)$ in the $xz$-plane." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields $$
f(n)=f(1)+(n-1)d.
$$

$$

$$

$$
d=17-19=-2.
$$

So, we substitute into the formula and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n) & =f(1)+(n-1)d \\  & =19+(n-1)(-2) \\  & =19-2n+2 \\  & =21-2n\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =18-5n \\ {a}_{33} & =18-5(33) \\  & =18-165 \\  & =-147\end{aligned}
$$

${a}_{24}=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}+(n-1)d.
$$

First, we will write the formula for the $n$th term of this sequence. From the first few terms

$$
-17,\,-12,\,-7,\,-2,\,…,
$$

we see that the first term is ${a}_{1}=-17$ and the common difference is 

$$
d=-12-(-17)=5.
$$

So, we substitute into the formula and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =-17+(n-1)(5) \\  & =-17+5n-5 \\  & =5n-22\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use our formula to find the $24$th term. All we have to do is substitute $n=24:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =5n-22 \\ {a}_{24} & =5(24)-22 \\  & =120-22 \\  & =98\end{aligned}

$x\in R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $3$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,3)$ to $x\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $f(x+6)=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$

II. $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R$

III. $f(x+2)=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f$ is the $3$-periodic extension of $F,$ we have 

- $f(x+3)=f(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,3).$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x+6)=f((x+3)+3)=f(x+3)=f(x)\end{aligned}
$$

for all $x\in R.$

- Statement II is false. For example, take $x=4.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(4)=f(1+3)=f(1)=F(1)=2(1)=2,\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}F(4)=2(4)=8.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x)\ne F(x)$ for $x=4.$

- Statement III is false. For example, take $x=2.$ Then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2+2)=f(4)=f(1+3)=f(1)=F(1)=2(1)=2\end{aligned}
$$

while 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2)=F(2)=2(2)=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x+2)\ne f(2)$ for $x=2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186164762 :answer-field/correct 17592186164763 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-d11bc330-9efc-55d1-a388-de4f864cc23e" :question/id #uuid "d11bc330-9efc-55d1-a388-de4f864cc23e" :question/math-academy-id "q-340511" :question/problem "Let $F(x)=4x-1$ for $x\in R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $6$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,6)$ to $x\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $f(x+12)=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$

II. $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R$

III. $f(x+3)=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f$ is the $6$-periodic extension of $F,$ we have 

- $f(x+6)=f(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,6).$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x+12)=f((x+6)+6)=f(x+6)=f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

for all $x\in R.$

- Statement II is false. For example, take $x=7.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(7)=f(1+6)=f(1)=F(1)=3,\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}F(7)=27.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x)\ne F(x)$ for $x=7.$

- Statement III is false. For example, take $x=2.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2+3)=f(5)=F(5)=19\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2)=F(2)=7.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x+3)\ne f(x)$ for $x=2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-67d9a9a1-d4bf-5f85-97bb-b57a4ffb6644"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-67d9a9a1-d4bf-5f85-97bb-b57a4ffb6644" :answer-field/id #uuid "67d9a9a1-d4bf-5f85-97bb-b57a4ffb6644" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-f962769d-467c-5c55-b93f-dae3d07918c0" :answer-field/choices ["answer-513baa56-f91e-5c3b-99a2-c83dbfe5f274" "answer-f962769d-467c-5c55-b93f-dae3d07918c0" "answer-316390e2-a9a1-557a-b993-1eb5daa5337e" "answer-1091f7e8-6330-5e59-9a2c-9f9973d68732" "answer-95757a8f-1751-58fa-98e7-c089f0afadab"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-513baa56-f91e-5c3b-99a2-c83dbfe5f274" :answer/id #uuid "513baa56-f91e-5c3b-99a2-c83dbfe5f274" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f962769d-467c-5c55-b93f-dae3d07918c0" :answer/id #uuid "f962769d-467c-5c55-b93f-dae3d07918c0" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-316390e2-a9a1-557a-b993-1eb5daa5337e" :answer/id #uuid "316390e2-a9a1-557a-b993-1eb5daa5337e" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1091f7e8-6330-5e59-9a2c-9f9973d68732" :answer/id #uuid "1091f7e8-6330-5e59-9a2c-9f9973d68732" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-95757a8f-1751-58fa-98e7-c089f0afadab" :answer/id #uuid "95757a8f-1751-58fa-98e7-c089f0afadab" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186315084 :question/problem "$$

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)).
$$

Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient ${b}_{2}$ below, where $⟨\,,⟩$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[0,2\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{2} & ={{field-1}} \\  & ={{field-2}}\,\cdot \,{{field-3}}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [0,2\pi )$ is given by

$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that's piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,2\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),
$$

where ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. 

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & = \\ \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the functions
$1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$
are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is

$$
{b}_{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩.
$$

Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(8\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain that

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & ={b}_{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ \\ {b}_{2} & =\frac{⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩}{⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩} \\ {b}_{2} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2{x}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-74ef7a6c-fb00-53a3-972e-01dd7c23eeb4" "answer-field-ab111ab9-2939-595a-a735-21f1af4492c6" #uuid "3db32c22-3de8-5264-9b28-9916a3aeb5f2" :question/math-academy-id "q-340659" :question/problem "Let $F(x)=2{x}^{4}-4{x}^{3}$ for $x\in R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [0,2\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)).
$$

Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient ${b}_{3}$ below, where $⟨\,,⟩$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[0,2\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{3} & ={{field-1}} \\  & ={{field-2}}\,\cdot \,{{field-3}}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [0,2\pi )$ is given by

$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that's piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,2\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),
$$

where ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. 

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩ & = \\ \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the functions
$1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$
are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is

$$
{b}_{3}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩.
$$

Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{12}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(12\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain that

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩ & ={b}_{3}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩ \\ {b}_{3} & =\frac{⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩}{⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩} \\ {b}_{3} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(2{x}^{4}-4{x}^{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1f978f14-7743-5e8c-b891-41d5a5372431" "answer-field-4ea577f4-edb3-5442-83b4-270041c2560c" "510f41a7-5712-55db-b50d-5c80967bb9fb" :question/math-academy-id "q-12889" :question/problem "Given that

$$
{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+4)}^{4}=A{x}^{8}+B{x}^{6}+C{x}^{4}+128{x}^{2}+256
$$

where $A,B$ and $C$ are constants, find the value of $A+B+C.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
$$

Here we have that $n=4,$ $a=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2},$ and $b=4.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{4}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{3}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{3},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{4}.
$$

The $4$th row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,4,6,4,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+4)}^{4} & =1{a}^{4}+4{a}^{3}b+6{a}^{2}{b}^{2}+4a{b}^{3}+1{b}^{4} \\  & =1{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{4}(4)^{0}+4{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{3}{(4)}^{1}+6{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{2}{(4)}^{2} \\  & \,+4{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{1}{(4)}^{3}+1{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{0}{(4)}^{4} \\  & =1(\frac{{x}^{8}}{16})(1)+4(\frac{{x}^{6}}{8})(4)+6(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4})(16) \\  & \,+4(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})(64)+1(1)(256) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8}}{16}+\frac{16{x}^{6}}{8}+\frac{96{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{256{x}^{2}}{2}+256 \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8}}{16}+2{x}^{6}+24{x}^{4}+128{x}^{2}+256.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have $A=\frac{1}{16},B=2$ and $C=24.$ So, finally

$$
A+B+C=\frac{1}{16}+2+24=\frac{417}{16}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-69965209-526e-5658-899a-44e6dd8b07be"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-12891" :question/problem "Find, in descending powers of $z,$ the first three terms of the binomial expansion of ${(1-{z}^{2})}^{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
$$

Here we have that $n=4,$ $a=1,$ and $b=-{z}^{2}.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{4}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{3}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{3},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{4}.
$$

The $4$th row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,4,6,4,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{(1-{z}^{2})}^{4} & =1{a}^{4}+4{a}^{3}b+6{a}^{2}{b}^{2}+4a{b}^{3}+1{b}^{4} \\  & =1(1)^{4}(-{z}^{2})^{0}+4(1)^{3}(-{z}^{2})^{1}+6(1)^{2}(-{z}^{2})^{2}+4(1)^{1}(-{z}^{2})^{3}+1(1)^{0}(-{z}^{2})^{4} \\  & =1(1)(1)+4(1)(-{z}^{2})+6(1)({z}^{4})+4(1)(-{z}^{6})+1(1)({z}^{8}) \\  & =1-4{z}^{2}+6{z}^{4}-4{z}^{6}+{z}^{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We rewrite the binomial expansion in descending powers of $z$ as follows:

$$
(1-{z}^{2})^{4}={z}^{8}-4{z}^{6}+6{z}^{4}-4{z}^{2}+1
$$

Finally, in descending powers of $z,$ the first three terms of the binomial expansion are

"700411f4-106e-5592-a547-8738d64ef693" :question/math-academy-id "q-110676" :question/problem "Given that 

$$
{(2s-{u}^{2})}^{4}=16{s}^{4}+A{s}^{3}{u}^{2}+B{s}^{2}{u}^{4}+Cs{u}^{6}+{u}^{8}
$$

where $A,B$ and $C$ are constants, determine the value of $A+B+C.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
$$

Here we have that $n=4,$ $a=2s,$ and $b=-{u}^{2}.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{4}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{3}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{3},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{4}.
$$

The $4$th row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,4,6,4,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}(2s-{u}^{2})^{4} & =1{a}^{4}{b}^{0}+4{a}^{3}b+6{a}^{2}{b}^{2}+4a{b}^{3}+1{a}^{0}{b}^{4} \\  & =1(2s)^{4}{(-{u}^{2})}^{0}+4(2s)^{3}{(-{u}^{2})}^{1}+6(2s)^{2}{(-{u}^{2})}^{2} \\  & \,+4(2s)^{1}{(-{u}^{2})}^{3}+1(2s)^{0}{(-{u}^{2})}^{4} \\  & =1(16{s}^{4})(1)+4(8{s}^{3})(-{u}^{2})+6(4{s}^{2})({u}^{4}) \\  & \,+4(2s)(-{u}^{6})+1(1)({u}^{8}) \\  & =16{s}^{4}-32{s}^{3}{u}^{2}+24{s}^{2}{u}^{4}-8s{u}^{6}+{u}^{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $A=-32,B=24,$ and $C=-8.$ Finally, then

$$
A+B+C=-32+24-8=-16.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fe5bbd0a-c356-5392-bd90-c3fba4a83d1d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096479 :question/problem "Evaluate $\displaystyle \int (x^4-3x) \cos(x) \textrm{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "For this integral we choose $u = x^4-3x$ and $\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \cos(x).$ Filling in the table gives the following:

| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same-color Products** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^4-3x$ | $\cos(x)$ |  |  |
| $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 4x^3-3$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} \sin(x)$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} +$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} (x^4-3x)\sin(x)$ |
| $\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 12x^2$ | $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}   -\cos(x)$ | $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -$ | $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}  -(4x^3-3)(-\cos(x))$ |
| $\color[rgb]{1,0,1} 24x$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0,1}  -\sin(x)$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0,1} +$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 12x^2(-\sin(x))$ |
| $\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1} 24$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,1} \cos(x)$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,1} -$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,1}- 24x\cos(x)$ |
| $0$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}  \sin(x)$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}+$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}  24\sin(x)$ |

We add up all the terms of the last column to get the answer for our integral. 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({x}^{4}-3x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\text{d}x & =({x}^{4}-3x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+(4{x}^{3}-3)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) \\  & \,\,-12{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)-24x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+24\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+C \\  & =({x}^{4}-12{x}^{2}-3x+24)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) \\  & \,\,+(4{x}^{3}-24x-3)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+C\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096681 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-1051456d-d936-5dd0-8e18-6d4a40dca9fc" "question-d35b604c-10fb-5e20-9163-ae0fba981c99" "question-09b2a1cb-b590-5e4c-af65-76fb35a22b46" "question-c451ec1c-6a2b-54c4-80d7-187b41f5f298"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096482 :question/problem "Evaluate $\displaystyle \int (x^2-1)(x+2)^5 \textrm{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "For this integral, we choose $u = x^2-1$ and $\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} =(x+2)^5.$ Filling in our table gives the following:

| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same-color Products** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^2-1$ | $(x+2)^5$ |  |  |
| $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 2x$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\dfrac{(x+2)^6}{6}$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} +$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\dfrac{(x^2-1)(x+2)^6}{6}$ |
| $\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 2$ | $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} \dfrac{(x+2)^7}{42}$ | $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -$ | $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -\,\dfrac{x(x+2)^7}{21}$ |
| $0$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\dfrac{(x+2)^8}{336}$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0,1} +$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0,1}  \dfrac{(x+2)^8}{168}$ |

We add up all the terms of the last column to get the answer for our integral. 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({x}^{2}-1)(x+2)^{5}\text{d}x & =\frac{({x}^{2}-1)(x+2)^{6}}{6}-\frac{x(x+2)^{7}}{21}+\frac{(x+2)^{8}}{168}+C \\  & =\frac{(x+2)^{6}}{168}(28({x}^{2}-1)-8x(x+2)+(x+2)^{2})+C \\  & =\frac{(x+2)^{6}}{168}(21{x}^{2}-12x-24)+C\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-1627a960-4b89-5682-9e7a-8ebccade355e" :question/id #uuid "1627a960-4b89-5682-9e7a-8ebccade355e" :question/math-academy-id "q-51229" :question/problem "Evaluate $\int ({x}^{3}+x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "For this integral we choose $u={x}^{3}+x$ and $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).$ Filling in the table gives the following:

| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same-color Products** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${x}^{3}+x$ | $\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)$ |  |  |
| $3{x}^{2}+1$ | $\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}$ | $+$ | $({x}^{3}+x)\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}$ |
| $6x$ | $-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{4}$ | $-$ | $(3{x}^{2}+1)\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{4}$ |
| $6$ | $-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{8}$ | $+$ | $-\frac{3x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{4}$ |
| $0$ | $\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{16}$ | $-$ | $-\frac{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{8}$ |

We add up all the terms of the last column to get the answer for our integral. 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({x}^{3}+x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =({x}^{3}+x)\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+(3{x}^{2}+1)\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{4}-\frac{3x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{4}-\frac{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{8}+C \\  & =(2{x}^{3}-x)\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{4}+(6{x}^{2}-1)\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{8}+C\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5647034f-2aaf-5579-99cc-ba72d358adba"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-13147" :question/problem "Evaluate $\int (2{x}^{4}+4x){e}^{3x}\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "For this integral, we choose $u=2{x}^{4}+4x$ and | **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same-color Products** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $2{x}^{4}+4x$ | ${e}^{3x}$ |  |  |
| $8{x}^{3}+4$ | $\frac{{e}^{3x}}{3}$ | $+$ | $\frac{(2{x}^{4}+4x){e}^{3x}}{3}$ |
| $24{x}^{2}$ | $\frac{{e}^{3x}}{9}$ | $-$ | $-\frac{(8{x}^{3}+4){e}^{3x}}{9}$ |
| $48x$ | $\frac{{e}^{3x}}{27}$ | $+$ | $\frac{8{x}^{2}{e}^{3x}}{9}$ |
| $48$ | $\frac{{e}^{3x}}{81}$ | $-$ | $-\frac{16x{e}^{3x}}{27}$ |
| $0$ | $\frac{{e}^{3x}}{243}$ | $+$ | $\frac{16{e}^{3x}}{81}$ |

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (2{x}^{4}+4x){e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{e}^{3x}}{81}(27(2{x}^{4}+4x)-9(8{x}^{3}+4)+9(8{x}^{2})-3(16x)+16)+C \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3x}}{81}(54{x}^{4}-72{x}^{3}+72{x}^{2}+60x-20)+C \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{3x}}{81}(27{x}^{4}-36{x}^{3}+36{x}^{2}+30x-10)+C\end{aligned}

"\frac{{e}^{3x}}{81}(27{x}^{4}-27{x}^{3}+36{x}^{2}+20x-20)+C" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097928 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to evaluate $\displaystyle \int x^3e^{x/2} \textrm{d}x.$ We can do it by applying integration by parts three times, but the calculation is pretty long. How can we speed it up?

Multiple applications of integration by parts become quick and easy if we use the **tabular method**.

Let's start by picking our $u$ and $\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}$ as normal:

$$
u = x^3\,,\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = e^{x/2}\,.
$$

We put this in a table, as shown below:

| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same Color Products** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3$ | $e^{x/2}$ |  |  |

To fill in the second row of the table, we differentiate the function in the first column and integrate the function in the second column. Doing this, we find

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(x^3\right) = 3x^2\,,\quad \int e^{x/2} \textrm{d}x = 2e^{x/2}\,.
$$

Filling in our table, we get the following:

| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same Color Products** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3$ | $e^{x/2}$ |  |  |
| $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 3x^2$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2e^{x/2}$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} +$ |  |

At this step, we begin filling the third column. It always starts with a "$+$" and then the signs alternate at each subsequent step.

We continue by differentiating the expression in the first column and integrating the expression in the second column until we get zero in the first column.

| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same Color Products** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color[rgb]{1,0,0}  x^3$ | $e^{x/2}$ |  |  |
| $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 3x^2$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2e^{x/2}$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} +$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0}$ |
| $\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 6x$ | $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}  4e^{x/2}$ | $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0.5,0}$ |
| $\color[rgb]{1,0,1} 6$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 8e^{x/2}$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0,1} +$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0,1}$ |
| $0$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,1}16e^{x/2}$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,1} -$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,1}$ |

Now we multiply the same-colored terms along with the same-colored sign. Specifically we multiply $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3$ with ${\color[rgb]{1,0,0} 2e^{x/2}},$ $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}3x^2$ with $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}4e^{x/2},$ and so on. We get

| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same Color Products** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color[rgb]{1,0,0}  x^3$ | $e^{x/2}$ |  |  |
| $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}3x^2$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2e^{x/2}$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} +$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} 2x^3e^{x/2}$ |
| $\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 6x$ | $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}  4e^{x/2}$ | $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -$ | $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}  -12x^2e^{x/2}$ |
| $\color[rgb]{1,0,1} 6$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 8e^{x/2}$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0,1} +$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 48xe^{x/2}$ |
| $0$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,1}16e^{x/2}$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,1} -$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,1} -96e^{x/2}$ |

Finally, we add up all the terms of the last column to get the answer for our integral. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{3}{e}^{x/2}\text{d}x & =2{x}^{3}{e}^{x/2}-12{x}^{2}{e}^{x/2}+48x{e}^{x/2}-96{e}^{x/2}+C \\  & ={e}^{x/2}(2{x}^{3}-12{x}^{2}+48x-96)+C.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096911 :activity/expected-seconds 840.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186278512 :question/problem "For a surface $S$ given by $x=k(y,z)$ for $(y,z)\in D,$ the flux of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

17592186119535 :question/problem "The figure below shows the graph of $f(x).$ Evaluate $\lim_\limits{x \to \,4} f(x).$

![](images/16/168433761f6629ad555a70acf5764f93246484c253f3c7ecba8fdfdfd87c2adf.png)" :question/worked-solution "We see from the graph that as $x$ approaches $4$ from the left, the function $f(x)$ approaches $-\infty.$ So, the left-hand limit is

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 4^-} f(x) = -\infty \, .
$$

Likewise, as $x$ approaches $4$ from the right, the function $f(x)$ again approaches $-\infty.$ So, the right-hand limit is

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 4^+} f(x) = -\infty \, .
$$

Consequently,

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 4} f(x)=-\infty \, .
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119869 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-50fa8042-1b8b-5648-8556-3cccc6bf538e" "question-e817a4fb-b6c9-5bc7-b2be-45b00395342a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119528 :question/problem "The figure below shows the graph of $f(x).$ What is $\lim_\limits{x \to \,-\,4} f(x)?$

![](images/ab/ab2abe13314c2005907dcd5d7077af8e87b7126474bbb0261f757d8ec7c00698.png)" :question/worked-solution "As $x$ approaches $-4$ from the right, the function value $f(x)$ grows to infinity, and therefore

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to -4^+} f(x)=\infty.
$$

However, the function $f(x)$ is not defined for $x<-4,$ and consequently we cannot approach $x=-4$ from the left. So we have

For example, consider the function $f(x)$ whose graph is shown below. This function has a vertical asymptote at $x=1,$ and the function value $f(x)$ grows without bound as $x$ approaches the asymptote $x=1.$ What is the limit $\lim_\limits{x\to 1} f(x)$? 

![](images/ab/ab9d57d3952fe0221616f9e64e1295fd0511703bdd5ed3a5fe91113cc7c8bf1b.png)

Remember that in order for computing any limit, in this case, $\lim_\limits{x\to 1} f(x),$ we have to compute the left and right-sided limits separately and ensure that they match up.

- **Left-sided limit:** As we approach $x=1$ (the vertical asymptote) from the left side of the graph, the function $f(x)$ increases without bound, approaching $\infty.$ We conclude that

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to 1^-} f(x) = \infty.
$$

- **Right-sided limit:** Likewise, as we approach the vertical asymptote $x=1$ from the right side of the graph, $f(x)$ still approaches $\infty.$ Consequently, 

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to 1^+ } f(x) = \infty.
$$

We see that both the left and right limits exist and are equal to $\infty\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to 1^-} f(x) = \lim_\limits{x\to 1^+} f(x) = \infty
$$

As a result, the overall limit is also equal to $\infty\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to 1} f(x) = \infty
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186120022 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092254 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-84522aa8-0251-51f3-8f96-c1848baee4b0"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-84522aa8-0251-51f3-8f96-c1848baee4b0" :question/id #uuid "84522aa8-0251-51f3-8f96-c1848baee4b0" :question/math-academy-id "q-67300" :question/problem "${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }10{(\frac{1}{2})}^{n}=$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the given series is a geometric series because it is in the form $\sum a{r}^{n}.$ 

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

The first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=10{(\frac{1}{2})}^{1}=5.
$$

 

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{10{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}}{10{(\frac{1}{2})}^{1}}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }10{(\frac{1}{2})}^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{5}{(1-\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =\frac{5}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =5\cdot \frac{2}{1} \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-da4c8753-aa62-5b12-846b-3fa944adeb01"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-b85d1cfe-34fb-5d55-ad84-699fc2c94f6d" :question/id #uuid "b85d1cfe-34fb-5d55-ad84-699fc2c94f6d" :question/math-academy-id "q-350640" :question/problem "Evaluate the geometric series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{5}{2}{(-0.4)}^{2n}.$ Do not round the answer.

${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{5}{2}{(-0.4)}^{2n}=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1.
$$

The first term is 

$$
{a}_{1}=\frac{5}{2}{(-0.4)}^{2(1)}=\frac{5}{2}{(-0.4)}^{2}
$$

 

and the second term is 

$$
{a}_{2}=\frac{5}{2}{(-0.4)}^{2(2)}=\frac{5}{2}{(-0.4)}^{4}.
$$

Therefore, the common ratio is 

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{\frac{5}{2}{(-0.4)}^{4}}{\frac{5}{2}{(-0.4)}^{2}}={(-0.4)}^{2}=0.16.
$$

 

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{5}{2}{(-0.4)}^{2n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{\frac{5}{2}{(-0.4)}^{2}}{1-0.16} \\  & =\frac{\frac{5}{2}(0.16)}{0.84} \\  & =\frac{0.4}{0.84} \\  & =\frac{10}{21}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-282a0a0f-efee-52cd-8a05-a07f215cbb39"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-282a0a0f-efee-52cd-8a05-a07f215cbb39" :answer-field/id #uuid "282a0a0f-efee-52cd-8a05-a07f215cbb39" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-7d0264cc-d7dc-5c37-b30f-16424540ced2" :answer-field/choices ["answer-7d0264cc-d7dc-5c37-b30f-16424540ced2"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7d0264cc-d7dc-5c37-b30f-16424540ced2" :answer/id #uuid "7d0264cc-d7dc-5c37-b30f-16424540ced2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{10}{21}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-4c0fb001-b215-5979-89f5-05a01ae52266" :question/id #uuid "4c0fb001-b215-5979-89f5-05a01ae52266" :question/math-academy-id "q-350641" :question/problem "Evaluate the geometric series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{9}{4}{(-\frac{1}{3})}^{2n}.$ Do not round the answer.

${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{9}{4}{(-\frac{1}{3})}^{2n}=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1.
$$

The first term is 

$$
{a}_{1}=\frac{9}{4}{(-\frac{1}{3})}^{2(1)}=\frac{9}{4}{(-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}
$$

 

and the second term is 

$$
{a}_{2}=\frac{9}{4}{(-\frac{1}{3})}^{2(2)}=\frac{9}{4}{(-\frac{1}{3})}^{4}.
$$

Therefore, the common ratio is 

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{\frac{9}{4}{(-\frac{1}{3})}^{4}}{\frac{9}{4}{(-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}}={(-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}=\frac{1}{9}.
$$

 

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{9}{4}{(-\frac{1}{3})}^{2n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{\frac{9}{4}(\frac{1}{9})}{(1-\frac{1}{9})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{4})}{(\frac{8}{9})} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{9}{8} \\  & =\frac{9}{32}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b1a4447f-3bfa-5239-8811-1f6dff980305"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}2y\operatorname{cos}⁡x, & \,0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the expected value of $Y.$" :question/worked-solution "The marginal density function for $Y$ when $0\le y\le 1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2y[\operatorname{sin}⁡x]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =2y(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =2y(1-0) \\  & =2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for ${f}_{X}(x)$ is given by

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}2y, & 0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the  expected value of $Y$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot 2y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{2}{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-76f810c9-6c36-550e-ba2c-f211b1f812da"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Find its average position of the fly between $0$ and $2$ minutes." :question/worked-solution "To calculate the average value of the position on $[{t}_{1},{t}_{2}],$ we use the average value formula

$$
{x}_{\text{avg}}=\frac{1}{{t}_{2}-{t}_{1}}\,{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{2-0}\,{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{t}{2}-\frac{\pi }{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{8}t))\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{8}t))|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((\frac{{2}^{2}}{4}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{8}\cdot 2))-(\frac{{0}^{2}}{4}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{8}\cdot 0))) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((1+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})-(0+1)) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the average position is $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\,\text{m}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1f66651c-8f9c-52e6-9972-14e6f7d0c2a3"] $$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{6-2}\,{\int }_{2}^{6}(\frac{{2}^{t}}{12})\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 12\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡2}({2}^{t}){|}_{2}^{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{48\operatorname{ln}⁡2}({2}^{6}-{2}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{60}{48\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =\frac{5}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/id #uuid "f05a5b67-91d9-5027-a739-e465c398f589" :question/math-academy-id "q-353941" :question/problem "A robotic sled moves along a straight track with velocity 
$v(t)={t}^{3}-t,$ where $t$ is measured in seconds and $v$ is measured in meters per second.

Find the average acceleration ${a}_{\text{avg}}$ over the time interval $t\in [1,3].$ Do not round your answer.

${a}_{\text{avg}}=$ 
{{field-1}}
${\text{m/s}}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "The average acceleration is the average rate of change of the velocity, so

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{v(b)-v(a)}{b-a} \\  & =\frac{v(3)-v(1)}{3-1} \\  & =\frac{[(3)^{3}-(3)]-[(1)^{3}-(1)]}{2} \\  & =\frac{(27-3)-(1-1)}{2} \\  & =\frac{24-0}{2} \\  & =\frac{24}{2} \\  & =12\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the average acceleration is $12\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4686715d-a18c-51be-a9b1-884139acad2f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-4686715d-a18c-51be-a9b1-884139acad2f" :answer-field/id #uuid "4686715d-a18c-51be-a9b1-884139acad2f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-37a3d483-228d-5bd2-9d7d-ce2ef8b4ae21" :answer-field/choices ["answer-37a3d483-228d-5bd2-9d7d-ce2ef8b4ae21"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-37a3d483-228d-5bd2-9d7d-ce2ef8b4ae21" :answer/id #uuid "37a3d483-228d-5bd2-9d7d-ce2ef8b4ae21" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "12" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-a7420375-7675-57fc-8640-9f218c433ea5" :question/id #uuid "a7420375-7675-57fc-8640-9f218c433ea5" :question/math-academy-id "q-353947" :question/problem "A test cart moves in a straight line with velocity

"question-c68b418a-a9c2-512b-93fe-1e0b537572e9" :question/id #uuid "c68b418a-a9c2-512b-93fe-1e0b537572e9" :question/math-academy-id "q-340768" :question/problem "$$

$$

Let $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ be $2\pi $-periodic extensions of some functions from $x\in [-\pi ,\pi )$ to $x\in R$ with the Fourier series shown above. What is the $6\text{th}$ Fourier sine coefficient of $-3f(x)-2g(x)?$" :question/worked-solution "Let $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ be $2\pi $-periodic functions with Fourier series

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)), \\ g(x) & ∼\frac{{c}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({c}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{d}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)).\end{aligned}
$$

Then for any constants $\alpha $ and $\beta $,

$$
\alpha f(x)+\beta g(x)∼\frac{\alpha {a}_{0}+\beta {c}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }((\alpha {a}_{n}+\beta {c}_{n})\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+(\alpha {b}_{n}+\beta {d}_{n})\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)).
$$

Using the linearity property of Fourier series, the corresponding Fourier coefficients of $-3f(x)-2g(x)$ are

- $-3{a}_{0}-2{c}_{0}$ for the constant coefficient,

- $-3{a}_{n}-2{c}_{n},$ $n\ge 1$ for the cosine coefficients, and

- $-3{b}_{n}-2{d}_{n},$ $n\ge 1$ for the sine coefficients.

Therefore, the $6$th sine coefficient of $-3f(x)-2g(x)$ is

$$
-3{b}_{6}-2{d}_{6}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b50ec26a-cc99-5796-8813-5d5595ca224f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b50ec26a-cc99-5796-8813-5d5595ca224f" :answer-field/id #uuid "b50ec26a-cc99-5796-8813-5d5595ca224f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-8a1fe503-e29c-50c9-8135-cba5a2e7f1c7" :answer-field/choices ["answer-369e06e2-73c3-5dd4-a343-09337ede43bc" "answer-539fdd72-d074-5ca4-bc19-a05dcd278d54" "answer-af9e08fd-f24c-56c3-9400-df7628dd678d" "answer-d8ef8838-eb42-5147-9f27-de7711e9fd4b" "answer-8a1fe503-e29c-50c9-8135-cba5a2e7f1c7"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-369e06e2-73c3-5dd4-a343-09337ede43bc" :answer/id #uuid "369e06e2-73c3-5dd4-a343-09337ede43bc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3{a}_{0}-2{c}_{0}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-539fdd72-d074-5ca4-bc19-a05dcd278d54" :answer/id #uuid "539fdd72-d074-5ca4-bc19-a05dcd278d54" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3{a}_{6}-2{c}_{6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-af9e08fd-f24c-56c3-9400-df7628dd678d" :answer/id #uuid "af9e08fd-f24c-56c3-9400-df7628dd678d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3{b}_{0}-2{d}_{0}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d8ef8838-eb42-5147-9f27-de7711e9fd4b" :answer/id #uuid "d8ef8838-eb42-5147-9f27-de7711e9fd4b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3{b}_{6}-2{c}_{6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8a1fe503-e29c-50c9-8135-cba5a2e7f1c7" :answer/id #uuid "8a1fe503-e29c-50c9-8135-cba5a2e7f1c7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3{b}_{6}-2{d}_{6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-2c275290-69db-55d0-83e9-26518022c1c5" :question/id #uuid "2c275290-69db-55d0-83e9-26518022c1c5" :question/math-academy-id "q-340760" :question/problem "$$

in the corresponding Fourier series of $f(x)$ must be zero." :question/worked-solution "To determine whether $f$ is even or odd, we compare $f(-x)$ and $f(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)^{3} \\  & =-{x}^{3} \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(-x)=-f(x),$ we have that $f$ is odd.

For Fourier series on $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ the cosine coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x,
$$

and the constant coefficient is

$$
{a}_{0}=\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Here, $f(x)$ is odd and $\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)$ is even, so $f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)$ is odd. Also, $f(x)$ itself is odd.

Now, the integral of an odd function over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$ is $0.$ Thus, ${a}_{n}=0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and ${a}_{0}=0.$

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ is $\text{odd}$ and the $\text{cosine terms}$ in its Fourier series must be zero." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields $$
{P}^{′}=kP(a-P),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>P$ is the carrying capacity.

For a logistic growth model, the fastest rate of growth occurs when $P=\frac{1}{2}a.$

![](images/90/9019b26b417c757bbfab79afb39379c1fc7a892bc44e934c6f23c339deacfd68.png)

From our equation, we see that $a=5000.$ Hence, the carrying capacity is $5000,$ and $P$ grows at its fastest possible rate when 

$$
P=\frac{1}{2}a=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 5000=2500.
$$"] ["question-fbdb7241-60ea-5f22-afcd-5e46de779c9a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-dbb704d4-511c-5244-871d-d498a47768aa" :answer-field/id #uuid "dbb704d4-511c-5244-871d-d498a47768aa"] ["answer-e33b7888-14e2-559e-bca1-077f0916190c" :answer/id #uuid "e33b7888-14e2-559e-bca1-077f0916190c"] ["answer-e33b7888-14e2-559e-bca1-077f0916190c" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-e33b7888-14e2-559e-bca1-077f0916190c" :answer/value "2500"] ["answer-field-dbb704d4-511c-5244-871d-d498a47768aa" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-dbb704d4-511c-5244-871d-d498a47768aa" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-dbb704d4-511c-5244-871d-d498a47768aa" :answer-field/correct "answer-e33b7888-14e2-559e-bca1-077f0916190c"] ["answer-field-dbb704d4-511c-5244-871d-d498a47768aa" :answer-field/choices "answer-e33b7888-14e2-559e-bca1-077f0916190c"] ["question-fbdb7241-60ea-5f22-afcd-5e46de779c9a" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-dbb704d4-511c-5244-871d-d498a47768aa"] [17592186175957 :knowledge-point/questions "question-fbdb7241-60ea-5f22-afcd-5e46de779c9a"] ["question-8023cebc-048b-5288-9c32-1da095db126f" :question/id #uuid "8023cebc-048b-5288-9c32-1da095db126f"] ["question-8023cebc-048b-5288-9c32-1da095db126f" :question/math-academy-id "q-103827"] ["question-8023cebc-048b-5288-9c32-1da095db126f" :question/problem "Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=\theta +{e}^{\theta }$ for $-\pi \le \theta \le \pi ?$"] ["question-8023cebc-048b-5288-9c32-1da095db126f" :question/worked-solution "The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\theta +{e}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=1+{e}^{\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\sqrt{(\theta +{e}^{\theta })^{2}+(1+{e}^{\theta })^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\sqrt{{\theta }^{2}+2\theta {e}^{\theta }+{e}^{2\theta }+1+2{e}^{\theta }+{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\sqrt{{\theta }^{2}+2{e}^{\theta }(\theta +1)+2{e}^{2\theta }+1}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-8023cebc-048b-5288-9c32-1da095db126f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-17a97da4-f06a-512c-b0f2-d273f0e4876b" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "In a factory, the average amount of sugar in a cookie is $15$ grams. However, $10%$ of cookies contain no more than $14$ grams of sugar. Assuming that the amount of sugar in each cookie is normally distributed, find the standard deviation of the amount of sugar in a cookie, rounded to $2$ decimal places.

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $p$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.10\,$ | $\,0.15\,$ | $\,0.20\,$ | $\,0.25\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,-2.3263\,$ | $\,-1.8808\,$ | $\,-1.6449\,$ | $\,-1.2816\,$ | $\,-1.0364\,$ | $\,-0.8416\,$ | $\,-0.6745\,$ |"] ["question-b642f61b-90d3-52e8-a698-ed0e6fdd52ac" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the amount (in grams) of sugar in a cookie. Then we have $X∼N(15,{\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find the standard deviation $\sigma .$ 

We know that $P(X\le 14)=0.10.$ Converting $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 14) & =0.10 \\ P(Z\le \frac{14-15}{\sigma }) & =0.10 \\ Φ(-\frac{1}{\sigma }) & =0.10 \\ -\frac{1}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.10).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.10)=-1.2816.
$$

Finally then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sigma } & =-1.2816 \\ \frac{1}{\sigma } & =1.2816 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{1}{1.2816} \\  & ≈0.78.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-b642f61b-90d3-52e8-a698-ed0e6fdd52ac" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-c889ce98-c36c-5100-9ccc-2833887780d6" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-1938b4fe-a4da-5df4-945e-a4ba43cb2798" :question/worked-solution "To solve the equation $\sqrt{-3x-8}=x+2,$ we raise both sides to the power of $2.$  This allows us to get rid of the radical, and gives us a quadratic equation that is easier to solve:

$$

$$

$$

- Second, we check whether the obtained value $x=5$ is a solution of the original equation:

$$

["question-698b79dc-de1f-5472-8b54-18da46bc32a4" :question/problem "The function 
$f(x,y)$
has the first derivative

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}x{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2} & y{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2}\end{aligned}]
$$

and has a stationary point at $(0,0).$ If $H$ denotes the Hessian determinant of $f,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. $H(0,0)<0$

II. $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(0,0)>0$

III. The point $(0,0)$ is a local minimum of $f$"] ["question-698b79dc-de1f-5472-8b54-18da46bc32a4" :question/worked-solution "The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}x{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2} & y{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2}\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=x\text{ }\,{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=y\text{ }\,{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2}.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\text{ }\,{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2})=(1+{x}^{2}){e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\text{ }\,{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2})=(1+{y}^{2}){e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\text{ }\,{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2})=xy\text{ }\,{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}(1+{x}^{2}){e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2} & xy\text{ }\,{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2} \\ xy\text{ }\,{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2} & (1+{y}^{2}){e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,0)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(0,0),$ we get

$$
H(0,0)=det({f}^{″}(0,0))={1}^{2}-{0}^{2}=1>0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(0,0)=({f}^{″}(0,0))_{11}=1>0.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $H(0,0)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(0,0)>0,$ the point $(0,0)$ is a local minimum by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""] ["question-698b79dc-de1f-5472-8b54-18da46bc32a4" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] function $y=2f(x)$ represents a stretch of the function $y=f(x)$ by a factor of $2$ parallel to the $y$-axis. This has the effect of multiplying the $y$-coordinates of all points on $y=f(x)$ by $2.$

The point $Q(10,q)$ on $f(x)$ is mapped to the point $P(10,8)$ on $y=2f(x).$ Since we know that the $y$-coordinate of $P$ is $2$ times the $y$-coordinate of $Q,$ we can form the following equation:

$$
2q=8
$$

Solving this equation, we get $q=4.$ Therefore, the coordinates of $Q$ are $(10,4).$"] ["question-370ca68a-a4c7-585b-aa83-7cfb70ebc27e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] :question/worked-solution "First, we let

$$
I=\int \frac{{ln}^{8}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{8}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{8{ln}^{7}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{x}\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{8}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{8}⁡x(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)(\frac{8{ln}^{7}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{9}⁡x-8\int \frac{{ln}^{8}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{9}⁡x-8I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $I,$ remembering to add a constant of integration $C$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={ln}^{9}⁡x-8I \\ 9I & ={ln}^{9}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{9}⁡x}{9}+C\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-d34958ec-5dd9-5a10-8bd6-7504a0d293c1" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-4338b54c-776e-5c97-9d8a-821ddad0e1e9" :answer-field/id #uuid
