{{field-1}}"] ["question-1d4ef9d9-890a-5da6-8625-b613890df574" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int \frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{6x}\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{4}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{4{ln}^{3}⁡x}{x}, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{6x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{6x}\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{6x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{4}⁡x)(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{6})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{6})(\frac{4{ln}^{3}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{6}-4\int \frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{6x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{6}-4I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $I.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{6}-4I \\ 5I & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{6} \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{30}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}\frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{6x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{30}({ln}^{5}⁡x)\,{|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{30}({ln}^{5}⁡({e}^{3})-{ln}^{5}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{30}((3\operatorname{ln}⁡e)^{5}-{0}^{5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{30}({3}^{5}-0) \\  & =\frac{81}{10}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-1d4ef9d9-890a-5da6-8625-b613890df574" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-1146e643-4cd0-54ef-a3e2-eff97703cea4" :answer-field/id #uuid "1146e643-4cd0-54ef-a3e2-eff97703cea4"] ["answer-c033b7b5-f0bb-5912-ac93-d7393c96dac2" :answer/id #uuid "c033b7b5-f0bb-5912-ac93-d7393c96dac2"] ["answer-c033b7b5-f0bb-5912-ac93-d7393c96dac2" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-c033b7b5-f0bb-5912-ac93-d7393c96dac2" :answer/value "\frac{81}{10}"] ["answer-field-1146e643-4cd0-54ef-a3e2-eff97703cea4" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-1146e643-4cd0-54ef-a3e2-eff97703cea4" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-1146e643-4cd0-54ef-a3e2-eff97703cea4" :answer-field/correct "answer-c033b7b5-f0bb-5912-ac93-d7393c96dac2"] ["answer-field-1146e643-4cd0-54ef-a3e2-eff97703cea4" :answer-field/choices "answer-c033b7b5-f0bb-5912-ac93-d7393c96dac2"] ["question-1d4ef9d9-890a-5da6-8625-b613890df574" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-1146e643-4cd0-54ef-a3e2-eff97703cea4"] [17592186068734 :knowledge-point/questions "question-1d4ef9d9-890a-5da6-8625-b613890df574"] ["question-1d5e523f-cb45-5cb6-96e4-37ea7521523c" :question/id #uuid "1d5e523f-cb45-5cb6-96e4-37ea7521523c"] ["question-1d5e523f-cb45-5cb6-96e4-37ea7521523c" :question/math-academy-id "q-348848"] ["question-1d5e523f-cb45-5cb6-96e4-37ea7521523c" :question/problem "Evaluate ${\int }_{1}^{{e}^{5}}\frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{3x}\,\text{d}x$ using integration by parts. To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{4}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{4{ln}^{3}⁡x}{x}, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{3x}\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3}.\end{aligned}

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{4}⁡x)(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3})(\frac{4{ln}^{3}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{3}-4\int \frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{3}-4I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $I.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{3}-4I \\ 5I & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{3} \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{15}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{5}}\frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{3x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{15}({ln}^{5}⁡x)\,{|}_{1}^{{e}^{5}} \\  & =\frac{1}{15}({ln}^{5}⁡({e}^{5})-{ln}^{5}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{15}((5\operatorname{ln}⁡e)^{5}-{0}^{5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{15}({5}^{5}-0) \\  & =\frac{625}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-1d5e523f-cb45-5cb6-96e4-37ea7521523c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-c3a039a4-2ad9-58c4-9de9-69c93ba57a90" :answer-field/id #uuid "c3a039a4-2ad9-58c4-9de9-69c93ba57a90"] ["answer-ff5d37fa-afb4-58b9-ac62-05838ab2df59" :answer/id #uuid "ff5d37fa-afb4-58b9-ac62-05838ab2df59"] ["answer-ff5d37fa-afb4-58b9-ac62-05838ab2df59" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-ff5d37fa-afb4-58b9-ac62-05838ab2df59" :answer/value "\frac{625}{3}"] ["answer-field-c3a039a4-2ad9-58c4-9de9-69c93ba57a90" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-c3a039a4-2ad9-58c4-9de9-69c93ba57a90" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-c3a039a4-2ad9-58c4-9de9-69c93ba57a90" :answer-field/correct "answer-ff5d37fa-afb4-58b9-ac62-05838ab2df59"] ["answer-field-c3a039a4-2ad9-58c4-9de9-69c93ba57a90" :answer-field/choices "answer-ff5d37fa-afb4-58b9-ac62-05838ab2df59"] ["question-1d5e523f-cb45-5cb6-96e4-37ea7521523c" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-c3a039a4-2ad9-58c4-9de9-69c93ba57a90"] [17592186068734 :knowledge-point/questions "question-1d5e523f-cb45-5cb6-96e4-37ea7521523c"] [17592186069401 :question/problem "Evaluate ${\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡z}{z}\,\text{d}z$ using integration by parts."] [17592186069401 :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int \frac{{ln}^{3}⁡z}{z}\,\text{d}z.$

\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)({e}^{x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)({e}^{x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-J \\ I & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-(-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+I) \\ I & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-I \\ 2I & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}+C\end{aligned}

{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2})(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2})(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}J \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}I) \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{4}-\frac{1}{4}I \\ \frac{5}{4}I & =\frac{2{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{4} \\ I & =\frac{1}{5}{e}^{-x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{1}{5}{e}^{-x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(\frac{1}{5}{e}^{-\pi /2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})))-(\frac{1}{5}{e}^{-0}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(0))-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(0)))) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi /2}}{5}+\frac{1}{5} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi /2}+1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-509669b5-ef46-5eb1-8d54-7bbaca5f8fc9" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-2392f4ba-bd38-5a07-8e70-90353132c90f" :answer-field/id #uuid To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2J \\ I & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2(-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2I) \\ I & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-4I \\ 5I & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x)){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(\frac{{e}^{-2\pi /2}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})))-(\frac{{e}^{-2(0)}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡0-2\operatorname{cos}⁡0)) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi }}{5}+\frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}({e}^{-\pi }+2)\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-0b786a85-3015-50d7-b6da-f38d91ed719a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-2abcc4ca-4f5a-5ee4-b3d4-9f4549d9ca5d" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+J \\ I & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-I) \\ I & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-I \\ 2I & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{{e}^{-x}}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)){|}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =(\frac{{e}^{-\pi }}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ))-(\frac{{e}^{\pi }}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi ))) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi }}{2}-\frac{{e}^{\pi }}{2} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi }-{e}^{\pi }}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-ce3e4235-61fa-5c48-8fde-1e9523a76255" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-feba3f58-6495-56d8-aeb6-29990aa6bdd2" :answer-field/id #uuid "answer-field-feba3f58-6495-56d8-aeb6-29990aa6bdd2"] [17592186068801 :knowledge-point/questions "question-ce3e4235-61fa-5c48-8fde-1e9523a76255"] [17592186070032 :tutorial/content "In some cases, applying integration by parts can lead to a cyclic pattern, where the original integral reappears after a few steps. This cyclic behavior allows us to solve the integral by forming an equation that can be solved algebraically.

To illustrate, let's consider the following example:

$$
I = \int \dfrac{\ln x}{x} \textrm{d}x
$$

Let's try using the method of integration by parts. We suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{x}\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)(\frac{1}{x})\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{2}⁡x-\int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{2}⁡x-I\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We now have the same integral $I$ on both sides of the equality. Thinking about $I$ as some unknown variable, we can easily solve this equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={ln}^{2}⁡x-I \\ I+I & ={ln}^{2}⁡x \\ 2I & ={ln}^{2}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{2}+C\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we added a constant of integration right at the very end of the calculation."] [17592186069630 :step/math-academy-id 640946] [17592186069631 :step/math-academy-id 640947] [17592186069632 :step/math-academy-id 640950] [17592186069725 :step/math-academy-id 640953] [17592186068957 :activity/expected-seconds 1500.0] ["question-e707f526-b15a-5f98-b415-f7cf137b340a" :question/id #uuid "e707f526-b15a-5f98-b415-f7cf137b340a"] ["question-e707f526-b15a-5f98-b415-f7cf137b340a" :question/math-academy-id "q-146207"] ["question-e707f526-b15a-5f98-b415-f7cf137b340a" :question/problem "| $y$ | $2$ | $4$ |

["question-b82a91db-40b3-51bf-b539-d94cf7913732" :question/math-academy-id "q-146284"] ["question-b82a91db-40b3-51bf-b539-d94cf7913732" :question/problem "| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ |

| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ |

Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Find $\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=4]$ given that the random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above and the corresponding conditional expected value is ${\mu }_{X|4}=\frac{3}{2}.$"] ["question-b82a91db-40b3-51bf-b539-d94cf7913732" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[(X-{\mu }_{X|y})^{2}\,|\,Y=y] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ let's first find the marginal distribution of $Y,$ corresponding to the column totals: 

| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ |
| $X=2$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{12}$ |
| $X=3$ | $\frac{1}{12}$ | $\frac{1}{12}$ |
| ${f}_{Y}(y)$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |

The conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y$ is

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

Therefore, dividing each joint probability by the corresponding column total, we obtain the conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y:$

| ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{2}{3}$ |
| $X=2$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ |
| $X=3$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ |
|  | $1$ | $1$ |

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=4] & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,4)]-{\mu }_{X|4}^{2} \\  & =[{1}^{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}+{2}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{6}+{3}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{6}]-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{3}{2}-\frac{9}{4} \\  & =\frac{7}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-b82a91db-40b3-51bf-b539-d94cf7913732" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-caa5996b-3602-50fb-816f-2fafeaae3fc0" :answer-field/id #uuid to have a common base.

To do this, we write $27$ as ${3}^{3},$ and then rewrite the left-hand side using the power rule of exponents:

$$
\begin{aligned}{27}^{x+2} & ={3}^{4x} \\ {({3}^{3})}^{x+2} & ={3}^{4x} \\ {3}^{3(x+2)} & ={3}^{4x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since both sides of the equation share the same base $(3)$, we equate the exponents and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3(x+2) & =4x \\ 3x+6 & =4x \\ x & =6\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-6adee969-6d90-563b-a4ef-2a55fc2a8432" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-d7feacf0-2600-5627-831e-b74ae6dc5e57" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-49bb96bd-7826-5c22-b9da-330c6f2a3a6b" :question/worked-solution "To solve this equation, we need both exponential terms to have a common base. To do this, we rewrite the equation using $9={3}^{2}$ and $27={3}^{3},$ as follows:

$$
{({3}^{2})}^{y}={({3}^{3})}^{y-3}
$$

Then, we apply the power rule of exponents. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{2y}={3}^{3(y-3)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since both sides of the equation share the same base $(3)$, we equate the exponents and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2y & =3(y-3) \\ 2y & =3y-9 \\ y & =9\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-49bb96bd-7826-5c22-b9da-330c6f2a3a6b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-b6e10a49-5bb8-53f2-b412-c67176d7bbe6" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-6679348c-4b94-5c71-ad1e-c5e2e39219c8" :question/math-academy-id "q-23909"] ["question-6679348c-4b94-5c71-ad1e-c5e2e39219c8" :question/problem "Consider the equation ${x}^{2}+1=k.$ For which values of $k$ does this equation have no real solutions?"] ["question-6679348c-4b94-5c71-ad1e-c5e2e39219c8" :question/worked-solution "Let's try and solve using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+1 & =k \\ {x}^{2} & =k-1 \\ \sqrt{{x}^{2}} & =\sqrt{k-1} \\ |x| & =\sqrt{k-1}\end{aligned}
$$

The equation will have no real solutions if the expression under the square root is negative, which gives the following condition:

$$
k-1<0
$$

We solve this inequality for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}k-1 & <0 \\ k & <1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, any value of $k$ that is less than $1$ will give an equation with no real solutions."] ["question-6679348c-4b94-5c71-ad1e-c5e2e39219c8" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] $$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-h & =2 \\ {x}^{2} & =2+h \\ \sqrt{{x}^{2}} & =\sqrt{2+h} \\ |x| & =\sqrt{2+h}\end{aligned}
$$

The equation has only one solution if the right-hand side is equal to zero, and the right-hand side is zero only if the expression underneath the radical is zero. So, we solve for the value of $h$ that makes the expression under the radical equal to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}2+h & =0 \\ h & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{3}^{n+1}{(x+\frac{1}{4})}^{n+1}}{n+3}\cdot \frac{n+2}{{3}^{n}{(x+\frac{1}{4})}^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{3(n+2)}{n+3}(x+\frac{1}{4})| \\  & =|x+\frac{1}{4}|{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{3(n+2)}{n+3} \\  & =|x+\frac{1}{4}|\cdot 3 \\  & =3|x+\frac{1}{4}|\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem "Given that the power series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}(x-1)^{n}$ converges at  $x=-3,$ which of the following **must** be true?

I. The series converges at $x=5$

II. The series diverges at $x=-4$

III. The series converges at $x=-2$"] ["question-654aa15f-b5e0-5714-95bd-cdd476eb0257" :question/worked-solution "The center of the expansion is $x=1,$ and since the series is convergent for $x=-3,$ this means that the radius of convergence $R$ is *at least* $4,$ i.e., $R\ge 4.$ So, the series is convergent for every point in the interval $[-3,5).$ However, we know nothing about the convergence of the series at any point outside the interval $[-3,5).$

![](images/1f/1f6d98b7983946bf60df9bb29bc527af17a63a38834457404c5284b19165e7d5.png)

 

With this in mind, let's check each of our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $5\notin [-3,5),$ we cannot guarantee that the series is convergent at $x=5.$

- Statement II is false. Since $-4\notin [-3,5),$ we cannot guarantee that the series is divergent at $x=-4.$

- Statement III is true. Since $-2\in [-3,5),$ the series is convergent at $x=-2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only.""] ["question-654aa15f-b5e0-5714-95bd-cdd476eb0257" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-ed2165e7-e994-5fc0-830d-7875786845b0" II. As $x\to {3}^{-},\,$ $f(x)\to \infty $

III. As $x\to {3}^{+},\,$ $f(x)\to -\infty $"] ["question-b21470c3-1ee9-52ab-ab28-1768b780f6d2" :question/worked-solution "The notation $x\to -{2}^{-}$ means that $x$ approaches $-2$ *from the left*. In the same way, the notation $x\to {3}^{-}$ means that $x$ approaches $3$ *from the left* while $x\to {3}^{+}$ means that $x$ approaches $3$ *from the right*. 

![](images/37/37af0eeb28d271efa4bd8f296b8c530b82a7f368f82fa96e025695317b81519d.png)

From the given graph, we see that:

- As $x$ approaches $-2$ from the left, the values of $f(x)$ do not approach $\infty .$ So, statement I is false.

- As $x$ approaches $3$ from the left, the values of $f(x)$ increase, approaching $\infty .$ So, statement II is true.

- As $x$ approaches $3$ from the right, the values of $f(x)$ do not approach $-\infty .$ So, statement III is false.

Consider the graph of $y=f(x)$ shown above. What are the equations of its vertical asymptotes?"] ["question-b6d62580-c7ef-590e-96ab-faddfa2655e8" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $x=a$ is called a vertical asymptote of $y=f(x)$ if $f(x)\to \infty $ or $f(x)\to -\infty $ as $x\to {a}^{+}$ or $x\to {a}^{-}.$

![](images/e6/e6d80874f9150371204f12b2e933085f9b2666ac77fce5430f9645e5af073a36.png)

From the given graph, we see that as $x$ approaches $-2$ from the left, the values of $f(x)$ decrease, approaching $-\infty .$ Also, notice that as $x$ approaches $-2$ from the right, the values of $f(x)$ decrease, approaching $-\infty .$

We also see that as $x$ approaches $0$ from the left, the values of $f(x)$ decrease, approaching $-\infty .$ And, as $x$ approaches $0$ from the right, the values of $f(x)$ decrease, approaching $-\infty .$

So, we can write: 

- $f(x)\to -\infty $ as $x\to -{2}^{-}$

- $f(x)\to -\infty $ as $x\to -{2}^{+}$

- $f(x)\to -\infty $ as $x\to {0}^{-}$

- $f(x)\to -\infty $ as $x\to {0}^{+}$

These give us the asymptotes $x=-2$ and $x=0.$"] ["question-b6d62580-c7ef-590e-96ab-faddfa2655e8" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-b475a21f-3809-5b3b-b4c4-760fa5caf3a4" When this happens, we say that the function approaches "infinity", or that it has an **infinite limit** at $x=1.$ We can write this mathematically, as follows:

$$
f(x) \rightarrow \infty\quad \text{as}\quad x \rightarrow 1
$$

In words, this reads "the function $f(x)$ approaches infinity as $x$ approaches $1$".

Now, consider the function $y = g(x),$ shown below. This is an example of a function that *decreases* without bound.

The function $g(x)$ approaches negative infinity as $x$ approaches $1.$ So, we can write

$$
g(x) \rightarrow -\infty\quad  \text{as } \quad x \rightarrow 1.
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm{E}[X^2] - \textrm{E}[X]^2,
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X] \cdot \textrm{E}[Y].
$$

First, we find $\textrm{Var}[X].$
We compute $\textrm{E}[X^2]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}(x+\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{3}+\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{4}y+\frac{1}{6}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{6} \\  & =\frac{5}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{12}-{(\frac{7}{12})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{11}{144}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\textrm{E}[Y^2]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}(x+\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(x{y}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}{y}^{4})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x{y}^{4}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}{y}^{4})\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{6}{y}^{3}+\frac{3}{10}{y}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}+\frac{3}{10} \\  & =\frac{7}{15}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{15}-{(\frac{5}{8})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{73}{960}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's find $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y].$ Using the given results, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{17}{48}-(\frac{7}{12})\cdot (\frac{5}{8}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{96}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=2.2$ and $\text{E}[Y]=1.4,$ find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y.$"] ["question-498cfd6b-9969-58ee-9468-55dacd0e9142" :question/worked-solution "For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $Σ$ is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=2$ | $0.55$ | $0.25$ | $0.8$ |
| $X=3$ | $0.05$ | $0.15$ | $0.2$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.6$ | $0.4$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a support ${S}_{X},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={2}^{2}\cdot 0.8+{3}^{2}\cdot 0.2 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =5-{2.2}^{2} \\  & =0.16.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a support ${S}_{Y},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 0.6+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.4 \\  & =2.2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =2.2-{1.4}^{2} \\  & =0.24.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\text{E}[XY]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =(2)(1)f(2,1)+(3)(1)f(3,1)+(2)(2)f(2,2)+(3)(2)f(3,2) \\  & =2\cdot 0.55+3\cdot 0.05+4\cdot 0.25+6\cdot 0.15 \\  & =3.15.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =3.15-2.2\cdot 1.4 \\  & =0.07.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.16 & 0.07 \\ 0.07 & 0.24\end{aligned}].
$$"] ["question-498cfd6b-9969-58ee-9468-55dacd0e9142" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-c7d1b7f0-9375-5f6f-bc52-a79347709299" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}].

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| $X=2$ | $0.3$ | $0.4$ | $0.7$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.4$ | $0.6$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a support ${S}_{X},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 0.3+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.7 \\  & =3.1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =3.1-{1.7}^{2} \\  & =0.21.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a support ${S}_{Y},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.4+{1}^{2}\cdot 0.6 \\  & =0.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =0.6-{0.6}^{2} \\  & =0.24.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\text{E}[XY]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =(1)(0)f(1,0)+(2)(0)f(2,0)+(1)(1)f(1,1)+(2)(1)f(2,1) \\  & =0\cdot 0.1+0\cdot 0.3+1\cdot 0.2+2\cdot 0.4 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=2$ | $0.15$ | $0.1$ | $0.25$ |
| $X=6$ | $0.5$ | $0.25$ | $0.75$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.65$ | $0.35$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a support ${S}_{X},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={2}^{2}\cdot 0.25+{6}^{2}\cdot 0.75 \\  & =28.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =28-{5}^{2} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a support ${S}_{Y},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={2}^{2}\cdot 0.65+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.35 \\  & =8.2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =8.2-{2.7}^{2} \\  & =0.91.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\text{E}[XY]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =(2)(2)f(2,2)+(6)(2)f(6,2)+(2)(4)f(2,4)+(6)(4)f(6,4) \\  & =4\cdot 0.15+12\cdot 0.5+8\cdot 0.1+24\cdot 0.25 \\  & =13.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =13.4-5\cdot 2.7 \\  & =-0.1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & -0.1 \\ -0.1 & 0.91\end{aligned}].

$$

$$

$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =1.3-1.6\cdot 0.8 \\  & =0.02.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.24 & 0.02 \\ 0.02 & 0.16\end{aligned}].

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, we find $\text{Var}[X].$ Using the given results, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}-{(\frac{4}{5})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{75}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}48{y}^{3}(x-y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}(x{y}^{3}-{y}^{4})\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}x{y}^{4}-\frac{1}{5}{y}^{5}]}_{y=0}^{y=x/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{64}{x}^{5}-\frac{1}{160}{x}^{5})\text{d}x \\  & =48\cdot \frac{3}{320}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{5}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{9}{20}{[\frac{1}{6}{x}^{6}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{40}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{40}-{(\frac{1}{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{80}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\text{E}[XY]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}xy\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}48x{y}^{2}(x-y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}-x{y}^{3})\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{4}x{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=x/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{24}{x}^{5}-\frac{1}{64}{x}^{5})\text{d}x \\  & =48\cdot \frac{5}{192}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{5}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{[\frac{1}{6}{x}^{6}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{5}{24}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{5}{24}-(\frac{4}{5})\cdot (\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{120}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{75} & \frac{1}{120} \\ \frac{1}{120} & \frac{1}{80}\end{aligned}].

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}.
$$

We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{4}\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}]}_{-1}^{1}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{-1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}-{(0)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{y}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{4}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{4}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{-1}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{5}{y}^{5}]}_{-1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{33}{5} \\  & =\frac{11}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{11}{5}-{(\frac{5}{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{51}{80}.\end{aligned}

Hence, $X$ and $Y$ are independent, and consequently $\text{Cov}[X,Y]=0.$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}.
$$

We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}x{y}^{3})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}]}_{0}^{1}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot 4 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{18}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}x{y}^{3})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{5}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{5}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {[\frac{1}{6}{y}^{6}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{32}{3} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}-{(\frac{8}{5})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{75}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the covariance of $X$ and $Y.$ The joint support of $X$ and $Y$ is given by the rectangle

$$
S=[0,1]\times [0,2].
$$

Moreover, we can write

$$
f(x,y)=g(x)\cdot h(y),
$$

where $g(x)=2x$ and $h(y)=\frac{{y}^{3}}{4}.$

Hence, $X$ and $Y$ are independent, and consequently $\text{Cov}[X,Y]=0.$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{18} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{8}{75}\end{aligned}].

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, we find $\text{Var}[X].$
We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\frac{5}{16}{x}^{2}({x}^{2}-y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}({x}^{4}-y{x}^{2})\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[y{x}^{4}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}{x}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y={x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{6})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{32}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{6}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{32}{[\frac{1}{7}{x}^{7}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{20}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{20}{7}-{(\frac{5}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{63}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{Var}[Y].$ Using the given results, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{40}{27}-{(\frac{20}{21})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{760}{1\,323}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\text{E}[XY]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}xy\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\frac{5}{16}xy({x}^{2}-y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}({x}^{3}y-x{y}^{2})\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}x]}_{y=0}^{y={x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{1}{6}{x}^{7})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{96}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{7}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{96}{[\frac{1}{8}{x}^{8}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{5}{3}-(\frac{5}{3})\cdot (\frac{20}{21}) \\  & =\frac{5}{63}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{63} & \frac{5}{63} \\ \frac{5}{63} & \frac{760}{1\,323}\end{aligned}].

Moreover, it is a positive semi-definite matrix.*"] [17592186188521 :activity/expected-seconds 900.0] ["question-8dc89317-431f-536c-84f1-f80a52b02432" :question/id #uuid "8dc89317-431f-536c-84f1-f80a52b02432"] ["question-8dc89317-431f-536c-84f1-f80a52b02432" :question/math-academy-id "q-152279"] ["question-8dc89317-431f-536c-84f1-f80a52b02432" :question/problem "The parabola $y={x}^{2}+2x+2$ and the line $y=2-2x$ intersect at the points $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})$ and $({x}_{2},{y}_{2}),$ where ${x}_{1}<{x}_{2}.$ What is the value of ${y}_{1}+{y}_{2}?$"] ["question-8dc89317-431f-536c-84f1-f80a52b02432" :question/worked-solution "We need to solve the following system consisting of the equations of the curves:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y={x}^{2}+2x+2 \\ y=2-2x\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the equations equal to one another and solving, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2x+2 & =2-2x \\ {x}^{2}+4x & =0 \\ x(x+4) & =0 \\ x & =-4,0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${x}_{1}<{x}_{2},$ the $x$-coordinates of the intersection points are ${x}_{1}=-4$ and ${x}_{2}=0.$ 

To find the $y$-coordinates of the intersection points, we plug these values into either curve. Let's choose the line since it's simpler.

- Substituting ${x}_{1}=-4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & =2-2{x}_{1} \\  & =2-2(-4) \\  & =10,\end{aligned}
$$

so one point of intersection is $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(-4,10).$

- Substituting ${x}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2} & =2-2{x}_{2} \\  & =2-2(0) \\  & =2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the other point of intersection is $({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(0,2).$

Therefore, ${y}_{1}=10,\,{y}_{2}=2,$ and

$$
{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}=10+2=12.
$$

:question/problem "Given that the line $y=x+k$ does **not** intersect the parabola $y={x}^{2}+1,$ what is the range of possible values of $k?$"] ["question-95764a8d-23d1-5507-836a-2817991f65d9" :question/worked-solution "To determine whether the line $y=x+k$ intersects the parabola $y={x}^{2}+1,$ we need to solve the following system of equations for the two curves:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y={x}^{2}+1 \\ y=x+k\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the equations equal to one another and writing in standard form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+1 & =x+k \\ {x}^{2}-x+1-k & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve this equation using the quadratic formula with $a=1,\,b=-1,$ and $c=1-k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{-(-1)\pm \sqrt{(-1)^{2}-4(1)(1-k)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{1\pm \sqrt{1-4+4k}}{2} \\  & =\frac{1\pm \sqrt{4k-3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the line and parabola do not intersect, our quadratic equation must have no real solutions; hence, the expression inside the square root must be negative.
Setting up and solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4k-3 & <0 \\ 4k & <3 \\ k & <\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the range of possible values of $k$ is $k<\frac{3}{4}.$"] ["question-95764a8d-23d1-5507-836a-2817991f65d9" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] $$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+5x-1 & =-2x-13 \\ {x}^{2}+7x+12 & =0 \\ (x+4)(x+3) & =0 \\ x & =-4,-3.\end{aligned}

Since ${x}_{1}<{x}_{2},$ the $x$-coordinates of the intersection points are ${x}_{1}=-4$ and ${x}_{2}=-3.$

$$

so one point of intersection is $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(-4,-5).$

- Substituting ${x}_{2}=-3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2} & =-2{x}_{2}-13 \\  & =-2(-3)-13 \\  & =-7,\end{aligned}
$$

so the other point of intersection is $({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(-3,-7).$

$$

:question/problem "The parabola $y={x}^{2}+x+4$ and the line $y=5x$ intersect at the point $P.$ Find the coordinates of $P.$

The coordinates of $P$ are
$(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$"] ["question-28de8699-3497-5296-9483-734e67042dfa" :question/worked-solution "We need to solve the following system consisting of the equations of the curves:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y={x}^{2}+x+4 \\ y=5x\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the equations equal to one another and solving, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+x+4 & =5x \\ {x}^{2}-4x+4 & =0 \\ (x-2)(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $x$-coordinate of the intersection point is $x=2.$

To find the $y$-coordinate of the intersection point, we plug this value into either curve. Let's choose the equation of the line. Substituting $x=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =5x \\  & =5(2) \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only point of intersection is $(2,10).$

{{field-1}}"] ["question-a4bf276d-b40b-5d47-b840-e4ace9d966fe" :question/worked-solution "To find an expression for the second derivative, we differentiate the equation with respect to $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}) \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =2x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}+\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x) \\  & =2x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}\cdot 2 \\  & =-\frac{2xy}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given expression for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ into the above and simplify the resulting expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =-\frac{2xy}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\cdot 2x\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}+2\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =-4{x}^{2}y+2\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the point $(0,0)$ lies on $f,$ we substitute the coordinates of our point into the above expression for the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}|}_{(0,0)} & =-4\cdot {0}^{2}\cdot 0+2\sqrt{1-{0}^{2}}=2\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-a4bf276d-b40b-5d47-b840-e4ace9d966fe" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-72a14dfe-4aac-5b96-99e1-2adb2bdf2921" :answer-field/id #uuid "72a14dfe-4aac-5b96-99e1-2adb2bdf2921"] ["answer-a94de121-a4bc-5c49-b381-af42e7f0741f" :answer/id #uuid "a94de121-a4bc-5c49-b381-af42e7f0741f"] ["answer-a94de121-a4bc-5c49-b381-af42e7f0741f" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-a94de121-a4bc-5c49-b381-af42e7f0741f" :answer/value "2"] ["answer-field-72a14dfe-4aac-5b96-99e1-2adb2bdf2921" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-72a14dfe-4aac-5b96-99e1-2adb2bdf2921" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-72a14dfe-4aac-5b96-99e1-2adb2bdf2921" :answer-field/correct "answer-a94de121-a4bc-5c49-b381-af42e7f0741f"] ["answer-field-72a14dfe-4aac-5b96-99e1-2adb2bdf2921" :answer-field/choices "answer-a94de121-a4bc-5c49-b381-af42e7f0741f"] ["question-a4bf276d-b40b-5d47-b840-e4ace9d966fe" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-72a14dfe-4aac-5b96-99e1-2adb2bdf2921"] [17592186157367 :knowledge-point/questions "question-a4bf276d-b40b-5d47-b840-e4ace9d966fe"] ["question-9b186f94-2456-5e8b-8019-128c4ccb5b71" :question/id #uuid "9b186f94-2456-5e8b-8019-128c4ccb5b71"] ["question-9b186f94-2456-5e8b-8019-128c4ccb5b71" :question/math-academy-id "q-126764"] ["question-9b186f94-2456-5e8b-8019-128c4ccb5b71" :question/problem "Use Euler's method to find an approximation to $y(0.2)$ using two steps of equal size.

{{field-1}}"] ["question-9b186f94-2456-5e8b-8019-128c4ccb5b71" :question/worked-solution "First, note that we are given $y(0)$ and asked to find $y(0.2).$ The distance from $x=0$ to $x=0.2$ is $0.2,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be 

$$
Δx=\frac{0.2-0}{2}=0.1.
$$

Now, let's proceed with Euler's method. We'll start by creating a table that includes the initial condition data $y(0)=0.$

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ | $$ | $$ |

**Step 1.** We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy$ (using the values of $x$ and $y$ in the first row) and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}}$ and ${y}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2x\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}=2\cdot 0\cdot \sqrt{1-{0}^{2}}=0 \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=0\cdot 0.1=0 \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=0+0.1=0.1 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=0+0=0\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| $0.1$ | $0$ | $$ | $$ |

**Step 2.** We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy$ (using the values of $x$ and $y$ in the second row) and new values of ${x}_{\text{new}}$ and ${y}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2x\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}=2\cdot 0.1\cdot \sqrt{1-{0}^{2}}=0.2 \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=0.2\cdot 0.1=0.02 \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=0.1+0.1=0.2 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=0+0.02=0.02\end{aligned}
$$

 

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| $0.1$ | $0$ | $0.2$ | $0.02$ |
| $0.2$ | $0.02$ | $$ | $$ |

{{field-1}}"] ["question-a3b460f4-8f03-59ea-8d4e-3d88c9d8d99f" :question/worked-solution "We have that

$$
f(x)≈{x}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{6}}{6}.

We can approximate $\int f(x)\,\text{d}x$ by integrating the above series term-by-term, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ≈{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{6}}{6})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{42}{x}^{6})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{42}]-0 \\  & =\frac{13}{42}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-a3b460f4-8f03-59ea-8d4e-3d88c9d8d99f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-96f0fd95-c9b0-5cbe-abcc-ca8956c4e2ea" :answer-field/id #uuid "96f0fd95-c9b0-5cbe-abcc-ca8956c4e2ea"] ["answer-2c6372b2-3f3a-5d2d-9b9b-d69b71a08c40" :answer/id #uuid "2c6372b2-3f3a-5d2d-9b9b-d69b71a08c40"] ["answer-2c6372b2-3f3a-5d2d-9b9b-d69b71a08c40" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-2c6372b2-3f3a-5d2d-9b9b-d69b71a08c40" :answer/value "\frac{13}{42}"] ["answer-field-96f0fd95-c9b0-5cbe-abcc-ca8956c4e2ea" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-96f0fd95-c9b0-5cbe-abcc-ca8956c4e2ea" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-96f0fd95-c9b0-5cbe-abcc-ca8956c4e2ea" :answer-field/correct "answer-2c6372b2-3f3a-5d2d-9b9b-d69b71a08c40"] ["answer-field-96f0fd95-c9b0-5cbe-abcc-ca8956c4e2ea" :answer-field/choices "answer-2c6372b2-3f3a-5d2d-9b9b-d69b71a08c40"] ["question-a3b460f4-8f03-59ea-8d4e-3d88c9d8d99f" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-96f0fd95-c9b0-5cbe-abcc-ca8956c4e2ea"] [17592186087794 :knowledge-point/questions "question-a3b460f4-8f03-59ea-8d4e-3d88c9d8d99f"] ["question-8679792d-1ee6-50ba-bf59-17896dc979de" :question/id #uuid "8679792d-1ee6-50ba-bf59-17896dc979de"] ["question-8679792d-1ee6-50ba-bf59-17896dc979de" :question/math-academy-id "q-126769"] ["question-8679792d-1ee6-50ba-bf59-17896dc979de" :question/problem "Given that the Maclaurin expansion of $f(x)$ can be represented as

{{field-1}}"] ["question-8679792d-1ee6-50ba-bf59-17896dc979de" :question/worked-solution "To find the radius of convergence, we apply the ratio test.

So, let's denote ${a}_{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n}{x}^{4n+2}}{(2n+1)!}.$ Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(-1)^{n+1}{x}^{4n+6}}{(2n+3)!}\cdot \frac{(2n+1)!}{(-1)^{n}{x}^{4n+2}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|-\frac{{x}^{4}}{(2n+2)(2n+3)}| \\  & ={x}^{4}{lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{1}{(2n+2)(2n+3)}| \\  & ={x}^{4}\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if $L<1.$ In this case, the convergence condition is satisfied for all $-\infty <x<\infty .$ Therefore, we conclude that the radius of convergence is $R=\infty .$"] ["question-8679792d-1ee6-50ba-bf59-17896dc979de" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-ee13cf7b-506a-556c-9c39-4af06c9d75a9" :answer-field/id #uuid "ee13cf7b-506a-556c-9c39-4af06c9d75a9"] ["answer-c0ee0055-9260-50e8-82d0-59ef2f03f218" :answer/id #uuid "c0ee0055-9260-50e8-82d0-59ef2f03f218"] ["answer-c0ee0055-9260-50e8-82d0-59ef2f03f218" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-c0ee0055-9260-50e8-82d0-59ef2f03f218" :answer/value "\infty"] ["answer-field-ee13cf7b-506a-556c-9c39-4af06c9d75a9" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-ee13cf7b-506a-556c-9c39-4af06c9d75a9" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-ee13cf7b-506a-556c-9c39-4af06c9d75a9" :answer-field/correct "answer-c0ee0055-9260-50e8-82d0-59ef2f03f218"] ["answer-field-ee13cf7b-506a-556c-9c39-4af06c9d75a9" :answer-field/choices "answer-c0ee0055-9260-50e8-82d0-59ef2f03f218"] ["question-8679792d-1ee6-50ba-bf59-17896dc979de" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-ee13cf7b-506a-556c-9c39-4af06c9d75a9"] [17592186092269 :knowledge-point/questions "question-8679792d-1ee6-50ba-bf59-17896dc979de"] ["question-1f6c3d65-e721-5449-9ddc-958a81a54048" :question/id #uuid "1f6c3d65-e721-5449-9ddc-958a81a54048"] ["question-1f6c3d65-e721-5449-9ddc-958a81a54048" :question/math-academy-id "q-126770"] ["question-1f6c3d65-e721-5449-9ddc-958a81a54048" :question/problem "Calculate the first three non-zero terms of the Maclaurin expansion of ${f}^{′}(x).$

["question-aad779ca-b824-50cb-b4dc-f0dd2ba06356" :question/problem "Which of the following best describes the projection of the intersection between the elliptic cone ${x}^{2}+(y-1)^{2}={z}^{2}$ and the plane $2x-y=0$ onto the $xz$-plane?"] ["question-aad779ca-b824-50cb-b4dc-f0dd2ba06356" :question/worked-solution "Since we want to find the projection onto the $xz$-plane, we need to eliminate the variable $y.$ First, we solve the equation of the plane for $y,$ as follows:

$$
2x-y=0\,⟹\,y=2x
$$

Substituting the expression for $y$ into the equation of the elliptic cone, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(2x-1)^{2} & ={z}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+4{x}^{2}-4x+1 & ={z}^{2} \\ {z}^{2}-5{x}^{2}+4x & =1 \\ {z}^{2}-5({x}^{2}-\frac{4}{5}x+\frac{4}{25})+\frac{4}{5} & =1 \\ {z}^{2}-5{({x}^{2}-\frac{2}{5})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{5} \\ 5{z}^{2}-25{(x-\frac{2}{5})}^{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is the equation of a hyperbola centered at $(\frac{2}{5},0)$ in the $xz$-plane."] ["question-aad779ca-b824-50cb-b4dc-f0dd2ba06356" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] :question/worked-solution "Since we want to find the projection onto the $xy$-plane, we need to eliminate the variable $z.$ First, we solve the equation of the plane for $z,$ as follows:

$$
2z-x+1=0\,⟹\,z=\frac{x}{2}-\frac{1}{2}
$$

Substituting the expression for $z$ into the equation of the elliptic cone, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2} & =2{(\frac{x}{2}-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+3{y}^{2} & =2(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{1}{4}) \\ {x}^{2}+3{y}^{2} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-x+\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+x+3{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}(x+1)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}+3{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{2}+3{y}^{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is the equation of an ellipse centered at $(-1,0)$ in the $xy$-plane."] ["question-1c9e9df7-050b-54af-a7dc-34ce03f716ac" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ${a}_{10}=23$ is $9$ jumps after ${a}_{1},$ we can determine the first term of the sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{10} & ={a}_{1}+9d \\ 23 & ={a}_{1}+9(3) \\ 23 & ={a}_{1}+27 \\ -4 & ={a}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the formula for the $n$th term is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =-4+(n-1)(3) \\  & =-4+3n-3 \\  & =3n-7\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-3a1942e4-caa0-5f58-aeeb-9eef16c2b831" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-3600f700-81aa-539b-9b1e-e8b15201fad2" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
f(n)=f(1)+(n-1)d.
$$

From the first few terms

$$
19,\,17,\,15,\,…
$$

we see that the first term is $f(1)=19$ and the common difference is 

$$
d=17-19=-2.
$$

So, we substitute into the formula and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n) & =f(1)+(n-1)d \\  & =19+(n-1)(-2) \\  & =19-2n+2 \\  & =21-2n\end{aligned}
$$

    

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is $f(n)=21-2n.$"] ["question-89937c4c-b18e-5039-ba6e-7940ef191d3c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] :question/problem "Find the $33$rd term of the following arithmetic sequence.

$$

$$"] ["question-985912e6-de0a-5f5e-a520-8f2ffaee1968" :question/worked-solution "The formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}+(n-1)d.
$$

First, we will write the formula for the $n$th term of this sequence. From the first few terms

$$
13,\,8,\,3,\,-2,\,…
$$

we see that the first term is ${a}_{1}=13$ and the common difference is 

$$
d=8-13=-5.
$$

So, we substitute into the formula and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =13+(n-1)(-5) \\  & =13-5n+5 \\  & =18-5n\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use our formula to find the $33$rd term. All we have to do is substitute $n=33:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =18-5n \\ {a}_{33} & =18-5(33) \\  & =18-165 \\  & =-147\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $33$rd term of the sequence is ${a}_{33}=-147.$"] ["question-985912e6-de0a-5f5e-a520-8f2ffaee1968" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["activity-b2e9f259-a49d-50fe-8d81-4ae722fca5d0" :activity/first-step "step-b95bdef4-950e-5d9f-9010-46130d47212a"] [17592186167264 :question/problem "Let $F(x)=2x$ for $x\in R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $3$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,3)$ to $x\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $f(x+6)=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$

II. $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R$

III. $f(x+2)=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$"] [17592186167264 :question/worked-solution "Since $f$ is the $3$-periodic extension of $F,$ we have 

- $f(x+3)=f(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,3).$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x+6)=f((x+3)+3)=f(x+3)=f(x)\end{aligned}
$$

for all $x\in R.$

- Statement II is false. For example, take $x=4.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(4)=f(1+3)=f(1)=F(1)=2(1)=2,\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"."] [17592186167264 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] [17592186164762 :answer-field/correct 17592186164763] ["question-d11bc330-9efc-55d1-a388-de4f864cc23e" :question/id #uuid "d11bc330-9efc-55d1-a388-de4f864cc23e"] ["question-d11bc330-9efc-55d1-a388-de4f864cc23e" :question/math-academy-id "q-340511"] ["question-d11bc330-9efc-55d1-a388-de4f864cc23e" :question/problem "Let $F(x)=4x-1$ for $x\in R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $6$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,6)$ to $x\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $f(x+12)=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$

II. $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R$

III. $f(x+3)=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$"] ["question-d11bc330-9efc-55d1-a388-de4f864cc23e" :question/worked-solution "Since $f$ is the $6$-periodic extension of $F,$ we have 

- $f(x+6)=f(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,6).$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x+12)=f((x+6)+6)=f(x+6)=f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

for all $x\in R.$

- Statement II is false. For example, take $x=7.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(7)=f(1+6)=f(1)=F(1)=3,\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}F(7)=27.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x)\ne F(x)$ for $x=7.$

- Statement III is false. For example, take $x=2.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2+3)=f(5)=F(5)=19\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2)=F(2)=7.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x+3)\ne f(x)$ for $x=2.$

The functions $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)$ and $g(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)$ 
{{field-2}}."] [17592186314101 :answer-field/correct 17592186312207] ["question-dc02bcc8-5f0f-5f17-99b3-d1e75d3135c1" :question/id #uuid "dc02bcc8-5f0f-5f17-99b3-d1e75d3135c1"] ["question-dc02bcc8-5f0f-5f17-99b3-d1e75d3135c1" :question/math-academy-id "q-340658"] ["question-dc02bcc8-5f0f-5f17-99b3-d1e75d3135c1" :question/problem "Let $F(x)=2{x}^{3}$ for $x\in R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [0,2\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)).
$$

Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient ${b}_{2}$ below, where $⟨\,,⟩$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[0,2\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{2} & ={{field-1}} \\  & ={{field-2}}\,\cdot \,{{field-3}}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-dc02bcc8-5f0f-5f17-99b3-d1e75d3135c1" :question/worked-solution "The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [0,2\pi )$ is given by

$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that's piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,2\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),
$$

where ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. 

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & = \\ \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the functions
$1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$
are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is

$$
{b}_{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩.
$$

Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(8\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain that

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & ={b}_{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ \\ {b}_{2} & =\frac{⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩}{⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩} \\ {b}_{2} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2{x}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-dc02bcc8-5f0f-5f17-99b3-d1e75d3135c1" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-74ef7a6c-fb00-53a3-972e-01dd7c23eeb4" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-3db32c22-3de8-5264-9b28-9916a3aeb5f2" :question/math-academy-id "q-340659"] ["question-3db32c22-3de8-5264-9b28-9916a3aeb5f2" :question/problem "Let $F(x)=2{x}^{4}-4{x}^{3}$ for $x\in R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [0,2\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)).
$$

Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient ${b}_{3}$ below, where $⟨\,,⟩$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[0,2\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{3} & ={{field-1}} \\  & ={{field-2}}\,\cdot \,{{field-3}}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-3db32c22-3de8-5264-9b28-9916a3aeb5f2" :question/worked-solution "The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [0,2\pi )$ is given by

$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that's piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,2\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),
$$

where ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. 

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩ & = \\ \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the functions
$1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$
are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is

$$
{b}_{3}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩.
$$

Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{12}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(12\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain that

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩ & ={b}_{3}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩ \\ {b}_{3} & =\frac{⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩}{⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩} \\ {b}_{3} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(2{x}^{4}-4{x}^{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-3db32c22-3de8-5264-9b28-9916a3aeb5f2" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-1f978f14-7743-5e8c-b891-41d5a5372431" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-510f41a7-5712-55db-b50d-5c80967bb9fb" :question/math-academy-id "q-12889"] ["question-510f41a7-5712-55db-b50d-5c80967bb9fb" :question/problem "Given that

$$
{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+4)}^{4}=A{x}^{8}+B{x}^{6}+C{x}^{4}+128{x}^{2}+256
$$

where $A,B$ and $C$ are constants, find the value of $A+B+C.$"] ["question-510f41a7-5712-55db-b50d-5c80967bb9fb" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
$$

Here we have that $n=4,$ $a=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2},$ and $b=4.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{4}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{3}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{3},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{4}.
$$

The $4$th row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,4,6,4,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+4)}^{4} & =1{a}^{4}+4{a}^{3}b+6{a}^{2}{b}^{2}+4a{b}^{3}+1{b}^{4} \\  & =1{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{4}(4)^{0}+4{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{3}{(4)}^{1}+6{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{2}{(4)}^{2} \\  & \,+4{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{1}{(4)}^{3}+1{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{0}{(4)}^{4} \\  & =1(\frac{{x}^{8}}{16})(1)+4(\frac{{x}^{6}}{8})(4)+6(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4})(16) \\  & \,+4(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})(64)+1(1)(256) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8}}{16}+\frac{16{x}^{6}}{8}+\frac{96{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{256{x}^{2}}{2}+256 \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8}}{16}+2{x}^{6}+24{x}^{4}+128{x}^{2}+256.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have $A=\frac{1}{16},B=2$ and $C=24.$ So, finally

$$
A+B+C=\frac{1}{16}+2+24=\frac{417}{16}.
$$"] ["question-510f41a7-5712-55db-b50d-5c80967bb9fb" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-69965209-526e-5658-899a-44e6dd8b07be" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
$$

Here we have that $n=4,$ $a=1,$ and $b=-{z}^{2}.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{4}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{3}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{3},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{4}.
$$

The $4$th row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,4,6,4,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{(1-{z}^{2})}^{4} & =1{a}^{4}+4{a}^{3}b+6{a}^{2}{b}^{2}+4a{b}^{3}+1{b}^{4} \\  & =1(1)^{4}(-{z}^{2})^{0}+4(1)^{3}(-{z}^{2})^{1}+6(1)^{2}(-{z}^{2})^{2}+4(1)^{1}(-{z}^{2})^{3}+1(1)^{0}(-{z}^{2})^{4} \\  & =1(1)(1)+4(1)(-{z}^{2})+6(1)({z}^{4})+4(1)(-{z}^{6})+1(1)({z}^{8}) \\  & =1-4{z}^{2}+6{z}^{4}-4{z}^{6}+{z}^{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We rewrite the binomial expansion in descending powers of $z$ as follows:

$$
(1-{z}^{2})^{4}={z}^{8}-4{z}^{6}+6{z}^{4}-4{z}^{2}+1
$$

Finally, in descending powers of $z,$ the first three terms of the binomial expansion are

$$
{z}^{8}-4{z}^{6}+6{z}^{4}.
$$"] ["question-c9b934c2-8c57-56f1-8a65-42f138da7b11" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-a9807bbb-6450-5bec-9d6e-2cb5e0bc2c61" :answer-field/id #uuid where $A,B$ and $C$ are constants, determine the value of $A+B+C.$"] ["question-700411f4-106e-5592-a547-8738d64ef693" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
$$

Here we have that $n=4,$ $a=2s,$ and $b=-{u}^{2}.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{4}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{3}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{3},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{4}.
$$

The $4$th row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,4,6,4,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}(2s-{u}^{2})^{4} & =1{a}^{4}{b}^{0}+4{a}^{3}b+6{a}^{2}{b}^{2}+4a{b}^{3}+1{a}^{0}{b}^{4} \\  & =1(2s)^{4}{(-{u}^{2})}^{0}+4(2s)^{3}{(-{u}^{2})}^{1}+6(2s)^{2}{(-{u}^{2})}^{2} \\  & \,+4(2s)^{1}{(-{u}^{2})}^{3}+1(2s)^{0}{(-{u}^{2})}^{4} \\  & =1(16{s}^{4})(1)+4(8{s}^{3})(-{u}^{2})+6(4{s}^{2})({u}^{4}) \\  & \,+4(2s)(-{u}^{6})+1(1)({u}^{8}) \\  & =16{s}^{4}-32{s}^{3}{u}^{2}+24{s}^{2}{u}^{4}-8s{u}^{6}+{u}^{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $A=-32,B=24,$ and $C=-8.$ Finally, then

$$
A+B+C=-32+24-8=-16.
$$"] ["question-700411f4-106e-5592-a547-8738d64ef693" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-fe5bbd0a-c356-5392-bd90-c3fba4a83d1d" :answer-field/id #uuid :knowledge-point/questions "question-c451ec1c-6a2b-54c4-80d7-187b41f5f298"] [17592186097928 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to evaluate $\displaystyle \int x^3e^{x/2} \textrm{d}x.$ We can do it by applying integration by parts three times, but the calculation is pretty long. How can we speed it up?

Multiple applications of integration by parts become quick and easy if we use the **tabular method**.

Let's start by picking our $u$ and $\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}$ as normal:

$$
u = x^3\,,\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = e^{x/2}\,.
$$

We put this in a table, as shown below:

| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same Color Products** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3$ | $e^{x/2}$ |  |  |

To fill in the second row of the table, we differentiate the function in the first column and integrate the function in the second column. Doing this, we find

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(x^3\right) = 3x^2\,,\quad \int e^{x/2} \textrm{d}x = 2e^{x/2}\,.
$$

Filling in our table, we get the following:

| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same Color Products** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3$ | $e^{x/2}$ |  |  |
| $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 3x^2$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2e^{x/2}$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} +$ |  |

At this step, we begin filling the third column. It always starts with a "$+$" and then the signs alternate at each subsequent step.

We continue by differentiating the expression in the first column and integrating the expression in the second column until we get zero in the first column.

| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same Color Products** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color[rgb]{1,0,0}  x^3$ | $e^{x/2}$ |  |  |
| $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 3x^2$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2e^{x/2}$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} +$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0}$ |
| $\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 6x$ | $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}  4e^{x/2}$ | $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0.5,0}$ |
| $\color[rgb]{1,0,1} 6$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 8e^{x/2}$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0,1} +$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0,1}$ |
| $0$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,1}16e^{x/2}$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,1} -$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,1}$ |

Now we multiply the same-colored terms along with the same-colored sign. Specifically we multiply $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3$ with ${\color[rgb]{1,0,0} 2e^{x/2}},$ $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}3x^2$ with $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}4e^{x/2},$ and so on. We get

| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same Color Products** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color[rgb]{1,0,0}  x^3$ | $e^{x/2}$ |  |  |
| $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}3x^2$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2e^{x/2}$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} +$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} 2x^3e^{x/2}$ |
| $\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 6x$ | $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}  4e^{x/2}$ | $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -$ | $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}  -12x^2e^{x/2}$ |
| $\color[rgb]{1,0,1} 6$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 8e^{x/2}$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0,1} +$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 48xe^{x/2}$ |
| $0$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,1}16e^{x/2}$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,1} -$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,1} -96e^{x/2}$ |

Finally, we add up all the terms of the last column to get the answer for our integral. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{3}{e}^{x/2}\text{d}x & =2{x}^{3}{e}^{x/2}-12{x}^{2}{e}^{x/2}+48x{e}^{x/2}-96{e}^{x/2}+C \\  & ={e}^{x/2}(2{x}^{3}-12{x}^{2}+48x-96)+C.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186096911 :activity/expected-seconds 840.0] [17592186278512 :question/problem "For a surface $S$ given by $x=k(y,z)$ for $(y,z)\in D,$ the flux of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by
