For example, consider the function $f(x)$ whose graph is shown below. This function has a vertical asymptote at $x=1,$ and the function value $f(x)$ grows without bound as $x$ approaches the asymptote $x=1.$ What is the limit $\lim_\limits{x\to 1} f(x)$? 

![](images/ab/ab9d57d3952fe0221616f9e64e1295fd0511703bdd5ed3a5fe91113cc7c8bf1b.png)

Remember that in order for computing any limit, in this case, $\lim_\limits{x\to 1} f(x),$ we have to compute the left and right-sided limits separately and ensure that they match up.

- **Left-sided limit:** As we approach $x=1$ (the vertical asymptote) from the left side of the graph, the function $f(x)$ increases without bound, approaching $\infty.$ We conclude that

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to 1^-} f(x) = \infty.
$$

- **Right-sided limit:** Likewise, as we approach the vertical asymptote $x=1$ from the right side of the graph, $f(x)$ still approaches $\infty.$ Consequently, 

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to 1^+ } f(x) = \infty.
$$

We see that both the left and right limits exist and are equal to $\infty\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to 1^-} f(x) = \lim_\limits{x\to 1^+} f(x) = \infty
$$

As a result, the overall limit is also equal to $\infty\mathbin{:}$

["question-4bc6d1d2-09ee-5cec-a2ab-850e837a407d" :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}2y\operatorname{cos}⁡x, & \,0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the expected value of $Y.$"] ["question-4bc6d1d2-09ee-5cec-a2ab-850e837a407d" :question/worked-solution "The marginal density function for $Y$ when $0\le y\le 1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2y[\operatorname{sin}⁡x]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =2y(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =2y(1-0) \\  & =2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for ${f}_{X}(x)$ is given by

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}2y, & 0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the  expected value of $Y$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot 2y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{2}{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-4bc6d1d2-09ee-5cec-a2ab-850e837a407d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-76f810c9-6c36-550e-ba2c-f211b1f812da" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-fbeb0099-1c78-5b43-8e43-b8ec47f11368" :question/problem "A fly’s position relative to a fixed origin $O$ is given by the function $x(t)=\frac{t}{2}-\frac{\pi }{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{8}t)\,\text{m},$ where $t$ is the time in minutes. Find its average position of the fly between $0$ and $2$ minutes."] ["question-fbeb0099-1c78-5b43-8e43-b8ec47f11368" :question/worked-solution "To calculate the average value of the position on $[{t}_{1},{t}_{2}],$ we use the average value formula

$$
{x}_{\text{avg}}=\frac{1}{{t}_{2}-{t}_{1}}\,{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{2-0}\,{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{t}{2}-\frac{\pi }{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{8}t))\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{8}t))|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((\frac{{2}^{2}}{4}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{8}\cdot 2))-(\frac{{0}^{2}}{4}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{8}\cdot 0))) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((1+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})-(0+1)) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the average position is $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\,\text{m}.$"] ["question-fbeb0099-1c78-5b43-8e43-b8ec47f11368" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] $$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{6-2}\,{\int }_{2}^{6}(\frac{{2}^{t}}{12})\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 12\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡2}({2}^{t}){|}_{2}^{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{48\operatorname{ln}⁡2}({2}^{6}-{2}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{60}{48\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =\frac{5}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/worked-solution "To calculate the average value of the acceleration on $[{t}_{1},{t}_{2}],$ we use the average value formula

$$
{a}_{\text{avg}}=\frac{1}{{t}_{2}-{t}_{1}}\,{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}a(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{2-0}\,{\int }_{0}^{2}({e}^{t}+2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{t}+{t}^{2}){|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[({e}^{2}+{2}^{2})-({e}^{0}+{0}^{2})] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{2}+4-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{2}+3).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the average acceleration is $\frac{1}{2}({e}^{2}+3)\,{\text{mm/s}}^{2}.$"] ["question-a23536ce-7cba-5974-838f-a84131e7f6d9" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["question-c68b418a-a9c2-512b-93fe-1e0b537572e9" :question/problem "$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx) \\ g(x) & ∼\frac{{c}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{c}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{d}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Let $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ be $2\pi $-periodic extensions of some functions from $x\in [-\pi ,\pi )$ to $x\in R$ with the Fourier series shown above. What is the $6\text{th}$ Fourier sine coefficient of $-3f(x)-2g(x)?$"] ["question-c68b418a-a9c2-512b-93fe-1e0b537572e9" :question/worked-solution "Let $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ be $2\pi $-periodic functions with Fourier series

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)), \\ g(x) & ∼\frac{{c}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({c}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{d}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)).\end{aligned}
$$

Then for any constants $\alpha $ and $\beta $,

$$
\alpha f(x)+\beta g(x)∼\frac{\alpha {a}_{0}+\beta {c}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }((\alpha {a}_{n}+\beta {c}_{n})\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+(\alpha {b}_{n}+\beta {d}_{n})\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)).
$$

Using the linearity property of Fourier series, the corresponding Fourier coefficients of $-3f(x)-2g(x)$ are

- $-3{a}_{0}-2{c}_{0}$ for the constant coefficient,

- $-3{a}_{n}-2{c}_{n},$ $n\ge 1$ for the cosine coefficients, and

- $-3{b}_{n}-2{d}_{n},$ $n\ge 1$ for the sine coefficients.

Therefore, the $6$th sine coefficient of $-3f(x)-2g(x)$ is

$$
-3{b}_{6}-2{d}_{6}.
$$"] ["question-c68b418a-a9c2-512b-93fe-1e0b537572e9" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-b50ec26a-cc99-5796-8813-5d5595ca224f" :answer-field/id #uuid in the corresponding Fourier series of $f(x)$ must be zero."] ["question-1c3a98af-770d-5596-b478-235b18fb3ea6" :question/worked-solution "To determine whether $f$ is even or odd, we compare $f(-x)$ and $f(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)^{3} \\  & =-{x}^{3} \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(-x)=-f(x),$ we have that $f$ is odd.

For Fourier series on $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ the cosine coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x,
$$

and the constant coefficient is

$$
{a}_{0}=\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Here, $f(x)$ is odd and $\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)$ is even, so $f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)$ is odd. Also, $f(x)$ itself is odd.

Now, the integral of an odd function over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$ is $0.$ Thus, ${a}_{n}=0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and ${a}_{0}=0.$

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ is $\text{odd}$ and the $\text{cosine terms}$ in its Fourier series must be zero."] ["question-1c3a98af-770d-5596-b478-235b18fb3ea6" :question/difficulty To illustrate, let's consider the following example:

$$
I = \int \dfrac{\ln x}{x} \textrm{d}x
$$

Let's try using the method of integration by parts. We suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}x & \,\Rightarrow \,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x} & \,\Rightarrow \,v=\int \frac{1}{x}\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}x(\operatorname{ln}x)-\int (\operatorname{ln}x)(\frac{1}{x})\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{2}x-\int \frac{\operatorname{ln}x}{x}\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{2}x-I\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We now have the same integral $I$ on both sides of the equality. Thinking about $I$ as some unknown variable, we can easily solve this equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={ln}^{2}x-I \\ I+I & ={ln}^{2}x \\ 2I & ={ln}^{2}x \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{2}x}{2}+C\,.\end{aligned}
$$

| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same Color Products** |

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(x^3\right) = 3x^2\,,\quad \int e^{x/2} \textrm{d}x = 2e^{x/2}\,
$$

| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same Color Products** |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3$ | $e^{x/2}$ |  |  |
| $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 3x^2$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2e^{x/2}$ | $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} +$ |  |

At this step, we begin filling the third column. It always starts with a "$+$" and then the signs alternate at each subsequent step.

We continue by differentiating the expression in the first column and integrating the expression in the second column until we get zero in the first column.

| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same Color Products** |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |

| $\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 6x$ | $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 4e^{x/2}$ | $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -$ | $\color[rgb]{0,0.5,0}$ |

Now we multiply the same colored terms along with the same colored sign. Specifically we multiply $\color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3$ with ${\color[rgb]{1,0,0} 2e^{x/2}}$, $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}3x^2$ with $\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}4e^{x/2}$, and so on. We get

| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same Color Products** |

to work out the definite integral.\n\nIn this case, we define\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}u=(\\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2} & \\,⟹\\,\\frac{\\text{d}u}{\\text{d}x}=\\frac{2\\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}\\,, \\\\ \\frac{\\text{d}v}{\\text{d}x}=18{x}^{2} & \\,⟹\\,v=\\int \\frac{\\text{d}v}{\\text{d}x}\\,\\text{d}x=\\int 18{x}^{2}\\,\\text{d}x=6{x}^{3}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nUsing the formula of integration by parts, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int 18{x}^{2}(\\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\\,\\text{d}x & =\\int u\\frac{\\text{d}v}{\\text{d}x}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =uv-\\int v\\frac{\\text{d}u}{\\text{d}x}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={(\\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}(6{x}^{3})-\\int (6{x}^{3})(\\frac{2\\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =6{x}^{3}{(\\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-12\\int {x}^{2}\\operatorname{ln}⁡x\\,\\text{d}x.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\\int {x}^{2}\\operatorname{ln}⁡x\\,\\text{d}x.$ We take\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}u=\\operatorname{ln}⁡x & \\,⟹\\,\\frac{\\text{d}u}{\\text{d}x}=\\frac{1}{x}\\,, \\\\ \\frac{\\text{d}v}{\\text{d}x}={x}^{2} & \\,⟹\\,v=\\int \\frac{\\text{d}v}{\\text{d}x}\\,\\text{d}x=\\int {x}^{2}\\,\\text{d}x=\\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\\,.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nIn this case, the formula for integration by parts gives\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int {x}^{2}\\operatorname{ln}⁡x\\,\\text{d}x & =\\int u\\frac{\\text{d}v}{\\text{d}x}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =uv-\\int v\\frac{\\text{d}u}{\\text{d}x}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =\\operatorname{ln}⁡x(\\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\\int (\\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\\frac{1}{x})\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =\\frac{{x}^{3}\\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3}-\\frac{1}{3}\\int {x}^{2}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =\\frac{{x}^{3}\\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3}-\\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $D$ is an integral constant. \n\nSo, we get that the indefinite integral is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int 18{x}^{2}(\\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\\,\\text{d}x & =6{x}^{3}{(\\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-12\\int {x}^{2}\\operatorname{ln}⁡x\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =6{x}^{3}{(\\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-12(\\frac{{x}^{3}\\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3}-\\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D) \\\\  & =6{x}^{3}{(\\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-4{x}^{3}\\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3}-12D \\\\  & ={x}^{3}(6{(\\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-4\\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\\frac{4}{3})+C,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $C=-12D.$\n\nFinally, we can work out the definite integral:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{1}^{e}18{x}^{2}(\\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\\text{d}x & ={[{x}^{3}(6{(\\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-4\\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\\frac{4}{3})]}_{1}^{e} \\\\  & =[{e}^{3}(6{(\\operatorname{ln}⁡e)}^{2}-4\\operatorname{ln}⁡e+\\frac{4}{3})]-[{1}^{3}(6{(\\operatorname{ln}⁡1)}^{2}-4\\operatorname{ln}⁡1+\\frac{4}{3})] \\\\  & =[{e}^{3}(6-4+\\frac{4}{3})]-\\frac{4}{3} \\\\  & =\\frac{10{e}^{3}-4}{3}\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186547073 :question/id #uuid "eec4d3ca-fb39-5950-ae42-a7772eee1331" :question/math-academy-id Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.\n\n*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *\n\n| $z$ | $\\,0.00\\,$ | $\\,0.01\\,$ | $\\,0.02\\,$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| $\\,1.3\\,$ | $\\,0.9032\\,$ | $\\,0.9049\\,$ | $\\,0.9066\\,$ |\n| $\\,1.4\\,$ | $\\,0.9192\\,$ | $\\,0.9207\\,$ | $\\,0.9222\\,$ |\n| $\\,1.5\\,$ | $\\,0.9332\\,$ | $\\,0.9345\\,$ | $\\,0.9357\\,$ |" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the score of a randomly selected student. Assuming the volume of soda is normally distributed, find the percentage of cans containing less than $12.2$ ounces of soda, rounded to $1$ decimal place.\n\n*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*\n\n| $p$ | $\\,0.01\\,$ | $\\,0.03\\,$ | $\\,0.05\\,$ | $\\,0.10\\,$ | $\\,0.15\\,$ | $\\,0.20\\,$ | $\\,0.25\\,$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\\,-2.3263\\,$ | $\\,-1.8808\\,$ | $\\,-1.6449\\,$ | $\\,-1.2816\\,$ | $\\,-1.0364\\,$ | $\\,-0.8416\\,$ | $\\,-0.6745\\,$ |\n\n$$\n\n$$\n\n*In addition, you're given the following table of values for $p=Φ(z)$*.\n\n| $z$ | $\\,0.05\\,$ | $\\,0.06\\,$ | $\\,0.07\\,$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| $\\,1.0\\,$ | $\\,0.8531\\,$ | $\\,0.8554\\,$ | $\\,0.8577\\,$ |\n| $\\,1.1\\,$ | $\\,0.8749\\,$ | $\\,0.8770\\,$ | $\\,0.8790\\,$ |\n| $\\,1.2\\,$ | $\\,0.8944\\,$ | $\\,0.8962\\,$ | $\\,0.8980\\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the volume of soda in a randomly selected can. Then we have $X∼N(12,{\\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find $P(X<12.2).$ But first, we need to find the standard deviation $\\sigma .$\n\nWe know that $P(X<11.7)=0.03.$ First, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X<11.7) & =0.03 \\\\ P(Z\\le \\frac{11.7-12}{\\sigma }) & =0.03 \\\\ Φ(\\frac{-0.3}{\\sigma }) & =0.03 \\\\ \\frac{-0.3}{\\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.03)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFrom the table, \n\n$$\n{Φ}^{-1}(0.03)≈-1.8808.\n$$\n\nTherefore, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{-0.3}{\\sigma } & =-1.8808 \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sigma } & =6.26933 \\\\ \\sigma  & =\\frac{1}{6.26933} \\\\  & ≈0.1595.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nFinally, we can solve for $P(X<12.2)$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X<12.2) & =P(X\\le 12.2) \\\\  & =P(Z\\le \\frac{12.2-12}{0.1595}) \\\\  & ≈P(Z\\le 1.25) \\\\  & =Φ(1.25) \\\\  & ≈89.4%\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, approximately $89.4%$  of soda cans contain less than "A truck travels an average distance of $21\\,\\text{mi}$ with a gallon of gas. However, $15%$ of the time, a truck travels more than $26\\,\\text{mi}$ on a gallon of gas. Assuming that the distance the truck can travel with a gallon of gas is normally distributed, find, as a percent, the proportion of journeys that the truck travels less than $15\\,\\text{mi}$ on a gallon of gas. Round your answer to $1$ decimal place.\n\n*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *\n\n| $p$ | $\\,0.75\\,$ | $\\,0.80\\,$ | $\\,0.85\\,$ | $\\,0.90\\,$ | $\\,0.95\\,$ | $\\,0.97\\,$ | $\\,0.99\\,$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\\,0.6745\\,$ | $\\,0.8416\\,$ | $\\,1.0364\\,$ | $\\,1.2816\\,$ | $\\,1.6449\\,$ | $\\,1.8808\\,$ | $\\,2.3263\\,$ |\n\n$$\n\n$$\n\n*In addition, you're given the following table of values for $p=Φ(z)$*.\n\n| $z$ | $\\,0.03\\,$ | $\\,0.04\\,$ | $\\,0.05\\,$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| $\\,-1.3\\,$ | $\\,0.0918\\,$ | $\\,0.0901\\,$ | $\\,0.0885\\,$ |\n| $\\,-1.2\\,$ | $\\,0.1093\\,$ | $\\,0.1075\\,$ | $\\,0.1056\\,$ |\n| $\\,-1.1\\,$ | $\\,0.1292\\,$ | $\\,0.1271\\,$ | $\\,0.1251\\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the distance traveled by the truck with a gallon of gas. Then we have $X∼N(21,{\\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find $P(X\\le 15).$ But first, we need to find the standard deviation $\\sigma .$ \n\nWe know that $P(X>26)=0.15.$ First, we convert this to a cumulative probability:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X\\le 26) & =1-P(X>26) \\\\  & =1-0.15 \\\\  & =0.85\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring. We get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X\\le 26) & =0.85 \\\\ P(Z\\le \\frac{26-21}{\\sigma }) & =0.85 \\\\ Φ(\\frac{5}{\\sigma }) & =0.85 \\\\ \\frac{5}{\\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.85)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFrom the table, \n\n$$\n{Φ}^{-1}(0.85)≈1.0364.\n$$\n\nTherefore, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{5}{\\sigma } & =1.0364 \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sigma } & =0.2073 \\\\ \\sigma  & =\\frac{1}{0.2073} \\\\  & ≈4.8239.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we can solve for $P(X\\le 15)$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X\\le 15) & =P(Z\\le \\frac{15-21}{4.8239}) \\\\  & ≈P(Z\\le -1.24) \\\\  & =Φ(-1.24) \\\\  & =0.1075 \\\\  & ≈10.8%\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, approximately $10.8%$ of the time, a gallon of gas travels only $15\\,\\text{mi}$ or less."} {:db/id 17592186519585 :question/id #uuid "d34b6be0-737c-5c5c-907f-c713ce8e6b32" :question/math-academy-id "q-133236" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "09021ce8-047e-5b0d-92f8-36d32076c19b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "78.2%" :db/id 17592186519005} {:answer/id #uuid "2d58aa30-649a-5d30-86fd-836c82705dcb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "83.4%" :db/id 17592186519065} {:answer/id #uuid "7bce9ce0-a3ff-570e-86db-d819bc4f24bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "80.8%" :db/id 17592186519187} {:answer/id #uuid "99059b85-08c0-5911-bef5-b258cf55a646" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "76.9%" :db/id 17592186519244} {:answer/id #uuid "99eaaeec-7b23-5191-b1ac-c727b2e8bc60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "81.1%" :db/id 17592186519246}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186519005} :answer-field/id #uuid "3d8d7f1f-3c0d-5b85-87f8-4a2364ded62c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186519432}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The average height of a player in a particular professional basketball league is $78$ inches. Then we have $X∼N(78,{\\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find $P(X>75).$ But first, we need to find the standard deviation $\\sigma .$ \n\nWe know that $P(X>82)=0.15.$ First, we convert this to a cumulative probability:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X\\le 82) & =1-P(X>82) \\\\  & =1-0.15 \\\\  & =0.85\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring. We get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X\\le 82) & =0.85 \\\\ P(Z\\le \\frac{82-78}{\\sigma }) & =0.85 \\\\ Φ(\\frac{4}{\\sigma }) & =0.85 \\\\ \\frac{4}{\\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.85)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFrom the table, \n\n$$\n{Φ}^{-1}(0.85)≈1.0364.\n$$\n\nTherefore, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{4}{\\sigma } & =1.0364 \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sigma } & =0.2591 \\\\ \\sigma  & =\\frac{1}{0.2591} \\\\  & ≈3.85951.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we can solve for $P(X>75)$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X>75) & =1-P(X\\le 75) \\\\  & =1-P(Z\\le \\frac{75-78}{3.85951}) \\\\  & ≈1-P(Z\\le -0.78) \\\\  & =1-Φ(-0.78) \\\\  & =1-0.2177 \\\\  & =0.7823 \\\\  & ≈78.2%\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, approximately $78.2%$ of players are over $75$ inch tall."} {:db/id 17592186083342 :question/worked-solution "Applying the average value formula, we find that the average value of the function is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{\\text{avg}} & =\\frac{1}{b-a}{\\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\pi -0}{\\int }_{0}^{\\pi }{cos}^{8}⁡x\\operatorname{sin}⁡x\\,\\text{d}x.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe calculate this integral using a substitution $u=\\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Differentiating, we have \n\n$$\n\\frac{\\text{d}u}{\\text{d}x}=-\\operatorname{sin}⁡x\\,⟹\\,\\text{d}u=-\\operatorname{sin}⁡x\\,\\text{d}x.\n$$\n\nCalculating the limits for $u$ gives\n\n| $x$ | $0$ | $\\pi $ |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| $u$ | $1$ | $-1$ |\n\nWe now substitute and evaluate, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{\\text{avg}} & =\\frac{1}{\\pi }{\\int }_{0}^{\\pi }{cos}^{8}⁡x\\operatorname{sin}⁡x\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =-\\frac{1}{\\pi }{\\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{8}\\,\\text{d}u \\\\  & =-{\\frac{1}{\\pi }(\\frac{{u}^{9}}{9})|}_{1}^{-1} \\\\  & =-\\frac{1}{9\\pi }[(-1)^{9}-{1}^{9}] \\\\  & =-\\frac{1}{9\\pi }(-2) \\\\  & =\\frac{2}{9\\pi }.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186304792 :question/id #uuid "2e55b4cb-6c56-5cac-893d-482f84ce6bec" "![](images/df/dfa665cf99f35e5cd2edef04b3f334f0054bbce7fc9b66c519d59d30e77ba2a1.png)\n\nThe graph of the function $f(x),$ which is defined on $[0,10],$ is shown above. It consists of line segments.\n\nFind the average value ${f}_{\\text{avg}}$ of $f(x)$ on $[1,9].$ Do not round the answer.\n\n${f}_{\\text{avg}}=$\n{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The average value of a function on a given interval $[a,b]$ is \n\n$$\n{f}_{\\text{avg}}=\\frac{1}{b-a}{\\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x.\n$$\n\nUsing the additive property of the definite integral, we write\n\n$$\n{\\int }_{1}^{9}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x={{{\\int }_{1}^{5}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{1}}+{{{\\int }_{5}^{9}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{2}}.\n$$\n\nThe 1st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\\in [1,5].$ The corresponding region is a triangle, so we find the area using the formula:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\\frac{1}{2}bh \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}\\cdot 4\\cdot 2 \\\\  & =4.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have \n\n$$\n{\\int }_{1}^{5}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x=-{A}_{1}=-4.\n$$\n\nThe 2nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\\in [5,9].$ The corresponding region is a triangle, so we find the area using the formula:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\\frac{1}{2}bh \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}\\cdot 4\\cdot 3 \\\\  & =6.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we have \n\n$$\n{\\int }_{5}^{9}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x={A}_{2}=6.\n$$\n\nSo, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{1}^{9}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x & =-{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} \\\\  & =-4+6 \\\\  & =2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, using the formula for the average value, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{\\text{avg}} & =\\frac{1}{b-a}{\\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{9-1}\\cdot 2 \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186317533 For which value of $P$ is the number of people who heard the rumor growing at the fastest possible rate?" :question/worked-solution "A logistic growth equation has the form\n\n$$\n{P}^{′}=kP(a-P),\n$$\n\nwhere $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>P$ is the carrying capacity.\n\nFor a logistic growth model, the fastest rate of growth occurs when $P=\\frac{1}{2}a.$\n\n![](images/9d/9d8f5340bba4d3c407e43f2bc64a4aa2ea986be89b8024baaa4e8ae65e96e5d5.png)\n\nFirst, let's rewrite the right-hand side of the given equation so that it matches the form above:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{dP}{dt} & =12P-0.000\\,2{P}^{2} \\\\  & =0.000\\,02P(60\\,000-P)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFrom here, we see that $a=60\\,000.$ Hence, the carrying capacity is $60\\,000,$ and $P$ grows at its fastest possible rate when \n\n$$\nP=\\frac{1}{2}a=\\frac{1}{2}\\cdot 60\\,000=30\\,000.\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186516842 :question/id #uuid "b8a8e489-11e9-52ae-86cf-436bdb177f60" :question/math-academy-id "q-353486" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4083cc71-3bcb-5360-9978-e4ce2aebb68e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2500" :db/id 17592186516239}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186516239} :answer-field/id #uuid "aa8b8268-0d26-5cf4-8d60-0789f0a8afa9" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186516730}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The population $P(t)$ of elk in a protected national park follows the logistic growth model\n\n$$\n\\frac{dP}{dt}=5P-0.001{P}^{2},\\,P(0)=200,\n$$\n\nwhere $t$ is the time, measured in years. :tutorial/content "We know that we can use the method of integration by parts to evaluate $\\displaystyle \\int xe^{4x} \\textrm{d}x.$ Now, suppose that we want to calculate $\\displaystyle \\int x^2e^{4x} \\textrm{d}x.$ Can we use integration by parts in this case?\n\nLet's  try. We define $u$ and $v$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}u={x}^{2} & \\,⟹\\,\\frac{\\text{d}u}{\\text{d}x}=2x\\,, \\\\ \\frac{\\text{d}v}{\\text{d}x}={e}^{4x} & \\,⟹\\,v=\\int {e}^{4x}\\text{d}x=\\frac{1}{4}\\,{e}^{4x}\\,.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo the formula for integration by parts leads to\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int {x}^{2}{e}^{4x}\\text{d}x & =\\int u\\frac{\\text{d}v}{\\text{d}x}\\text{d}x \\\\  & =uv-\\int v\\frac{\\text{d}u}{\\text{d}x}\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={x}^{2}(\\frac{1}{4}\\,{e}^{4x})-\\int (\\frac{1}{4}\\,{e}^{4x})2x\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}\\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\\frac{1}{2}\\int x{e}^{4x}\\text{d}x.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe still don't have an answer, but the problem is reduced to the calculation of a simpler integral  $\\displaystyle \\int xe^{4x} \\textrm{d}x.$ To compute this integral, we just need to apply the integration by parts formula again. For this second integral, we take\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}u=x & \\,⟹\\,\\frac{\\text{d}u}{\\text{d}x}=1\\,, \\\\ \\frac{\\text{d}v}{\\text{d}x}={e}^{4x} & \\,⟹\\,v=\\int {e}^{4x}\\text{d}x=\\frac{1}{4}\\,{e}^{4x}\\,.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, integration by parts gives\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int x{e}^{4x}\\text{d}x & =\\int u\\frac{\\text{d}v}{\\text{d}x}\\text{d}x \\\\  & =uv-\\int v\\frac{\\text{d}u}{\\text{d}x}\\text{d}x \\\\  & =x(\\frac{1}{4}\\,{e}^{4x})-\\int (\\frac{1}{4}\\,{e}^{4x})\\cdot 1\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}\\,x{e}^{4x}-\\frac{1}{4}(\\frac{1}{4}\\,{e}^{4x})+{C}_{1} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}\\,x{e}^{4x}-\\frac{1}{16}\\,{e}^{4x}+{C}_{1}\\,,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $C_1$ is a constant of integration.\nSo we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int {x}^{2}{e}^{4x}\\text{d}x & =\\frac{1}{4}\\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\\frac{1}{2}\\int x{e}^{4x}\\text{d}x \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}\\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\\frac{1}{2}(\\frac{1}{4}\\,x{e}^{4x}-\\frac{1}{16}\\,{e}^{4x}+{C}_{1}) \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}\\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\\frac{1}{8}\\,x{e}^{4x}+\\frac{1}{32}\\,{e}^{4x}-\\frac{{C}_{1}}{2} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{32}\\,{e}^{4x}(8{x}^{2}-4x+1)+C\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $C = 17592186070031 :tutorial/content "We know that we can use the method of integration by parts to evaluate $\\displaystyle \\int xe^{4x} \\textrm{d}x.$ Now, suppose that we want to calculate $\\displaystyle \\int x^2e^{4x} \\textrm{d}x.$ Can we use integration by parts in this case?\n\nLet's  try. We define $u$ and $v$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}u={x}^{2} & \\,⟹\\,\\frac{\\text{d}u}{\\text{d}x}=2x\\,, \\\\ \\frac{\\text{d}v}{\\text{d}x}={e}^{4x} & \\,⟹\\,v=\\int {e}^{4x}\\text{d}x=\\frac{1}{4}\\,{e}^{4x}\\,.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo the formula for integration by parts leads to\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int {x}^{2}{e}^{4x}\\text{d}x & =\\int u\\frac{\\text{d}v}{\\text{d}x}\\text{d}x \\\\  & =uv-\\int v\\frac{\\text{d}u}{\\text{d}x}\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={x}^{2}(\\frac{1}{4}\\,{e}^{4x})-\\int (\\frac{1}{4}\\,{e}^{4x})2x\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}\\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\\frac{1}{2}\\int x{e}^{4x}\\text{d}x.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe still don't have an answer, but the problem is reduced to the calculation of a simpler integral  $\\displaystyle \\int xe^{4x} \\textrm{d}x.$ To compute this integral, we just need to apply the integration by parts formula again. For this second integral, we take\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}u=x & \\,⟹\\,\\frac{\\text{d}u}{\\text{d}x}=1\\,, \\\\ \\frac{\\text{d}v}{\\text{d}x}={e}^{4x} & \\,⟹\\,v=\\int {e}^{4x}\\text{d}x=\\frac{1}{4}\\,{e}^{4x}\\,.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, integration by parts gives\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int x{e}^{4x}\\text{d}x & =\\int u\\frac{\\text{d}v}{\\text{d}x}\\text{d}x \\\\  & =uv-\\int v\\frac{\\text{d}u}{\\text{d}x}\\text{d}x \\\\  & =x(\\frac{1}{4}\\,{e}^{4x})-\\int (\\frac{1}{4}\\,{e}^{4x})\\cdot 1\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}\\,x{e}^{4x}-\\frac{1}{4}(\\frac{1}{4}\\,{e}^{4x})+{C}_{1} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}\\,x{e}^{4x}-\\frac{1}{16}\\,{e}^{4x}+{C}_{1}\\,,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $C_1$ is a constant of integration.\nSo we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int {x}^{2}{e}^{4x}\\text{d}x & =\\frac{1}{4}\\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\\frac{1}{2}\\int x{e}^{4x}\\text{d}x \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}\\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\\frac{1}{2}(\\frac{1}{4}\\,x{e}^{4x}-\\frac{1}{16}\\,{e}^{4x}+{C}_{1}) \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}\\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\\frac{1}{8}\\,x{e}^{4x}+\\frac{1}{32}\\,{e}^{4x}-\\frac{{C}_{1}}{2} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{32}\\,{e}^{4x}(8{x}^{2}-4x+1)+C\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $C = -\\dfrac{C_1}{2}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "35a2eb7b-569b-5939-bcc0-2261596617e8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 901 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "944ebf60-fe41-58ac-91a8-63c93b565add" :step/math-academy-id 655420 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069906}} {:db/id 17592186070031 :tutorial/content "We know that we can use the method of integration by parts to evaluate $\\displaystyle \\int xe^{4x} \\textrm{d}x.$ Now, suppose that we want to calculate $\\displaystyle \\int x^2e^{4x} \\textrm{d}x.$ Can we use integration by parts in this case?\n\nLet's  try. 3{x}^{2}\\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\\,\\text{d}x & =\\int u\\frac{\\text{d}v}{\\text{d}x}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =uv-\\int v\\frac{\\text{d}u}{\\text{d}x}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =(3{x}^{2})(\\operatorname{sin}⁡(x))-\\int (\\operatorname{sin}⁡(x))(6x)\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =3{x}^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)-6\\int x\\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\\,\\text{d}x.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nAgain, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\\int x\\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\\,\\text{d}x.$ We take\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}u=x & \\,⟹\\,\\frac{\\text{d}u}{\\text{d}x}=1\\,, \\\\ \\frac{\\text{d}v}{\\text{d}x}=\\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) & \\,⟹\\,v=\\int \\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\\text{d}x=-\\operatorname{cos}⁡(x).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nIn this case, the formula for integration by parts gives\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int x\\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\\,\\text{d}x & =\\int u\\frac{\\text{d}v}{\\text{d}x}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =uv-\\int v\\frac{\\text{d}u}{\\text{d}x}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =x(-\\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))-\\int (-\\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))\\cdot 1\\,dx \\\\  & =-x\\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+\\int \\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\\,dx \\\\  & =-x\\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+\\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+D,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $D$ is an integral constant. \n\nSo, we get that the indefinite integral is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int =3{x}^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)-6(-x\\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+\\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+D) \\\\  & =3{x}^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+6x\\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)-6\\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+C,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $C=-6D.$\n\nFinally, we can work out the definite integral:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{0}^{\\pi }3{x}^{2}\\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\\,\\text{d}x & ={[3{x}^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+6x\\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)-6\\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)]}_{0}^{\\pi } ))-(3(0)^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+6(0)\\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)-6\\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\\\  & =0+6\\pi (-1)-0-0 \\\\  & =-6\\pi \\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "![](images/df/dfa665cf99f35e5cd2edef04b3f334f0054bbce7fc9b66c519d59d30e77ba2a1.png)\n\nThe graph of the function $f(x),$ which is defined on $[0,10],$ is shown above. It consists of line segments.\n\nFind the average value ${f}_{\\text{avg}}$ of $f(x)$ on $[1,9].$ Do not round the answer.\n\n${f}_{\\text{avg}}=$\n{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The average value of a function on a given interval $[a,b]$ is \n\n$$\n{f}_{\\text{avg}}=\\frac{1}{b-a}{\\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x.\n$$\n\nUsing the additive property of the definite integral, we write\n\n$$\n{\\int }_{1}^{9}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x={{{\\int }_{1}^{5}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{1}}+{{{\\int }_{5}^{9}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{2}}.\n$$\n\nThe 1st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\\in [1,5].$ The corresponding region is a triangle, so we find the area using the formula:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\\frac{1}{2}bh \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}\\cdot 4\\cdot 2 \\\\  & =4.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have \n\n$$\n{\\int }_{1}^{5}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x=-{A}_{1}=-4.\n$$\n\nThe 2nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\\in [5,9].$ The corresponding region is a triangle, so we find the area using the formula:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\\frac{1}{2}bh \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}\\cdot 4\\cdot 3 \\\\  & =6.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we have \n\n$$\n{\\int }_{5}^{9}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x={A}_{2}=6.\n$$\n\nSo, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{1}^{9}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x & =-{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} \\\\  & =-4+6 \\\\  & =2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, using the formula for the average value, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{\\text{avg}} & =\\frac{1}{b-a}{\\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{9-1}\\cdot 2 \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid :step/math-academy-id 35103 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176797}} {:db/id 17592186176799 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177031 :tutorial/content "In general, the logistic growth boundary value problem for the function $y(t)$ is given by\n\n$$\ny' = ky(a-y), \\qquad y(0) = y_0,\n$$\n\nwhere $k > 0,$ and $0 < y < a.$\n\nA diagram showing a typical logistic growth curve is shown below.\n\n![](images/00/00478583a9bc76980b898db4f846f323511026c1c6ac7b79e3f047575a015305.png)\n\nNote the following:\n\n- In practical situations, we usually set $t > 0.$ If we relax this constraint, we have\n\n$$\n\\displaystyle\\lim_{t\\to-\\infty}{y(t)} = 0.\n$$\n\n \nThis behavior can be confirmed using an analysis similar to what we saw earlier.\n\n- The parameter $a$ is the **carrying capacity,** and is the limiting value of $y(t)$ for large $t.$ We can write\n\n$$\n\\displaystyle\\lim_{t\\to\\infty}{y(t)} = a.\n$$\n\n \nIf $y(t)$ represents how some population changes with time, the carrying capacity gives the maximum possible population.\n\n- We have assumed that $0 < y < a$ for all $t.$ Other cases are possible, though we do not consider those here." :tutorial/id #uuid "3f070df6-1d9d-5050-b509-d48d330c4709" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5714 :tutorial/title "Some Key Features of a Logistic Growth Curve"} :step/id #uuid "2b3e0981-7dcf-5a80-b4a4-1a180100a2d1" :step/math-academy-id 35104 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176798}} {:db/id 17592186176802 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177033 :tutorial/content "For some differential equations, it's possible to sketch the solution curves *without* calculating the general solution. Instead, we gather information about the solutions using the differential equation itself.\n\nAs an example, consider the following logistic growth equation: \n\n$$\ny' = 5y(10-y)\n$$\n\nIn practical applications, we're usually interested in the domain $t > 0,$ so we will stick to this constraint for the moment.\n\nThe equation is autonomous, so let's start by finding the equilibrium solutions. Setting up the equation $y'(t) = 0$ gives\n\n$$\n5y(10-y) = 0.\n$$\n\nSo, there are two equilibrium solutions, $y=0,$ and $y=10.$ Let's create a diagram and plot these two solutions.\n\n![](images/98/98d52420673e65eedf5679e57b9c562f8a8eeabde24d0d2ed4fff827a6447fc2.png)\n\nWe will now sketch a solution curve that lies between these two equilibrium solutions. \n\nNotice the following:\n\n- Since $0 < y < 10$ for all $t,$ we have that $5y(10-y)$ is positive for all $t.$\n\n- Therefore, $y'(t)$ is positive for all $t.$\n\n- Hence, $y(t)$ is increasing for all $t.$\n\nUsing this information, we can start to sketch a solution curve.\n\n![](images/ce/ce6f493f4c2830acf42e189ace04027f8452ec3df92d24b9d223f92848832996.png)\n\nNext, we note the following regarding the end-behavior of our solution:\n\n- The expression $5y(10-y)\\to 0$ as $y\\to10.$\n\n- Therefore, $y'\\to 0$ as $y\\to 10.$\n\nIn other words, the curve flattens as $y$ approaches $10.$ Adding this behavior to our diagram, we get a complete sketch of the solution curve.\n\n![](images/f3/f329f3cd49d61c3a1e2838397521cdd6d3bbefc7dadd09d1dd25b00767a0cd37.png)\n\nGathering information about the solutions to a differential equation without solving it is called **qualitative analysis.**" :tutorial/id #uuid "05ebc248-7295-5381-964a-30c7e3b638e5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5718 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "ad747121-27b0-5c58-8372-2eae12c1e5f1" :step/math-academy-id 35114 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176799}} {:db/id 17592186176803 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177034 :tutorial/content "Let's go back to the following logistic growth equation:\n\n$$\ny' = 5y(10-y), \\qquad y(0) = y_0.\n$$\n\nThe logistic growth curve for this problem is sketched below.\n\n![](images/0a/0a225fd04f81bd65e1bad3ff14097563d112a16e3847aac26cc86591533ea5d0.png)\n\nThe curve contains an inflection point, that is, a point where $y(t)$ is growing at its fastest possible rate. What information can we deduce about this point? \n\nTo find the inflection point, we solve $y''(t) = 0.$ First, we differentiate the differential equation using implicit differentiation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{y}^{″} & =(5y)^{′}\\cdot (10-y)+(5y)\\cdot (10-y)^{′} \\\\  & =5\\cdot (10-y)\\cdot {y}^{′}+(5y)\\cdot (-1)\\cdot {y}^{′} \\\\  & ={y}^{′}\\cdot (5\\cdot (10-y)+(5y)\\cdot (-1)) \\\\  & ={y}^{′}\\cdot (50-5y-5y) \\\\  & ={y}^{′}\\cdot (50-10y)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe now need to solve $y''(t) = 0,$ i.e.,\n\n$$\ny'\\cdot\\left(50-10y\\right) = 0.\n$$\n\nWe know that $y'$ is increasing for all $t,$ so $y'\\neq 0.$ Therefore, we must have\n\n$$\n50-10y = 0\\quad \\Rightarrow\\quad y = 5.\n$$\n\nLet's mark this on our diagram.\n\n![](images/75/75d0363483e1bda70decb171466fe9e506eb0da80d0e78ed893bb61551ae9d44.png)\n\nThe fact that the inflection point occurs when $y$ is precisely half the carrying capacity is *not* a coincidence. In fact, this is always the case. equations, it's possible to sketch the solution curves *without* calculating the general solution. Instead, we gather information about the solutions using the differential equation itself.\n\nAs an example, consider the following logistic growth equation: \n\n$$\ny' = 5y(10-y)\n$$\n\nIn practical applications, we're usually interested in the domain $t > 0,$ so we will stick to this constraint for the moment.\n\nThe equation is autonomous, so let's start by finding the equilibrium solutions. Setting up the equation $y'(t) = 0$ gives\n\n$$\n5y(10-y) = 0.\n$$\n\nSo, there are two equilibrium solutions, $y=0,$ and $y=10.$ Let's create a diagram and plot these two solutions.\n\n![](images/98/98d52420673e65eedf5679e57b9c562f8a8eeabde24d0d2ed4fff827a6447fc2.png)\n\nWe will now sketch a solution curve that lies between these two equilibrium solutions. \n\nNotice the following:\n\n- Since $0 < y < 10$ for all $t,$ we have that $5y(10-y)$ is positive for all $t.$\n\n- Therefore, $y'(t)$ is positive for all $t.$\n\n- Hence, $y(t)$ is increasing for all $t.$\n\nUsing this information, we can start to sketch a solution curve.\n\n![](images/ce/ce6f493f4c2830acf42e189ace04027f8452ec3df92d24b9d223f92848832996.png)\n\nNext, we note the following regarding the end-behavior of our solution:\n\n- The expression $5y(10-y)\\to 0$ as $y\\to10.$\n\n- Therefore, $y'\\to 0$ as $y\\to 10.$\n\nIn other words, the curve flattens as $y$ approaches $10.$ Adding this behavior to our diagram, we get a complete sketch of the solution curve.\n\n![](images/f3/f329f3cd49d61c3a1e2838397521cdd6d3bbefc7dadd09d1dd25b00767a0cd37.png)\n\nGathering information about the solutions to a differential equation without solving it is called **qualitative analysis.**" :tutorial/id #uuid "05ebc248-7295-5381-964a-30c7e3b638e5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5718 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186177034 :tutorial/content "Let's go back to the following logistic growth equation:\n\n$$\ny' = 5y(10-y), \\qquad y(0) = y_0.\n$$\n\nThe logistic growth curve for this problem is sketched below.\n\n![](images/0a/0a225fd04f81bd65e1bad3ff14097563d112a16e3847aac26cc86591533ea5d0.png)\n\nThe curve contains an inflection point, that is, a point where $y(t)$ is growing at its fastest possible rate. What information can we deduce about this point? \n\nTo find the inflection point, we solve $y''(t) = 0.$ First, we differentiate the differential equation using implicit differentiation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{y}^{″} & =(5y)^{′}\\cdot (10-y)+(5y)\\cdot (10-y)^{′} \\\\  & =5\\cdot (10-y)\\cdot {y}^{′}+(5y)\\cdot (-1)\\cdot {y}^{′} \\\\  & ={y}^{′}\\cdot (5\\cdot (10-y)+(5y)\\cdot (-1)) \\\\  & ={y}^{′}\\cdot (50-5y-5y) \\\\  & ={y}^{′}\\cdot (50-10y)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe now need to solve $y''(t) = 0,$ i.e.,\n\n$$\ny'\\cdot\\left(50-10y\\right) = 0.\n$$\n\nWe know that $y'$ is increasing for all $t,$ so $y'\\neq 0.$ Therefore, we must have\n\n$$\n50-10y = 0\\quad \\Rightarrow\\quad y = 5.\n$$\n\nLet's mark this on our diagram.\n\n![](images/75/75d0363483e1bda70decb171466fe9e506eb0da80d0e78ed893bb61551ae9d44.png)\n\nThe fact that the inflection point occurs when $y$ is precisely half the carrying capacity is *not* a coincidence. In fact, this is always the case. Then the probability density function $f(x)$ of $X$ is a unimodal, bell-shaped curve. Moreover, it is symmetrical about the mean, median, and mode, which all equal $\\mu$.  \n\n![](images/0c/0c8951446f52cea9db6c0a2b600fc53cb564c3d64ff0afab15c9756dc0c0f29b.png)\n\nWe can use the normal distribution to model a wide range of real-life situations because many real-world distributions are roughly bell-shaped and symmetrical around a mean value. \n\nPatients' blood pressures, people's weights, measurement errors, and IQ scores are just some of the real-world examples that can be modeled as a normal distribution. \n\nTo determine whether a given data is normal, the first thing to do is to check the shape of the distribution. For example, if a data set is roughly bell-shaped, then it *might* be normally distributed. \n\nIt should be noted that, in practice, statisticians will often need to perform several tests on the data to check for normality (these are called **normality tests**). We cannot rely only on a distribution's shape since other distributions are also bell-shaped. However, checking the shape is often a good starting point." :tutorial/id #uuid "9f150bce-c1b4-502c-bcb1-da067550b958" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4966 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "Suppose that $X\\sim N(\\mu, \\sigma^2)$ is normally distributed. Then the probability density function $f(x)$ of $X$ is a unimodal, bell-shaped curve. Moreover, it is symmetrical about the mean, median, and mode, which all equal $\\mu$.  \n\n![](images/0c/0c8951446f52cea9db6c0a2b600fc53cb564c3d64ff0afab15c9756dc0c0f29b.png)\n\nWe can use the normal distribution to model a wide range of real-life situations because many real-world distributions are roughly bell-shaped and symmetrical around a mean value. \n\nPatients' blood pressures, people's weights, measurement errors, and IQ scores are just some of the real-world examples that can be modeled as a normal distribution. \n\nTo determine whether a given data is normal, the first thing to do is to check the shape of the distribution. For example, if a data set is roughly bell-shaped, then it *might* be normally distributed. \n\nIt should be noted that, in practice, statisticians will often need to perform several tests on the data to check for normality (these are called **normality tests**). We cannot rely only on a distribution's shape since other distributions are also bell-shaped. However, checking the shape is often a good starting point." :tutorial/id #uuid "9f150bce-c1b4-502c-bcb1-da067550b958" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4966 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "932c4862-d05e-5b90-85c8-d54c3a5130a8" :step/math-academy-id 30927 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084297}} {:db/id 17592186084482 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $X\\sim N(\\mu, \\sigma^2)$ is normally distributed. "The average duration (in minutes) of the videos produced by a popular content creator is $35\\,\\text{min}.$ Also, $5%$ of their videos have a duration of less than $20$ minutes. Assuming that the duration of the videos is normally distributed, find the standard deviation of the duration times, rounded to the near minute.\n\n*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*\n\n| $p$ | $\\,0.01\\,$ | $\\,0.03\\,$ | $\\,0.05\\,$ | $\\,0.10\\,$ | $\\,0.15\\,$ | $\\,0.20\\,$ | $\\,0.25\\,$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\\,-2.3263\\,$ | $\\,-1.8808\\,$ | $\\,-1.6449\\,$ | $\\,-1.2816\\,$ | $\\,-1.0364\\,$ | $\\,-0.8416\\,$ | $\\,-0.6745\\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the duration of a video. Then we have $X∼N(35,{\\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find the standard deviation $\\sigma .$ \n\nWe know that $P(X\\le 20)=0.05.$ Converting $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X\\le 20) & =0.05 \\\\ P(Z\\le \\frac{20-35}{\\sigma }) & =0.05 \\\\ Φ(-\\frac{15}{\\sigma }) & =0.05 \\\\ -\\frac{15}{\\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.05).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFrom the table, \n\n$$\n{Φ}^{-1}(0.05)=-1.6449.\n$$\n\nFinally then, \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}-\\frac{15}{\\sigma } & =-1.6449 \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sigma } & =0.1097 \\\\ \\sigma  & ≈9\\,\\text{minutes}.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "08ba30f8-c04b-524e-80f7-0ec881803edf" :step/next {:db/id 17592186415887}} {:db/id 17592186415884 :step/content {:db/id 17592186302161 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8ce3962b-9372-53e8-94dd-19aae1e9b687" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.51" :db/id 17592186300674}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186300674} :answer-field/id #uuid "752c40b7-22f4-5848-b34a-2e00b4e7dbd7" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186301589}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "6829b460-7921-509d-b187-5e5360672369" :question/math-academy-id "q-324314" :question/problem "The lengths of metal rods produced by a certain factory are normally distributed with a mean of $100$ centimeters and a standard deviation of $4$ centimeters. What is the probability that a randomly selected rod is longer or equal to $96.8\\,cm$ but shorter than $102.4\\,cm?$ **Round your answer to two decimal places**.\n\n*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *\n\n| | $z$ | $\\,0.00\\,$ | $\\,0.01\\,$ | $\\,0.02\\,$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| $\\,-1.0\\,$ | $\\,0.1587\\,$ | $\\,0.1562\\,$ | $\\,0.1539\\,$ |\n| $\\,-0.9\\,$ | $\\,0.1841\\,$ | $\\,0.1814\\,$ | $\\,0.1788\\,$ |\n| $\\,-0.8\\,$ | $\\,0.2119\\,$ | $\\,0.2090\\,$ | $\\,0.2061\\,$ | |  | | $z$ | $\\,0.00\\,$ | $\\,0.01\\,$ | $\\,0.02\\,$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| $\\,0.4\\,$ | $\\,0.6554\\,$ | $\\,0.6591\\,$ | $\\,0.6628\\,$ |\n| $\\,0.5\\,$ | $\\,0.6915\\,$ | $\\,0.6944\\,$ | $\\,0.6985\\,$ |\n| $\\,0.6\\,$ | $\\,0.7257\\,$ | $\\,0.7291\\,$ | $\\,0.7324\\,$ | |  |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| $z$ | $\\,0.00\\,$ | $\\,0.01\\,$ | $\\,0.02\\,$ |\n| $\\,-1.0\\,$ | $\\,0.1587\\,$ | $\\,0.1562\\,$ | $\\,0.1539\\,$ |\n| $\\,-0.9\\,$ | $\\,0.1841\\,$ | $\\,0.1814\\,$ | $\\,0.1788\\,$ |\n| $\\,-0.8\\,$ | $\\,0.2119\\,$ | $\\,0.2090\\,$ | $\\,0.2061\\,$ |\n| $z$ | $\\,0.00\\,$ | $\\,0.01\\,$ | $\\,0.02\\,$ |\n| $\\,0.4\\,$ | $\\,0.6554\\,$ | $\\,0.6591\\,$ | $\\,0.6628\\,$ |\n| $\\,0.5\\,$ | $\\,0.6915\\,$ | $\\,0.6944\\,$ | $\\,0.6985\\,$ |\n| $\\,0.6\\,$ | $\\,0.7257\\,$ | $\\,0.7291\\,$ | $\\,0.7324\\,$ |\n\nThe probability that a randomly selected rod is longer or equal to $96.8\\,cm$ but shorter than $102.4\\,cm$ is approximately\n{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the rod length (in centimeters). Then we have $X∼N(100,{4}^{2}).$\n\nWe want to find $P(96.8\\le X<102.4).$ First, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(96.8\\le X<102.4) & =P(\\frac{96.8-100}{4}\\le Z<\\frac{102.4-100}{4}) \\\\  & =P(-0.80\\le Z<0.60)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we express the required probability in terms of $Φ(z):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(-0.80\\le Z<0.60) & =P(Z<0.60)-P(Z<-0.80) \\\\  & =P(Z\\le 0.60)-P(Z\\le -0.80) \\\\  & =Φ(0.60)-Φ(-0.80)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFrom the $z$-table, we see that\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Φ(0.60) & =0.7257 \\\\ Φ(-0.80) & =0.2119.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(-0.80<Z<0.60) & =Φ(0.60)-Φ(-0.80) \\\\  & =0.7257-0.2119 \\\\  & =0.5138 \\\\  & ≈0.51\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the probability that a randomly selected rod is longer or equal to $96.8\\,cm$ but shorter than $102.4\\,cm$ is approximately $0.51.$"} :step/id #uuid "13582afe-72fb-5625-8464-5f459b09da11" :step/next =-1.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nHowever, when we plug this result into the original equation, we get a false statement:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\sqrt{3-(-1)} & \\overset{?}{=}-2 \\\\ \\sqrt{4} & \\overset{?}{=}-2 \\\\ 2 & \\ne -2\\,\\,\\times \\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe value $x=-1$ does *not* satisfy the original equation, so we *cannot* accept it as a solution.\n\nTherefore, the equation solve:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{(\\sqrt{2x-1})}^{2} & ={(x)}^{2} \\\\ 2x-1 & ={x}^{2} \\\\ {x}^{2}-2x+1 & =0 \\\\ (x-1)^{2} & =0 \\\\ x & =1\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nRemember that in square root equations, we should always check the obtained value(s) to ensure that they are actually solutions of the original equation.\n\nHere, we check that the obtained value $x=1$ is actually a solution of the original equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\sqrt{2(1)-1} & \\overset{?}{=}(1) \\\\ \\sqrt{1} & \\overset{?}{=1} \\\\ 1 & =1\\,✓\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the equation $\\sqrt{2x-1}=x$ has the solution derivatives test is inconclusive.\n\nEvaluating the second derivative at $(1,1),$ we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,1)=\\begin{bmatrix}e & 0 \\\\ 0 & A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.\n\nThe second partial derivative test states that if $a\\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:\n\n- If $H(a)>0,$ then:\n\n- if $\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$\n\n- if $\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$\n\n- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$\n\n- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.\n\nFirst, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \\frac{∂f}{∂y}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1) & \\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1)\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2(x+y+1) & 2(x+3y+5)\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:\n\n$$\n\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}x+y+1 &=0 \\\\ x+3y+5 &=0.\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nSubtracting the first equation from the second one, we get\n\n$$\n2y+4=0\\,⟹\\,y=-2.\n$$\n\nThen, substituting this into the first equation, we obtain\n\n$$\nx+(-2)+1=0\\,⟹\\,x=1.\n$$\n\nHence, $(1,-2)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$\n\nTo classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.\n\nFirst, we compute the second partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+y+1))=2\\, & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+3y+5))=2 \\\\ \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+y+1))=2\\, & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+3y+5))=6\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, the second derivative  is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\\\ \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\\\ 2 & 6\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nEvaluating the second derivative at $(1,-2),$ we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-2)=[\\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\\\ 2 & 6\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nComputing the determinant $H(1,-2),$ we get\n\n$$\nH(1,-2)=det({f}^{″}(1,-2))=2\\cdot 6-{2}^{2}=8>0.\n$$\n\nFinally, notice that \n\n$$\n\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(1,-2)=({f}^{″}(1,-2))_{11}=2>0.\n$$\n\nTherefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(1,-2).$"} {:db/id 17592186125084 :question/id #uuid "e71f4d1b-7ab2-518d-aa98-4d69ed0f6542" :question/math-academy-id "q-37592" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices \\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}-2x & =0 \\\\ {x}^{4}-8x & =0 \\\\ x({x}^{3}-8) & =0 \\\\ x & =0,2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nBack-substituting these values into $y=\\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2},$ we stationary points and use it to categorize them:\n\n- Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,0),$ we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,0)=[\\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\\\ -6 & 0\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nComputing the determinant $H(0,0),$ we get\n\n$$\nH(0,0)=det({f}^{″}(0,0))=0\\cdot 0-(-6)^{2}=-36<0.\n$$\n\nTherefore, $f(0,0)$ is a saddle point.\n\n- $H(2,2),$ we get\n\n$$\nH(2,2)=det({f}^{″}(2,2))=12\\cdot 12-(-6)^{2}=108>0.\n$$\n\nFinally, since $H(2,2)>0$ and $\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(2,2)=({f}^{″}(2,2))_{11}=12>0,$ the function $f$ has a get\n\n$$\n4-4y-4x=0\\,⟹\\,x=1-y.\n$$\n\nThen, substituting this into the second equation, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}4-4(1-y)+{y}^{2} & =0 \\\\ {y}^{2}+4y & =0 \\\\ y(y+4) & =0 \\\\ y & 2y\\end{bmatrix}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:\n\n- Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,0),$ we :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.\n\nThe second partial derivative test states that if $a\\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:\n\n- If $H(a)>0,$ then:\n\n- if $\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$\n\n- if $\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$\n\n- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$\n\n- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.\n\nFirst, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=\\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}-y & 8{y}^{2}-x\\end{bmatrix},$ we must have\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂f}{∂x}={x}^{2}-y,\\,\\frac{∂f}{∂y}=8{y}^{2}-x.\n$$\n\nThe first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:\n\n$$\n\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-y &=0 \\\\ 8{y}^{2}-x &=0\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nSolving the first equation for $y,$ we get\n\n$$\n{x}^{2}-y=0\\,⟹\\,y={x}^{2}.\n$$\n\nThen, substituting this into the second equation, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}8{({x}^{2})}^{2}-x & =0 \\\\ 8{x}^{4}-x & =0 \\\\ x(8{x}^{3}-1) & =0 \\\\ x & =0,\\frac{1}{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nBack-substituting these values into $y={x}^{2},$ we obtain\n\n$$\nx=0\\,\\,\\,\\,⟹\\,y={0}^{2}=0,\\,\\,x=\\frac{1}{2}\\,⟹\\,y={(\\frac{1}{2})}^{2}=\\frac{1}{4}.\n$$\n\nHence, $(0,0)$ and $(\\frac{1}{2},\\frac{1}{4})$ are stationary points of $f(x,y).$\n\nTo classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test.\n\nFirst, we compute the second partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-y)=2x\\, & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{y}^{2}-x)=-1 \\\\ \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-y)=-1\\, & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & get\n\n$$\nH(1,2)=det({f}^{″}(1,2))=0\\cdot 2-{4}^{2}=-16<0.\n$$\n\nTherefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(1,2).$\n\nIn conclusion, :topic/math-academy-id 1944} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125649 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125889 :tutorial/content "The **critical points** of a function $f(\\mathbf x)$ are the points $\\mathbf x = \\mathbf a$ in the domain of $f$ such that $\\boldsymbol f'(\\mathbf a) =\\mathbf 0^T$ or $\\boldsymbol f'(\\mathbf a)$ does not exist. A critical point such that $\\boldsymbol f'(\\mathbf a) = \\mathbf 0^T$ is called a **stationary point**.\n\nFor example, consider the function $f(x,y) = x^2 - 2x + y^2+6y.$ The domain of $f$ is $\\mathbb{R}^2,$ and the first partial derivatives of $f$ are\n\n$$\n\\dfrac {\\partial f}{\\partial x} = 2x-2,\n\\qquad\n\\dfrac {\\partial f}{\\partial y} = 2y+6.\n$$\n\nSo, the first derivative of $f$ is\n![](images/9e/9ea3f2d1dd0994be64602aeaffcf5d8424f52daa03844e21e65469f779d9b009.svg)\n\nTo find the critical points, we need to find the points $(x,y) \\in \\mathbb{R}^2$ such that ![](images/23/23faa4c01362cad11c2ab6ad19045ca44a09460da1c719c8212480f27f21c5b1.svg) or $\\boldsymbol f'(x,y)$ does not exist:\n\n- Setting $\\boldsymbol f'(x,y) = \\mathbf{0}^T,$ we obtain the following system:\n\n$$\n\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}2x-2 &=0 \\\\ 2y+6 &=0\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nThis system has the solution $x=1$ and $y=-3.$ Consequently, $(1,-3)$ is a critical point of $f.$\n\n- $\\boldsymbol f'(x,y)$ exists everywhere, so there are no more critical points to be found.\n\nTherefore, the only critical point of $f$ is $(1,-3).$" :tutorial/id #uuid :tutorial/content "Recall that, for functions of two variables $f(x,y)$, there are typically three possible types of critical points that can occur:\n\n- Local minimum points. For example, the elliptic paraboloid $z = f(x,y) = x^2+y^2$ has a minimum point at $(0,0),$ as shown below.\n\n![](images/14/14e8d23a4bc649257c2f7351e0d2c1d62e39a8cd8eed1467e65853ee121b836e.png)\n\n- Local maximum points. For example, the elliptic paraboloid $z = f(x,y) = -x^2-y^2$ has a maximum point at $(0,0),$ as shown below.\n\n![](images/00/008803f43cb2161624f8ef295c70a125b8be64d93184928bd2176a6debaa9f85.png)\n\n- Saddle points. For example, the hyperbolic paraboloid $z = f(x,y) = y^2-x^2$ has a saddle point at $(0,0),$ as shown below.\n\n![](images/12/1214b413073ad87a302fb1297cef47208a922e368d680a9f69ec8fb18d9ca8a0.png)\n\nLocal maximum and local minimum points are analogous to what you would have seen in single-variable calculus. \n\nA saddle point occurs when the slopes are zero in all directions, yet it is not a local maximum or minimum. The hyperbolic paraboloid shown above reaches a local maximum at $(0,0)$ along the $xz$-plane, yet this is a local minimum along the $yz$-plane." :tutorial/id #uuid "fe3c5f00-f720-5573-a01f-c37f0a3e447f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7877 :tutorial/title "Classifying Stationary Points"} :step/id #uuid "c5093fcf-6163-5240-9022-125813bd45bf" :step/math-academy-id 45418 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125652}} {:db/id 17592186125652 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125891 :tutorial/content "The **second partial derivatives test** helps to determine whether a stationary point of a function of two variables gives rise to a local maximum, a local minimum, or a saddle point.\n\nSuppose that $\\mathbf x = \\mathbf{a}$ is a critical point of $f(\\mathbf x),$ and let $H(\\mathbf{a})$ denote the determinant of $\\boldsymbol f''(x,y)$ evaluated at $\\mathbf{a}$ (recall that $H(\\mathbf a)$ is called the *Hessian determinant* of $f$ at $\\mathbf a$).\n\nThe second partial derivative test states the following:\n\n- If $H(\\mathbf{a}) > 0,$ then:\n\n- if $\\dfrac{\\partial^2 f}{\\partial x^2}(\\mathbf{a}) < 0,$  then $f$ has a local maximum at $\\mathbf{a},$ and\n\n- if $\\dfrac{\\partial^2 f}{\\partial x^2}(\\mathbf{a}) > 0,$  then $f$ has a local minimum at $\\mathbf{a}.$\n\n- If $H(\\mathbf{a}) < 0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $\\mathbf{a}.$\n\n- If $H(\\mathbf{a}) = 0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive, and we need to classify the point using some other method.\n\nAs an example, consider the function $f (x, y) = 3 + 2x^2 - x y + y^2.$ Let's find the critical points of this function and then classify them using the second partial derivatives test.\n\nWe start by computing the partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\partial f}{\\partial x} = 4x -y, \\qquad \\dfrac{\\partial f}{\\partial y} = 2y -x\n$$\n\nThe first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $\\boldsymbol f'(x,y) = \\mathbf{0}^T,$ we obtain the following system:\n\n$$\n\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}4x-y &=0 \\\\ 2y-x &=0,\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nThe solution to this system is $x=0, y=0.$ Hence, $(0,0)$ is the only stationary point.  \n\nTo classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.\n\nFirst, we compute the second partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x-y)=4 \\\\ \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y-x)=2 \\\\ \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y-x)=-1\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, the second derivative is \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\\\ \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\\\ -1 & 2\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:\n\n- Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,0),$ we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,0)=[\\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\\\ -1 & 2\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nComputing the determinant $H(0,0),$ we get\n\n$$\nH(0,0) = \\det(\\boldsymbol f''(0,0)) = 4 \\cdot 2 - (-1)^2 = 7 > 0.\n$$\n\nFinally, since $H(0,0) > 0$ and $\\dfrac{\\partial^2 f}{\\partial x^2}(0,0) = (\\boldsymbol f''(0,0))_{11}= 4 >0,$ the function $f$ has a local minimum at $(0,0).$\n\nIn conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(0,0).$" 17592186125895 :tutorial/content "Suppose $\\mathbf{a} \\in \\mathbb{R}^2$ is a stationary point of a function $f(\\mathbf x).$\n\nIn a previous lesson, we saw that if $H(\\mathbf{a}) = \\det(\\boldsymbol{f}''(\\mathbf{a})) \\neq 0$, then we can classify $\\mathbf{a}$ as follows:\n\n- if $\\boldsymbol{f}''(\\mathbf{a})$ is positive definite, then $\\mathbf{a}$ is a local minimum\n\n- if $\\boldsymbol{f}''(\\mathbf{a})$ is negative definite, then $\\mathbf{a}$ is a local maximum\n\n- if $\\boldsymbol{f}''(\\mathbf{a})$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $\\mathbf{a}$ is a saddle point\n\nThe second derivatives test follows from these facts. To see why, we first recall Sylvester's criterion:\n\nThe quadratic form $\\mathbf{x}^TA\\mathbf{x}$ (as well as the $2\\times 2$ matrix $A$) is\n\n- positive definite if and only if $\\Delta_1 > 0$ and $\\Delta_2 > 0,$ and\n\n- negative definite if and only if $\\Delta_1 < 0$ and $\\Delta_2 > 0,$\n\nwhere $\\Delta_1$ and $\\Delta_2$ are the first and second principle minors of $A,$ respectively.\n\nFirst, notice the following:\n\n- The first principal minor of $\\boldsymbol f''(\\mathbf a)$ is\n\n$$\n\\Delta_1 = (\\boldsymbol{f}''(\\mathbf{a}))_{11} = \\dfrac{\\partial^2 f}{\\partial x^2}.\n$$\n\n- The second principal minor of $\\boldsymbol f''(\\mathbf a)$ is the Hessian determinant\n\n$$\n\\Delta_2 = \\det(\\boldsymbol{f}''(\\mathbf{a})) = H(\\mathbf{a}).\n$$\n\nKnowing this, we can go through each case:\n\n- If $H(\\mathbf a) < 0,$ then $\\Delta_2 < 0.$ Hence, by Sylvester's criterion, the Hessian matrix $\\boldsymbol f''(\\mathbf{a})$ The hyperbolic paraboloid shown above reaches a local maximum at $(0,0)$ along the $xz$-plane, yet this is a local minimum along the $yz$-plane." :tutorial/id #uuid "fe3c5f00-f720-5573-a01f-c37f0a3e447f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7877 :tutorial/title "Classifying Stationary Points"} {:db/id 17592186125652 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125891 :tutorial/content "The **second partial derivatives test** helps to determine whether a stationary point of a function of two variables gives rise to a local maximum, a local minimum, or a saddle point.\n\nSuppose that $\\mathbf x = \\mathbf{a}$ is a critical point of $f(\\mathbf x),$ and let $H(\\mathbf{a})$ denote the determinant of $\\boldsymbol f''(x,y)$ evaluated at $\\mathbf{a}$ (recall that $H(\\mathbf a)$ is called the *Hessian determinant* of $f$ at $\\mathbf a$).\n\nThe second partial derivative test states the following:\n\n- If $H(\\mathbf{a}) > 0,$ then:\n\n- if $\\dfrac{\\partial^2 f}{\\partial x^2}(\\mathbf{a}) < 0,$  then $f$ has a local maximum at $\\mathbf{a},$ and\n\n- if $\\dfrac{\\partial^2 f}{\\partial x^2}(\\mathbf{a}) > 0,$  then $f$ has a local minimum at $\\mathbf{a}.$\n\n- If $H(\\mathbf{a}) < 0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $\\mathbf{a}.$\n\n- If $H(\\mathbf{a}) = 0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive, and we need to classify the point using some other method.\n\nAs an example, consider the function $f (x, y) = 3 + 2x^2 - x y + y^2.$ Let's find the critical points of this function and then classify them using the second partial derivatives test.\n\nWe start by computing the partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\partial f}{\\partial x} = 4x -y, \\qquad \\dfrac{\\partial f}{\\partial y} = 2y -x\n$$\n\nThe first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $\\boldsymbol f'(x,y) = \\mathbf{0}^T,$ we obtain the following system:\n\n$$\n\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}4x-y &=0 \\\\ 2y-x &=0,\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nThe solution to this system is $x=0, y=0.$ Hence, $(0,0)$ is the only stationary point.  \n\nTo classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.\n\nFirst, we compute the second partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x-y)=4 \\\\ \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y-x)=2 \\\\ \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y-x)=-1\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, the second derivative is \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\\\ \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\\\ -1 & 2\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:\n\n- Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,0),$ we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,0)=[\\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\\\ -1 & 2\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nComputing the determinant $H(0,0),$ we get\n\n$$\nH(0,0) = \\det(\\boldsymbol f''(0,0)) = 4 \\cdot 2 - (-1)^2 = 7 > 0.\n$$\n\nFinally, since $H(0,0) > 0$ and $\\dfrac{\\partial^2 f}{\\partial x^2}(0,0) = (\\boldsymbol f''(0,0))_{11}= 4 >0,$ the function $f$ has a local minimum at $(0,0).$\n\nIn conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(0,0).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8248e727-7421-5535-ba58-b5ed98f7ac38" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7878 :tutorial/title "The Second Partial Derivatives Test"} :step/id #uuid "f1821258-7802-571e-a84f-0738986e608c" :step/math-academy-id 45419 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125653}} {:db/id 17592186125891 :tutorial/content "The **second partial derivatives test** helps to determine whether a stationary point of a function of two variables gives rise to a local maximum, a local minimum, or a saddle point.\n\nSuppose that $\\mathbf x = \\mathbf{a}$ is a critical point of $f(\\mathbf x),$ and let $H(\\mathbf{a})$ denote the determinant of $\\boldsymbol f''(x,y)$ evaluated at $\\mathbf{a}$ (recall that $H(\\mathbf a)$ is called the *Hessian determinant* of $f$ at $\\mathbf a$).\n\nThe second partial derivative test states the following:\n\n- If $H(\\mathbf{a}) > 0,$ then:\n\n- if $\\dfrac{\\partial^2 f}{\\partial x^2}(\\mathbf{a}) < 0,$  then $f$ has a local maximum at $\\mathbf{a},$ and\n\n- if $\\dfrac{\\partial^2 f}{\\partial x^2}(\\mathbf{a}) > 0,$  then $f$ has a local minimum at $\\mathbf{a}.$\n\n- If $H(\\mathbf{a}) < 0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $\\mathbf{a}.$\n\n- If $H(\\mathbf{a}) = 0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive, and we need to classify the point using some other method.\n\nAs an example, consider the function $f (x, y) = 3 + 2x^2 - A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.\n\nThe second partial derivative test states that if $a\\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:\n\n- If $H(a)>0,$ then:\n\n- if $\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$\n\n- if $\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$\n\n- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$\n\n- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.\n\nFirst, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \\frac{∂f}{∂y}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1) & \\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1)\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2(x+y+1) & 2(x+3y+5)\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:\n\n$$\n\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}x+y+1 &=0 \\\\ x+3y+5 &=0.\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nSubtracting the first equation from the second one, we get\n\n$$\n2y+4=0\\,⟹\\,y=-2.\n$$\n\nThen, substituting this into the first equation, we obtain\n\n$$\nx+(-2)+1=0\\,⟹\\,x=1.\n$$\n\nHence, $(1,-2)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$\n\nTo classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.\n\nFirst, we compute the second partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+y+1))=2\\, & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+3y+5))=2 \\\\ \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+y+1))=2\\, & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+3y+5))=6\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, the second derivative  is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\\\ \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\\\ 2 & 6\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nEvaluating the second derivative at $(1,-2),$ we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-2)=[\\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\\\ 2 & 6\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nComputing the determinant $H(1,-2),$ we get\n\n$$\nH(1,-2)=det({f}^{″}(1,-2))=2\\cdot 6-{2}^{2}=8>0.\n$$\n\nFinally, notice that \n\n$$\n\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(1,-2)=({f}^{″}(1,-2))_{11}=2>0.\n$$\n\nTherefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.\n\nThe second partial derivative test states that if $a\\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:\n\n- If $H(a)>0,$ then:\n\n- if $\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$\n\n- if $\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$\n\n- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$\n\n- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.\n\nFirst, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6y & 3{y}^{2}-6x\\end{aligned}],$ we must have\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂f}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}-6y,\\,\\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{y}^{2}-6x.\n$$\n\nThe first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:\n\n$$\n\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6y &=0 \\\\ 3{y}^{2}-6x &=0.\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nSolving the first equation for $y,$ we get\n\n$$\n3{x}^{2}-6y=0\\,⟹\\,y=\\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}.\n$$\n\nThen, substituting this into the second equation, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}3{(\\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})}^{2}-6x & =0 \\\\ \\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}-2x & =0 \\\\ {x}^{4}-8x & =0 \\\\ x({x}^{3}-8) & =0 \\\\ x & =0,2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nBack-substituting these values into $y=\\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2},$ we obtain\n\n$$\nx=0\\,⟹\\,y=\\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}=0,\\,\\,x=2\\,⟹\\,y=\\frac{1}{2}(2)^{2}=2.\n$$\n\nHence, $(0,0)$ and $(2,2)$ are stationary points of $f(x,y).$\n\nTo classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test.\n\nFirst, we compute the second partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-6y)=6x\\, & =\\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{y}^{2}-6x)=6y\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, the second derivative is \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\\\ \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}6x & -6 \\\\ -6 & 6y\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:\n\n- Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,0),$ we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,0)=[\\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\\\ -6 & 0\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nComputing the determinant $H(0,0),$ we get\n\n$$\nH(0,0)=det({f}^{″}(0,0))=0\\cdot 0-(-6)^{2}=-36<0.\n$$\n\nTherefore, $f(0,0)$ is a saddle point.\n\n- A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.\n\nThe second partial derivative test states that if $a\\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:\n\n- If $H(a)>0,$ then:\n\n- if $\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$\n\n- if $\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$\n\n- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$\n\n- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.\n\nFirst, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \\frac{∂f}{∂y}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1) & \\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1)\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2(x+y+1) & 2(x+3y+5)\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:\n\n$$\n\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}x+y+1 &=0 \\\\ x+3y+5 &=0.\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nSubtracting the first equation from the second one, we get\n\n$$\n2y+4=0\\,⟹\\,y=-2.\n$$\n\nThen, substituting this into the first equation, we obtain\n\n$$\nx+(-2)+1=0\\,⟹\\,x=1.\n$$\n\nHence, $(1,-2)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$\n\nTo classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.\n\nFirst, we compute the second partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+y+1))=2\\, & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+3y+5))=2 \\\\ \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+y+1))=2\\, & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+3y+5))=6\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\\\ 2 & 6\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nEvaluating the second derivative at $(1,-2),$ we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-2)=[\\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\\\ 2 & 6\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nComputing the determinant $H(1,-2),$ we get\n\n$$\nH(1,-2)=det({f}^{″}(1,-2))=2\\cdot 6-{2}^{2}=8>0.\n$$\n\nFinally, notice that \n\n$$\n\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(1,-2)=({f}^{″}(1,-2))_{11}=2>0.\n$$\n\nTherefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:\n\n$$\n\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6y &=0 \\\\ 3{y}^{2}-6x &=0.\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nSolving the first equation for $y,$ $H(2,2),$ we get\n\n$$\nH(2,2)=det({f}^{″}(2,2))=12\\cdot 12-(-6)^{2}=108>0.\n$$\n\nFinally, since $H(2,2)>0$ and $\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(2,2)=({f}^{″}(2,2))_{11}=12>0,$ the function $f$ has a Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:\n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}-4x=0 \\\\ e-{e}^{y}=0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSolving the first equation for $x,$ we get\n\n$$\n-4x=0\\,⟹\\,x=0.\n$$\n\nSolving the second  equation for $y,$ we get\n\n$$\ne-{e}^{y}=0\\,⟹\\,y=1.\n$$\n\nHence, $(0,1)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$   \n\nTo classify this stationary obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,1)=[\\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\\\ 0 & -e\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nComputing the determinant $H(0,1),$ we get\n\n$$\nH(0,1)=det({f}^{″}(0,1))=(-4)\\cdot (-e)-{0}^{2}=4e>0.\n$$\n\nFinally, notice that \n\n$$\n\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(0,0)=({f}^{″}(0,1))_{11}=-4<0.\n$$\n\nTherefore, applying the second
