A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.\n\nThe second partial derivative test states that if $a\\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:\n\n- If $H(a)>0,$ then:\n\n- if $\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$\n\n- if $\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$\n\n- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$\n\n- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.\n\nFirst, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \\frac{∂f}{∂y}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1) & \\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1)\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2(x+y+1) & 2(x+3y+5)\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:\n\n$$\n\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}x+y+1 &=0 \\\\ x+3y+5 &=0.\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nSubtracting the first equation from the second one, we get\n\n$$\n2y+4=0\\,⟹\\,y=-2.\n$$\n\nThen, substituting this into the first equation, we obtain\n\n$$\nx+(-2)+1=0\\,⟹\\,x=1.\n$$\n\nHence, $(1,-2)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$\n\nTo classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.\n\nFirst, we compute the second partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+y+1))=2\\, & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+3y+5))=2 \\\\ \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+y+1))=2\\, & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+3y+5))=6\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, the second derivative  is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\\\ \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\\\ 2 & 6\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nEvaluating the second derivative at $(1,-2),$ we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-2)=[\\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\\\ 2 & 6\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nComputing the determinant $H(1,-2),$ we get\n\n$$\nH(1,-2)=det({f}^{″}(1,-2))=2\\cdot 6-{2}^{2}=8>0.\n$$\n\nFinally, notice that \n\n$$\n\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(1,-2)=({f}^{″}(1,-2))_{11}=2>0.\n$$\n\nTherefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a The point $(3,-3)$ is a local minimum of $f$" :question/worked-solution "The second partial derivative test states that if $a\\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:\n\n- If $H(a)>0,$ then:\n\n- if $\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$\n\n- if $\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$\n\n- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$\n\n- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.\n\nFirst, we notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\\begin{aligned}4x+2y-6 & 2x+2y\\end{aligned}],$ we must have\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4x+2y-6,\\,\\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2x+2y.\n$$\n\nNow, we compute the second partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x+2y-6)=4 \\\\ \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+2y)=2 \\\\ \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+2y)=2\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, the second derivative is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\\\ \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\\\ 2 & 2\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nEvaluating the second derivative at $(3,-3),$ we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(3,-3)=[\\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\\\ 2 & 2\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWith that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.\n\n- Statement I is true. Indeed, computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(3,-3),$ we get\n\n$$\nH(3,-3)=det({f}^{″}(3,-3))=4\\cdot 2-{2}^{2}=4>0.\n$$\n\n- Statement II is false. We have $\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(3,-3)=({f}^{″}(3,-3))_{11}=4>0.$\n\n- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $H(3,-3)>0$ and $\\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(3,-3)>0,$ the point $(3,-3)$ is a local minimum by the second partial derivative test.\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I and III traversed once in the counterclockwise direction." :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula\n\n$$\n{∮}_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r={\\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\\,\\text{d}t.\n$$\n\nFirst, we need to parameterize a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as \n\n$$\nr(t)=\\operatorname{cos}⁡t\\,i+\\operatorname{sin}⁡t\\,j,\\,0\\le t\\le 2\\pi .\n$$\n\nSo, along the curve $C,$ we have\n\n$$\nx=\\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\\,y=\\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\n$$\n\nAs a result,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\\,i-x\\,j \\\\  & =\\operatorname{sin}⁡t\\,i-\\operatorname{cos}⁡t\\,j.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nComputing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\\frac{\\text{d}x}{\\text{d}t}\\,i+\\frac{\\text{d}y}{\\text{d}t}\\,j \\\\  & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}t}(\\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}t}(\\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\\\  & =-\\operatorname{sin}⁡t\\,i+\\operatorname{cos}⁡t\\,j.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\\operatorname{sin}⁡t\\,i-\\operatorname{cos}⁡t\\,j)\\cdot (-\\operatorname{sin}⁡t\\,i+\\operatorname{cos}⁡t\\,j) \\\\  & =-{sin}^{2}⁡t-{cos}^{2}⁡t \\\\  & =-({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\\\  & =-1.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F(r)\\cdot \\text{d}r & ={\\int }_{0}^{2\\pi }F(r(t))\\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{2\\pi }(-1)\\,dt \\\\  & ={-t|}_{0}^{2\\pi } \\\\  & =-2\\pi \\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186180172 :question/id #uuid "e19e4fc2-d0da-5e51-a13e-b5b2b6e03a48" :question/math-academy-id "q-39341"} {:db/id 17592186259784 :question/id #uuid It can be parameterized as \n\n$$\nr(t)=4\\operatorname{cos}⁡t\\,i+4\\operatorname{sin}⁡t\\,j,\\,0\\le t\\le \\frac{\\pi }{2}.\n$$\n\nSo, along the curve $C,$ we have\n\n$$\nx=4\\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\\,y=4\\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\n$$\n\nAs a result,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =3\\,i+\\frac{1}{x}\\,j \\\\  & =3\\,i+\\frac{1}{4\\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\\,j.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nComputing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =-4\\operatorname{sin}⁡t\\,i+4\\operatorname{cos}⁡t\\,j.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(3\\,i+\\frac{1}{4\\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\\,j)\\cdot (-4\\operatorname{sin}⁡t\\,i+4\\operatorname{cos}⁡t\\,j) \\\\  & =3\\cdot (-4\\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\\frac{1}{4\\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\\cdot 4\\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\\\  & =-12\\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{C}F(r)\\cdot \\text{d}r & ={\\int }_{0}^{\\pi /2}F(r(t))\\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{\\pi /2}(-12\\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)\\,dt \\\\  & =[12\\operatorname{cos}⁡t+t]_{0}^{\\pi /2} \\\\  & =(0+\\frac{\\pi }{2})-(12+0) \\\\  & =\\frac{\\pi }{2}-12\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186345269 :question/id #uuid "b1cf0636-8c91-5e55-83eb-9e319cf28463" :question/math-academy-id "q-77034"} {:db/id 17592186387616 :question/id #uuid have\n\n$$\nx=t,\\,y=\\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}.\n$$\n\nAs a result, \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =t\\,i+\\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}\\,j.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nComputing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get \\\\  & =t\\cdot 1+\\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}\\cdot \\frac{t}{\\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}} \\\\  & =2t.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{C}F\\cdot ${f}_{X|Y}(x\\,|\\,y),$ let's first find the marginal distribution of $Y,$ corresponding to the column totals: \n\n| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ | $Y=8$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| $X=3$ | $\\frac{1}{4}$ | $\\frac{1}{8}$ | $\\frac{1}{4}$ |\n| $X=9$ | $\\frac{1}{8}$ | $\\frac{3}{16}$ | $\\frac{1}{16}$ |\n| ${f}_{Y}(y)$ | $\\frac{3}{8}$ | $\\frac{5}{16}$ | $\\frac{5}{16}$ |\n\nThe conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y$ is\n\n$$\n{f}_{X|Y}(x\\,|\\,y)=\\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, dividing each joint probability by the corresponding column total, we obtain the conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y:$\n\n| ${f}_{X|Y}(x\\,|\\,y)$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ | $Y=8$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| $X=3$ | $\\frac{2}{3}$ | $\\frac{2}{5}$ | :tutorial/content "Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables, where the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is given by $\\mu_{X|y}.$ In other words,\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[X\\,|\\,Y=y] = \\mu_{X|y}.\n$$\n\nThe **conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$** is defined as\n\n$$\n\\textrm{Var}[X\\,|\\,Y=y] = \\textrm{E}\\big[(X - \\mu_{X|y} \\big)^2 \\,|\\, Y=y].\n$$\n\nThis is similar to the definition of $\\textrm{Var}[X]$ in that it represents the average  (squared) distance of the random variable $X$ from the mean. The difference here is that the expected values are now dependent on the outcome of $Y.$\n\nSimilarly to the case of $\\textrm{Var}[X],$ this often isn't the easiest formula to use in practice. However, it can be shown that the definition of conditional variance is equivalent to\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\text{Var}[X\\,|\\,Y=y] & =\\text{E}[{X}^{2}\\,|\\,Y=y]-{\\mu }_{X|y}^{2} \\\\  & =[{\\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\\,|\\,y)]-{\\mu }_{X|y}^{2},\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $f_{X|Y}(x \\,|\\, y)$ is the conditional PMF of $X$ given $Y.$ Note that these formulas are analogous to those for $\\textrm{Var}[X].$\n\nFinally, we have an analogous definition for the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X=x\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\text{Var}[Y\\,|\\,X=x] & =\\text{E}[(Y-{\\mu }_{Y|x})^{2}\\,|\\,X=x] \\\\  & =\\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\\,|\\,X=x]-{\\mu }_{Y|x}^{2} \\\\  & =[{\\sum }_{y}{y}^{2}\\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\\,|\\,x)]-{\\mu }_{Y|x}^{2}\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies\n\n$$\nτ(Δx)=O\\,((Δx)^{p+1})\\,\\text{as}\\,Δx\\to 0.\n$$\n\nThe order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.\n\nIn other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$\n\nIn our case, the step size decreases from $0.08$ to $0.02.$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\nk=\\frac{0.08}{0.02}=4.\n$$\n\nAs a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately\n\n$$\n{k}^{p+1}={4}^{p+1}.\n$$\n\nOn the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.13$ to $0.002.$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\n\\frac{0.13}{0.002}=65.\n$$\n\nComparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{4}^{p+1} & ≈65 \\\\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{4}⁡(65) \\\\ p+1 & ≈3.011… \\\\ p & ≈2.011….\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is $2.$"} {:db/id 17592186221987 :question/id #uuid "36473f35-3093-5439-832b-c821da150814" :question/math-academy-id "q-333706" :knowledge-point/_questions (LTE) satisfies\n\n$$\nτ(Δx)=O\\,((Δx)^{p+1})\\,\\text{as}\\,Δx\\to 0.\n$$\n\nThe order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.\n\nIn other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$\n\nFirst, we compute the LTE for the given step sizes:\n\n- With step size $Δx=0.5,$ the LTE is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}τ(0.5) & =7(0.5)^{4}-2(0.5)^{5} \\\\  & =7\\cdot 0.062\\,5-2\\cdot 0.031\\,25 \\\\  & =0.375.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- With step size $Δx=0.25,$ the LTE is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}τ(0.25) & =7(0.25)^{4}-2(0.25)^{5} \\\\  & =7\\cdot (0.003\\,906…)-2\\cdot (0.000\\,976…) \\\\  & =0.025\\,39… \\\\  & ≈0.025.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we determine the order by comparing the errors. The step size decreases from $0.5$ to $0.25.$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\nk=\\frac{0.5}{0.25}=2.\n$$\n\nAs a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately\n\n$$\n{k}^{p+1}={2}^{p+1}.\n$$\n\nOn the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.375$ to $0.025\\,39….$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\n\\frac{0.375}{(0.025\\,39…)}=14.769\\,23…≈14.769.\n$$\n\nComparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{2}^{p+1} & ≈14.769\\,23… \\\\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{2}⁡(14.769\\,23…) \\\\ p+1 & ≈3.884… \\\\ p & ≈2.884….\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is\n$3.$\n\nIndeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the LTE:\n\n$$\nτ(Δx)=7(Δx)^{4}-2(Δx)^{5}\\,⇒\\,τ(Δx)=O\\,((Δx)^{4})=O\\,((Δx)^{3+1}),\\,Δx\\to 0.\n$$\n\nHence, the order of the method is :question/problem "A numerical method is used to approximate the solution to an initial value problem.\n\n- With step size $Δx=0.15,$ the observed local truncation error is $τ(0.15)=0.54.$\n\n- With step size $Δx=0.05,$ the observed local truncation error is $τ(0.05)=0.003.$\n\nEstimate the order of the numerical method." :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies\n\n$$\nτ(Δx)=O\\,((Δx)^{p+1})\\,\\text{as}\\,Δx\\to 0.\n$$\n\nThe order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.\n\nIn other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$\n\nIn our case, the step size decreases from $0.15$ to $0.05.$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\nk=\\frac{0.15}{0.05}=3.\n$$\n\nAs a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately\n\n$$\n{k}^{p+1}={3}^{p+1}.\n$$\n\nOn the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.54$ to $0.003.$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\n\\frac{0.54}{0.003}=180.\n$$\n\nComparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{3}^{p+1} & ≈180 \\\\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{3}⁡(180) \\\\ p+1 & ≈4.726… \\\\ p & ≈3.726….\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is $4.$"} {:db/id 17592186308666 :question/id #uuid "6b20caa4-47fd-550a-81fb-67a189c54897" ≈0.004.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we determine the order by comparing the errors. approximately\n\n$$\n{k}^{p+1}={3}^{p+1}.\n$$\n\nOn the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.099\\,9$ to $0.003\\,9.$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\n\\frac{0.099\\,9}{0.003\\,9}=25.615\\,38…≈25.615.\n$$\n\nComparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{3}^{p+1} & ≈25.615\\,38… \\\\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{3}⁡(25.615\\,38…) \\\\ p+1 & ≈2.952… \\\\ p & ≈1.952….\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is\n$2.$\n\nIndeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the LTE:\n\n$$\nτ(Δx)=4(Δx)^{3}-(Δx)^{4}\\,⇒\\,τ(Δx)=O\\,((Δx)^{3})=O\\,((Δx)^{2+1}),\\,Δx\\to 0.\n$$\n\nHence, the order of the method is sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$\n\nIn our case, the step size decreases from $0.10$ to $0.05.$ So, it :topic/math-academy-id 6399} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186222294 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222498 :tutorial/content "Each step of a numerical method produces a local truncation error $\\tau,$ which, over multiple steps, accumulates into a global truncation error $e.$ Both LTE and GTE depend on step size $\\Delta x.$\n\nThe **order** of a numerical method describes how fast these errors shrink as $\\Delta x$ decreases.\nA numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the *largest positive* integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies\n\n$$\ne(\\Delta x) = \\mathcal O\\!\\left((\\Delta x)^p\\right)\\quad\\textrm{as}\\quad \\Delta x \\to 0.\n$$\n\nIn other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately $k^p{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}e(\\frac{Δx}{k}) & ≈K{(\\frac{Δx}{k})}^{p}=\\frac{K(Δx)^{p}}{{k}^{p}}≈\\frac{e(Δx)}{{k}^{p}}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nLet's demonstrate with an example. Suppose a numerical method is used to approximate the solution to an initial value problem.\n\n- With step size $\\Delta x = 0.21,$ the observed global truncation error is $e(0.21) = 0.785.$\n\n- With step size $\\Delta x = 0.07,$ the observed global truncation error is $e(0.07) = 0.010.$\n\nUsing this data, we can estimate the order of the numerical method.\n\nThe step size decreases from $0.21$ to $0.07.$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\nk = \\dfrac{0.21}{0.07} = 3.\n$$\n\nAs a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the GTE should decrease by a factor of approximately\n\n$$\nk^p = 3^p.\n$$\n\nOn the other hand, the GTE actually decreases from $0.785$ to $0.010.$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{0.785}{0.010} = 78.5.\n$$\n\nComparing the two scale factors for the GTE, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{3}^{p} & ≈78.5 \\\\ p & ≈{log}_{3}⁡(78.5) \\\\ p & ≈3.97….\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the approximate order of the method is $4.$\n\nBut why is order important? Well, a higher order means that the error decreases faster as $\\Delta x$ decreases. As a result, higher-order methods can achieve a target accuracy *with fewer steps*. In this way, order predicts the accuracy you gain when you make steps smaller." :tutorial/id #uuid "40e84a8b-32df-5566-99ff-2b37f338d69f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14500 :tutorial/title but equivalent, definition for the **order** can be made in terms of the local truncation error.\n\nA numerical method has **order** $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies\n\n$$\n\\tau(\\Delta x) = \\mathcal O\\!\\left((\\Delta x)^{p+1}\\right)\\quad\\textrm{as}\\quad \\Delta x \\to 0.\n$$\n\nIn other words, a numerical method has **order** $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately $k^{p+1}.$\n\nBut why is the power $p+1$ for LTE but only $p$ for GTE?\n\nEach local truncation error measures the error made in *one step* of the method. If a method has order $p,$ then the error made in a single step shrinks like\n\n$$\n\\tau(\\Delta x) = \\mathcal O\\!\\left((\\Delta x)^{p+1}\\right).\n$$\n\nHowever, on a fixed interval, using step size $\\Delta x$ requires about\n\n$$\nN \\approx \\dfrac1{\\Delta x}\n$$\n\nsteps. The global truncation error results from *accumulating* these local errors over all steps.\n\nHeuristically, adding up $N$ local errors of size $(\\Delta x)^{p+1}$ gives\n\n$$\ne(\\Delta x) \\sim N \\cdot (\\Delta x)^{p+1} \\sim \\dfrac1{\\Delta x} \\cdot (\\Delta x)^{p+1} = (\\Delta x)^p.\n$$\n\nThus, the local truncation error is one power of $\\Delta x$ higher than the global truncation error.\n\nNext, we will apply this definition to determine the order of a given numerical method." :tutorial/id #uuid "b5d4a6f3-fc92-557f-be1f-b14832313c21" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14501 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222512 :tutorial/content "We'll now show that the definition of order with respect to LTE is the same as with respect to GTE.\n\nIndeed, suppose a numerical method with increment formula $\\Delta y = \\Phi(x, y, \\Delta x) \\cdot \\Delta x$ satisfies the following:\n\n$$\n\\tau(\\Delta x) = \\mathcal O\\!\\left((\\Delta x)^{p+1}\\right)\\quad\\textrm{as}\\quad \\Delta x \\to 0\n$$\n\nOn a fixed interval of length $L,$ the number of steps is $N \\approx \\dfrac{L}{\\Delta x}.$ So,\n$N = \\mathcal O\\!\\left(\\dfrac{1}{\\Delta x}\\right)$ as $\\Delta x \\to 0.$\n\nNow, recall the relationship between GTE and LTE, given by\n\n$$\ne(\\Delta x) = e_N = e_{N-1} + \\left[ \\Phi(x_{N-1}, y(x_{N-1}), \\Delta x) - \\Phi(x_{N-1}, y_{N-1}, \\Delta x) \\right] \\cdot \\Delta x + \\tau_N.\n$$\n\nSince $y(x_{N-1}) - y_{N-1} = e_{N-1},$ it is natural to say that changing the input $y$ by $e_{N-1}$ changes $\\Phi$ by about a constant multiple of $e_{N-1}.$ So, heuristically,\n\n$$\n\\Phi(x_{N-1}, y(x_{N-1}), \\Delta x) - \\Phi(x_{N-1}, y_{N-1}, \\Delta x) \\approx Ce_{N-1}\n$$\n\nfor some $C$ that *doesn't* depend on $\\Delta x$ (on a fixed interval). Hence, the GTE satisfies approximately\n\n$$\ne(\\Delta x) = e_N \\approx (1+C\\Delta x)e_{N-1} + \\tau_N.\n$$\n\nAfter $N$ steps, we get\n\n$$\ne(\\Delta x) \\approx (1+C\\Delta x)^N e_0 + \\sum_{n=1}^N(1+C\\Delta x)^{N-n}\\tau_n.\n$$\n\nNext, note that $(1+C\\Delta x)^N \\approx e^{CN\\Delta x} \\approx e^{CL},$ which is $\\mathcal O(1)$ as $\\Delta x \\to 0.$ So, the weights $(1+C\\Delta x)^{N-n}$ don't change the *power* of $\\Delta x.$\n\nSo, we can treat the GTE as roughly the sum of the per-step local errors. Therefore,\n\n$$\ne(\\Delta x) \\approx \\sum_{n=1}^N \\tau_n\n$$\n\nWith $\\tau_n = \\mathcal O\\!\\left((\\Delta x)^{p+1}\\right)$ for each $n=1,\\ldots,N,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}e(Δx) & ={\\sum }_{n=1}^{N}O\\,((Δx)^{p+1}) \\\\  & =N\\cdot O\\,((Δx)^{p+1}) \\\\  & =O\\,(\\frac{1}{Δx})\\cdot O\\,((Δx)^{p+1}) \\\\  & =O\\,((Δx)^{p}).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNote that since $p$ is maximal in the LTE definition, this shows the GTE has order $p$ as well." :tutorial/id #uuid "380a28f7-f36f-50b0-982b-365f87b068bd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14656 :tutorial/title "Connecting the Definitions of the Order of Numerical Methods"} :step/id #uuid "a05640d9-1389-5d1b-b299-1230e633c270" :step/math-academy-id 593404}] :activity/title "Order of Numerical Methods" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186221478} {:db/id 17592186222294 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222498 :tutorial/content "Each step of a numerical method produces a local truncation error $\\tau,$ which, over multiple steps, accumulates into a global truncation error $e.$ Both LTE and GTE depend on step size $\\Delta x.$\n\nThe **order** of a numerical method describes how fast these errors shrink as $\\Delta x$ decreases.\nA numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the *largest positive* integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies\n\n$$\ne(\\Delta x) = \\mathcal O\\!\\left((\\Delta x)^p\\right)\\quad\\textrm{as}\\quad \\Delta x \\to 0.\n$$\n\nIn other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately $k^p{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}e(\\frac{Δx}{k}) & ≈K{(\\frac{Δx}{k})}^{p}=\\frac{K(Δx)^{p}}{{k}^{p}}≈\\frac{e(Δx)}{{k}^{p}}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nLet's demonstrate with an example. x)^{p+1}\\right)\\quad\\textrm{as}\\quad \\Delta x \\to 0\n$$\n\nOn a fixed interval of length $L,$ the number of steps is $N \\approx \\dfrac{L}{\\Delta x}.$ So,\n$N = \\mathcal O\\!\\left(\\dfrac{1}{\\Delta x}\\right)$ as $\\Delta x \\to 0.$\n\nNow, recall the relationship between GTE and LTE, given by\n\n$$\ne(\\Delta x) = e_N = e_{N-1} + \\left[ \\Phi(x_{N-1}, y(x_{N-1}), \\Delta x) - \\Phi(x_{N-1}, y_{N-1}, \\Delta x) \\right] \\cdot \\Delta x + \\tau_N.\n$$\n\nSince $y(x_{N-1}) - y_{N-1} = e_{N-1},$ it is natural to say that changing the input $y$ by $e_{N-1}$ changes $\\Phi$ by about a constant multiple of $e_{N-1}.$ So, heuristically,\n\n$$\n\\Phi(x_{N-1}, y(x_{N-1}), \\Delta x) - \\Phi(x_{N-1}, y_{N-1}, \\Delta x) \\approx Ce_{N-1}\n$$\n\nfor some $C$ that *doesn't* depend on $\\Delta x$ (on a fixed interval). is approximately\n{{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies\n\n$$\nτ(Δx)=O\\,((Δx)^{p+1})\\,\\text{as}\\,Δx\\to 0.\n$$\n\nThe order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.\n\nIn other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$\n\nFirst, we compute the LTE for the given step sizes:\n\n- With step size $Δx=0.5,$ the LTE is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}τ(0.5) & =8(0.5)^{5}+2(0.5)^{6} \\\\  & =8\\cdot 0.031\\,25+2\\cdot 0.015\\,625 \\\\  & =0.281\\,25 \\\\  & ≈0.281.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- With step size $Δx=0.2,$ the LTE is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}τ(0.2) & =8(0.2)^{5}+2(0.2)^{6} \\\\  & =8\\cdot 0.000\\,32+2\\cdot 0.000\\,064 \\\\  & =0.002\\,688 \\\\  & ≈0.003.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we determine the order by comparing the errors. The step size decreases from $0.5$ to $0.2.$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\nk=\\frac{0.5}{0.2}=2.5.\n$$\n\nAs a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately\n\n$$\n{k}^{p+1}={2.5}^{p+1}.\n$$\n\nOn the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.281\\,25$ to $0.002\\,688.$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\n\\frac{0.281\\,25}{0.002\\,688}=104.631\\,69…≈104.632.\n$$\n\nComparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{2.5}^{p+1} & ≈104.631\\,69… \\\\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{2.5}⁡(104.631\\,69…) \\\\ p+1 & ≈5.075… \\\\ p & ≈4.075….\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is\n$4.$\n\nIndeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the LTE:\n\n$$\nτ(Δx)=8(Δx)^{5}+2(Δx)^{6}\\,⇒\\,τ(Δx)=O\\,((Δx)^{5})=O\\,((Δx)^{4+1}),\\,Δx\\to 0.\n$$\n\nHence, the order of the method is that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies\n\n$$\nτ(Δx)=O\\,((Δx)^{p+1})\\,\\text{as}\\,Δx\\to 0.\n$$\n\nThe order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.\n\nWith that in mind, let's check each option in turn:\n\n- For $τ(Δx)=6(Δx)^{3},$ the dominant term as $Δx\\to 0$ is $6(Δx)^{3}=6(Δx)^{2+1}.$ So, statement I corresponds to an order $2$ method.\n\n- For $τ(Δx)=0.3(Δx)^{2}+2(Δx)^{3},$ the dominant term as $Δx\\to 0$ is $0.3(Δx)^{2}=0.3(Δx)^{1+1}.$ So, statement II corresponds to an order $1$ method.\n\n- For $τ(Δx)=9(Δx)^{3}+4(Δx)^{5},$ the dominant :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies\n\n$$\ne(Δx)=O\\,((Δx)^{p})\\,\\text{as}\\,Δx\\to 0.\n$$\n\nThe order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.\n\nIn other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p}.$\n\nIn our case, the step size decreases from $0.25$ to $0.10.$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\nk=\\frac{0.25}{0.10}=2.5.\n$$\n\nNow, since the numerical method is of order $3,$ the error is expected to decrease by a factor of\n\n$$\n{k}^{3}=(2.5)^{3}=15.625.\n$$\n\nTherefore, using a step size of $Δx=0.10,$ the expected GTE is\n\n$$\ne(0.10)≈\\frac{0.125}{15.625}=0.008.\n$$\n\nSo,\n\n$$\ne(0.10)≈0.008.\n$$"} :step/id :question/math-academy-id "q-334724" :question/problem "The local truncation error (LTE) of a numerical method with step size $Δx$ is\n\n$$\nτ(Δx)=8(Δx)^{5}+2(Δx)^{6}.\n$$\n\nComplete the following sentences.\n\n$\\,$ With step size $Δx=0.5,$ the local truncation error is $≈$\n{{field-1}}.\n\n$\\,$ With step size $Δx=0.2,$ the local truncation error is $≈$\n{{field-2}}.\n\n$\\,$ Decreasing from $Δx=0.5$ to $Δx=0.2,$ the LTE is reduced by a factor of $≈$\n{{field-3}}.\n\n$\\,$ According to this data, the order of the method is approximately\n{{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies\n\n$$\nτ(Δx)=O\\,((Δx)^{p+1})\\,\\text{as}\\,Δx\\to 0.\n$$\n\nThe order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.\n\nIn other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$\n\nFirst, we compute the LTE for the given step sizes:\n\n- With step size $Δx=0.5,$ the LTE is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}τ(0.5) & =8(0.5)^{5}+2(0.5)^{6} \\\\  & =8\\cdot 0.031\\,25+2\\cdot 0.015\\,625 \\\\  & =0.281\\,25 \\\\  & ≈0.281.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- With step size $Δx=0.2,$ the LTE is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}τ(0.2) & =8(0.2)^{5}+2(0.2)^{6} \\\\  & =8\\cdot 0.000\\,32+2\\cdot 0.000\\,064 \\\\  & =0.002\\,688 \\\\  & ≈0.003.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we determine the order by comparing the errors. The step size decreases from $0.5$ to $0.2.$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\nk=\\frac{0.5}{0.2}=2.5.\n$$\n\nAs a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately\n\n$$\n{k}^{p+1}={2.5}^{p+1}.\n$$\n\nOn the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.281\\,25$ to $0.002\\,688.$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\n\\frac{0.281\\,25}{0.002\\,688}=104.631\\,69…≈104.632.\n$$\n\nComparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{2.5}^{p+1} & ≈104.631\\,69… \\\\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{2.5}⁡(104.631\\,69…) \\\\ p+1 & ≈5.075… \\\\ p & ≈4.075….\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is\n$4.$\n\nIndeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the LTE:\n\n$$\nτ(Δx)=8(Δx)^{5}+2(Δx)^{6}\\,⇒\\,τ(Δx)=O\\,((Δx)^{5})=O\\,((Δx)^{4+1}),\\,Δx\\to 0.\n$$\n\nHence, the order of the method is problem is known to be order $4.$  Suppose that using step size $Δx=0.25$ produces a global truncation error (GTE) of $e(0.25)≈0.3125.$  If we instead use a step size $Δx=0.10,$ what GTE should we expect?\n\n$e(0.10)≈$\n{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies\n\n$$\ne(Δx)=O\\,((Δx)^{p})\\,\\text{as}\\,Δx\\to 0.\n$$\n\nThe order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.\n\nIn other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p}.$\n\nIn our case, the step size decreases from $0.25$ to $0.10.$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\nk=\\frac{0.25}{0.10}=2.5.\n$$\n\nNow, since the numerical method is of order $4,$ the error is expected to decrease by a factor of\n\n$$\n{k}^{4}=(2.5)^{4}=39.0625.\n$$\n\nTherefore, using a step size of $Δx=0.10,$ the expected GTE is\n\n$$\ne(0.10)≈\\frac{0.3125}{39.0625}=0.008.\n$$"} :step/id #uuid :question/math-academy-id "q-334763" :question/problem "A numerical method for approximating a solution to an initial value problem is known to be order $3.$  Suppose that using step size $Δx=0.2$ produces a global truncation error (GTE) of $e(0.2)≈0.064.$  If we instead use a step size $Δx=0.1,$ what GTE should we expect?\n\n$e(0.1)≈$\n{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies\n\n$$\ne(Δx)=O\\,((Δx)^{p})\\,\\text{as}\\,Δx\\to 0.\n$$\n\nThe order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.\n\nIn other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p}.$\n\nIn our case, the step size decreases from $0.2$ to $0.1.$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\nk=\\frac{0.2}{0.1}=2.\n$$\n\nNow, since the numerical method is of order $3,$ the error is expected to decrease by a factor of\n\n$$\n{k}^{3}={2}^{3}=8.\n$$\n\nTherefore, using a step size of $Δx=0.1,$ the expected GTE is\n\n$$\ne(0.1)≈\\frac{0.064}{8}=0.008.\n$$"} :step/id integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies\n\n$$\nτ(Δx)=O\\,((Δx)^{p+1})\\,\\text{as}\\,Δx\\to 0.\n$$\n\nThe order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.\n\nIn other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$\n\nFirst, we compute the LTE for the given step sizes:\n\n- With step size $Δx=0.3,$ the LTE is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}τ(0.3) & =4(0.3)^{3}-(0.3)^{4} \\\\  & =4\\cdot 0.027-0.008\\,1 \\\\  & =0.108-0.008\\,1 \\\\  & =0.099\\,9 \\\\  & ≈0.100.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- With step size $Δx=0.1,$ the LTE is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}τ(0.1) & =4(0.1)^{3}-(0.1)^{4} \\\\  & =4\\cdot 0.001-0.000\\,1 \\\\  & =0.004-0.000\\,1 \\\\  & =0.003\\,9 \\\\  & ≈0.004.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we determine the order by comparing the errors. The step size decreases from $0.3$ to $0.1.$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\nk=\\frac{0.3}{0.1}=3.\n$$\n\nAs a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately\n\n$$\n{k}^{p+1}={3}^{p+1}.\n$$\n\nOn the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.099\\,9$ to $0.003\\,9.$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\n\\frac{0.099\\,9}{0.003\\,9}=25.615\\,38…≈25.615.\n$$\n\nComparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{3}^{p+1} & ≈25.615\\,38… \\\\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{3}⁡(25.615\\,38…) \\\\ p+1 & ≈2.952… \\\\ p & ≈1.952….\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is\n$2.$\n\nIndeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the LTE:\n\n$$\nτ(Δx)=4(Δx)^{3}-(Δx)^{4}\\,⇒\\,τ(Δx)=O\\,((Δx)^{3})=O\\,((Δx)^{2+1}),\\,Δx\\to 0.\n$$\n\nHence, the order of the method is numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies\n\n$$\nτ(Δx)=O\\,((Δx)^{p+1})\\,\\text{as}\\,Δx\\to 0.\n$$\n\nThe order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.\n\nIn other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$\n\nFirst, we compute the LTE for the given step sizes:\n\n- With step size $Δx=0.3,$ the LTE is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}τ(0.3) & =4(0.3)^{3}-(0.3)^{4} \\\\  & =4\\cdot 0.027-0.008\\,1 \\\\  & =0.108-0.008\\,1 \\\\  & =0.099\\,9 \\\\  & ≈0.100.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- With step size $Δx=0.1,$ the LTE is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}τ(0.1) & =4(0.1)^{3}-(0.1)^{4} \\\\  & =4\\cdot 0.001-0.000\\,1 \\\\  & =0.004-0.000\\,1 \\\\  & =0.003\\,9 \\\\  & ≈0.004.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we determine the order by comparing the errors. The step size decreases from $0.3$ to $0.1.$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\nk=\\frac{0.3}{0.1}=3.\n$$\n\nAs a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately\n\n$$\n{k}^{p+1}={3}^{p+1}.\n$$\n\nOn the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.099\\,9$ to $0.003\\,9.$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\n\\frac{0.099\\,9}{0.003\\,9}=25.615\\,38…≈25.615.\n$$\n\nComparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{3}^{p+1} & ≈25.615\\,38… \\\\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{3}⁡(25.615\\,38…) \\\\ p+1 & ≈2.952… \\\\ p & ≈1.952….\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is\n$2.$\n\nIndeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the LTE:\n\n$$\nτ(Δx)=4(Δx)^{3}-(Δx)^{4}\\,⇒\\,τ(Δx)=O\\,((Δx)^{3})=O\\,((Δx)^{2+1}),\\,Δx\\to 0.\n$$\n\nHence, the order of the method is {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F,$ defined as\n\n$$\nF(x,y)=\\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\\,i+\\frac{y}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\\,j.\n$$\n\nEvaluate ${\\int }_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the curve $y={x}^{2}\\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)$ for $x\\in [0,1].$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that \n\n$$\n{\\int }_{C}∇f\\cdot \\text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).\n$$\n\n \n\nFirst, we define $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)$ as follows:\n\n$$\nF(x,y)={{\\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}_{⏟}}_{P(x,y)}\\,i+{{\\frac{y}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}_{⏟}}_{Q(x,y)}\\,j.\n$$\n\nTo apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we must first find a potential function $f$ (if it exists) such that $F=∇f.$ Notice that the domain of $F$ is ${R}^{2},$ and\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-\\frac{2xy}{(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}}.\n$$\n\nSince the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ there exists a potential function $f$ such that $F=∇f,$ and we must have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}, \\\\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\\frac{y}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nReconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get\n\n$$\nf(x,y)=\\frac{1}{2}\\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}).\n$$\n\nNote that we set $C=0$ for the arbitrary constant since we can use any function $f$ that satisfies $∇f=F.$\n\nWe're now ready to apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals. A suitable parametrization of the curve $C$ is given by\n\n$$\nr(t)=⟨t,{t}^{2}\\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)⟩,\\,t\\in [0,1].\n$$\n\nThe position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0⟩, \\\\ r(1) & =⟨1,\\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,0)$ and $(1,\\operatorname{ln}⁡2).$\n\nFinally, applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r & ={\\int }_{C}∇f\\cdot \\text{d}r \\\\  & =f(1,\\operatorname{ln}⁡2)-f(0,0) \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}\\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{1}^{2}+{ln}^{2}⁡2)-\\frac{1}{2}\\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}) \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}\\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{ln}^{2}⁡2)-0 \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}\\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{ln}^{2}⁡2).\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186134566 :question/id #uuid $t\\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that \n\n$$\n{\\int }_{C}∇f\\cdot \\text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).\n$$\n\nWe start by parametrizing the curve $C.$ A suitable parametrization is\n\n$$\nr(t)=⟨2\\sqrt{t},t⟩,\\,t\\in [1,4].\n$$\n\nThen, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨2,1⟩, \\\\ r(4) & =⟨4,4⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nApplying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{C}∇f\\cdot \\text{d}r & =f(r(4))-f(r(1)) \\\\  & =f(4,4)-f(2,1) \\\\  & =({4}^{2}+{e}^{4\\cdot 4})-({2}^{2}+{e}^{2\\cdot 1}) \\\\  & =(16+{e}^{16})-(4+{e}^{2}) \\\\  & ={e}^{16}-{e}^{2}+12.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "d45199d9-a99e-54aa-9c88-4b37e9921203"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5570ad04-a911-54fe-882f-cae6a0eccb35" :answer/type {:db/id {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "![](images/13/13e4c6a06a44099024ce91ef6c9ed4679af037c2e794351597a4d604bf39dc6f.png)\n\nConsider the ellipse $E$ and vector field $F$ shown above. Let $C$ be any path where $E$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction. Which of the following statements are true?\n\nI. ${∮}_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r=0$\n\nII. ${∮}_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r>0$\n\nIII. ${∮}_{-C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r>0$" :question/worked-solution "The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$\nIt is given by the formula\n\n$$\nΓ={∮}_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r={\\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\\,\\text{d}t.\n$$\n\nWe now recall the following:\n\n- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r>0.$\n\n- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r<0.$\n\nWith that in mind, let's check each statement.\n\n- Statement I is true, while statement II is false. Since the force $F$ acts perpendicular to the motion of the particle as it moves around $C,$ it neither helps nor hinders its motion. \n\n![](images/63/6371bb04d33719ee18c65a92354e84be0e9077e780eac9559dcb7ec42deb8d99.png)\n\nSo, ${∮}_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r=0.$\n\n- Statement III is false. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $F$ remains unchanged.\n\n![](images/0b/0bd9476fa9b19f04b40fbb9cca2986ed90495aa134307606622ef91070af19a7.png)\n\nSo, ${∮}_{-C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r=0.$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I only.\""} {:db/id 17592186455485 :question/id #uuid "a9318e5b-e833-584c-92bb-558dab7e94de" :question/math-academy-id "q-125640" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "029ef420-9eaa-5c6d-8287-3ef33710e976" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186454907} {:answer/id #uuid "3af01276-3947-5c77-abb0-001b7f9268cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186455000} {:answer/id #uuid "74a31f1c-47e3-545d-a815-1b80644ceb5a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186455118} {:answer/id #uuid "c134f711-db33-5b9e-bc96-94b44710886e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186455236} {:answer/id #uuid "ce1d9b86-ba57-557d-9af4-ca1029204f80" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186455261}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186455000} :answer-field/id #uuid "07b21c95-dc62-58a4-b763-c93eafdfda09" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186455342}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "![](images/a1/a1883ee3a3a99d43109bae2d2093aef35548dde9753cfb7dc19dfd77a104ec83.png)\n\nConsider the ellipse $E$ and the vector field $F,$ shown above. } \\\\  & =-4(2\\pi )-0 \\\\  & =-8\\pi \\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186415315 :question/id #uuid "b79e3fb3-3865-5932-ba2e-8b5992286bc0" :question/math-academy-id "q-125481" 17592186180496 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180719 :tutorial/content "Given a vector field $\\mathbf{F}$ and a path $C$ defined by $\\mathbf{r}=\\mathbf{r}(t)$ for $t \\in [a,b],$ the line integral \n\n$$\n\\int\\limits_C \\mathbf F \\cdot \\textrm d\\mathbf r\n$$\n\ngives the total work done by $\\mathbf F$ in moving a particle from the initial point $\\mathbf{r}(a)$ to the terminal point $\\mathbf{r}(b)$ on the curve.\n\nNow suppose that $C$ is a *closed* curve. The **circulation** of $\\mathbf{F}$ along $C,$ denoted using the Greek letter $\\Gamma$ (pronounced \"gamma\"), is given by the line integral\n\n$$\n\\Gamma = \\oint\\limits_C \\mathbf F \\cdot \\textrm d\\mathbf r = \\int_a^b \\mathbf F(r(t)) \\cdot \\mathbf r'(t) \\; \\textrm{d}t.\n$$\n\nRemember that the notation $\\displaystyle\\oint$ simply reminds us that we're integrating along a closed path.\n\nThe circulation $\\Gamma$ gives the total work done by $\\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along the entire closed path. We can also think of $\\Gamma$ as a measure of how much $\\mathbf F$ circulates around $C.$\n\nLet's build some intuition by considering some examples. \n\n- Consider the vector field $\\mathbf{F}$ and the closed curve $C$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction, shown below. \n\n![](images/9e/9e9de4e3734be4f7d8f59f6d54d0ed92c51db3a0beb8277f4b450531b7dab332.png)\n\nIt's clear from the picture that $\\mathbf{F}$ *assists* the motion of a particle as it moves counterclockwise along the path. Therefore, we can conclude that\n\n$$\n\\Gamma = \\displaystyle\\oint\\limits_{C}\\mathbf F\\cdot \\textrm d \\mathbf r >    0.\n$$\n\n- Now imagine that $C$ is traversed in the clockwise direction.\n\n![](images/16/16dd701d51e3b43714b58993f66e42359289f557ef86fd9091ab6b8bba7041e7.png)\n\nWe see that $\\mathbf F$ works *against* the particle's motion as it moves clockwise along the path. Therefore,\n\n$$\n\\Gamma = \\displaystyle\\oint\\limits_{C}\\mathbf F\\cdot \\textrm d \\mathbf r < 0.\n$$\n\n- Finally, consider the vector field $\\mathbf{G}$ and the closed curve $C$ traversed in the clockwise direction, shown below.\n\n![](images/8b/8bf269cecceeefc3e81b868a4fc4c54127f00432145782b24719bb49552868c7.png)\n\nSince the force $\\mathbf G$ acts perpendicular to the particle's motion as it moves around the path, it neither helps nor hinders its motion. Therefore, we conclude that\n\n$$\n\\Gamma = \\displaystyle\\oint\\limits_{C}\\mathbf G\\cdot \\textrm d \\mathbf r = 0.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4446c197-397c-5e41-a7a9-22d57126ffae" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5833 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "2145b39b-47ee-5ae2-ad16-55a2719cc2e0" :step/math-academy-id 35732 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180494}} {:db/id 17592186180499 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179743 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179605 :question/id #uuid "1e15ae93-0a63-506a-a0ae-b15e035f0494" :question/math-academy-id "e-9543"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1da220a9-2afc-5b63-a423-a4d2b3de9567" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049150}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180026} {:db/id 17592186180027} {:db/id 17592186259836} {:db/id 17592186259837} {:db/id 17592186259838} {:db/id 17592186259839} {:db/id 17592186259840} {:db/id 17592186259842} {:db/id 17592186369298} {:db/id 17592186369305} {:db/id 17592186369312} {:db/id 17592186415314}] :knowledge-point/title "Circulation in Conservative Vector Fields"} :step/id #uuid "3bb98ffd-856f-5d48-bd6b-55f3885cdca8" :step/math-academy-id 35749} {:db/id 17592186180500 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180721 :tutorial/content "The fundamental theorem of line integrals states that\n\n$$\n\\int_{C} \\nabla f \\cdot \\textrm{d}\\mathbf r = f(\\mathbf r(b)) - :step/math-academy-id 35756 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180499}} {:db/id 17592186180719 :tutorial/content "Given a vector field $\\mathbf{F}$ and a path $C$ defined by $\\mathbf{r}=\\mathbf{r}(t)$ for $t \\in [a,b],$ the line integral \n\n$$\n\\int\\limits_C \\mathbf F \\cdot \\textrm d\\mathbf r\n$$\n\ngives the total work done by $\\mathbf F$ in moving a particle from the initial point $\\mathbf{r}(a)$ to the terminal point $\\mathbf{r}(b)$ on the curve.\n\nNow suppose that $C$ is a *closed* curve. The **circulation** of $\\mathbf{F}$ along $C,$ denoted using the Greek letter $\\Gamma$ (pronounced \"gamma\"), is given by the line integral\n\n$$\n\\Gamma = \\oint\\limits_C \\mathbf F \\cdot \\textrm d\\mathbf r = \\int_a^b \\mathbf F(r(t)) \\cdot \\mathbf r'(t) \\; \\textrm{d}t.\n$$\n\nRemember that the notation $\\displaystyle\\oint$ simply reminds us that we're integrating along a closed path.\n\nThe circulation $\\Gamma$ gives the total work done by $\\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along the entire closed path. We can also think of $\\Gamma$ as a measure of how much $\\mathbf F$ circulates around $C.$\n\nLet's build some intuition by considering some examples. \n\n- Consider the vector field $\\mathbf{F}$ and the closed curve $C$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction, shown below. \n\n![](images/9e/9e9de4e3734be4f7d8f59f6d54d0ed92c51db3a0beb8277f4b450531b7dab332.png)\n\nIt's clear from the picture that $\\mathbf{F}$ *assists* the motion of a particle as it moves counterclockwise along the path. Therefore, we can conclude that\n\n$$\n\\Gamma = \\displaystyle\\oint\\limits_{C}\\mathbf F\\cdot \\textrm d \\mathbf r >    0.\n$$\n\n- Now imagine that $C$ is traversed in the clockwise direction.\n\n![](images/16/16dd701d51e3b43714b58993f66e42359289f557ef86fd9091ab6b8bba7041e7.png)\n\nWe see that $\\mathbf F$ works *against* the particle's motion as it moves clockwise along the path. Therefore,\n\n$$\n\\Gamma = \\displaystyle\\oint\\limits_{C}\\mathbf F\\cdot \\textrm d \\mathbf r < 0.\n$$\n\n- Finally, consider the vector field $\\mathbf{G}$ and the closed curve $C$ traversed in the clockwise direction, shown below.\n\n![](images/8b/8bf269cecceeefc3e81b868a4fc4c54127f00432145782b24719bb49552868c7.png)\n\nSince the force $\\mathbf G$ acts perpendicular to the particle's motion as it moves around the path, it neither helps nor hinders its motion. Therefore, we conclude that\n\n$$\n\\Gamma = \\displaystyle\\oint\\limits_{C}\\mathbf G\\cdot \\textrm d \\mathbf r = 0.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4446c197-397c-5e41-a7a9-22d57126ffae" Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the **clockwise** direction. Which of the following statements are true?\n\nI. ${∮}_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r=0$\n\nII. ${∮}_{-C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r=0$\n\nIII. ${∮}_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r>0$" :question/worked-solution "The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$\nIt is given by the formula\n\n$$\nΓ={∮}_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r={\\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\\,\\text{d}t.\n$$\n\nWe now recall the following:\n\n- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r>0.$\n\n- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r<0.$\n\nWith that in mind, let's check each statement.\n\n- Statement I is true, while statement III is false. Since the force $F$ acts perpendicular to the motion of the particle as it moves around $C,$ it neither helps nor hinders its motion. \n\n![](images/c4/c498ddeae8ba4325a4a1dfc0840520c4718bb50a0600970405374dde933e1b1d.png)\n\nSo, ${∮}_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r=0.$\n\n- Statement II is true. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $F$ remains unchanged.\n\n![](images/74/740429a29b5eb4b72bbfae11e08c9ac272e72e31d395b4dad2602beb4d4ba40a.png)\n\nSo, ${∮}_{-C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r=0.$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I and II only.\""} :step/id #uuid "23ee9455-766f-5586-95a2-a9ed8dfe87ce"} {:db/id 17592186455518 :step/content {:db/id 17592186455447 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b7d45a6-b7b5-5b6e-a82c-a1748d83e603" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-9\\pi " :db/id 17592186454946} {:answer/id #uuid "7e4f36c3-2d0c-50c9-a36d-272fd914e84a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\\pi " :db/id 17592186455133} {:answer/id #uuid "c26f1bdf-26e0-5acd-bbc9-1a8e6be78f5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3\\pi " :db/id 17592186455239} {:answer/id #uuid "c3275529-012a-5a31-82a4-2f28fcd1acb1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186455240} {:answer/id #uuid "ff6f64d6-184a-5394-8a28-a8c004572db7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9\\pi " :db/id 17592186455340}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186455240} :answer-field/id #uuid "bbf611c1-7a64-56ff-a8ce-599f171848cc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186455404}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "442b3fed-648b-5cc8-977b-6700ae26738b" :question/math-academy-id "q-125482" :question/problem "Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y)=\\frac{1}{y}\\,i+\\frac{1}{x}\\,j$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ oriented counterclockwise." :question/worked-solution "The closed curve $C$ is the circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as\n\n$$\nr(t)=3\\operatorname{cos}⁡t\\,i+3\\operatorname{sin}⁡t\\,j,\\,0\\le t\\le 2\\pi .\n$$\n\nThe circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$\nIt is given by the formula\n\n$$\nΓ={∮}_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r={\\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\\,\\text{d}t.\n$$\n\nAlong the curve $C,$ we have\n\n$$\nx=3\\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\\,y=3\\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\n$$\n\nSo,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\\frac{1}{y}\\,i+\\frac{1}{x}\\,j \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{3\\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\\,i+\\frac{1}{3\\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\\,j.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nComputing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}t}(3\\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\\,i+\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}t}(3\\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\\,j \\\\  & =-3\\operatorname{sin}⁡t\\,i+3\\operatorname{cos}⁡t\\,j.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\\frac{1}{3\\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\\,i+\\frac{1}{3\\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\\,j)\\cdot (-3\\operatorname{sin}⁡t\\,i+3\\operatorname{cos}⁡t\\,j) \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{3\\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\\cdot (-3\\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\\frac{1}{3\\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\\cdot 3\\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\\\  & =-1+1 \\\\  & =0.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nHence, we conclude that:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r & ={\\int }_{0}^{2\\pi }F(r(t))\\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\\,\\text{d}t=0\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "40211c38-7902-5a30-be18-54ba1e524e35" :step/next {:db/id 17592186455523}} {:db/id "![](images/13/13e4c6a06a44099024ce91ef6c9ed4679af037c2e794351597a4d604bf39dc6f.png)\n\nConsider the ellipse $E$ and vector field $F$ shown above. Let $C$ be any path where $E$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction. Which of the following statements are true?\n\nI. ${∮}_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r=0$\n\nII. ${∮}_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r>0$\n\nIII. ${∮}_{-C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r>0$" :question/worked-solution "The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$\nIt is given by the formula\n\n$$\nΓ={∮}_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r={\\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\\,\\text{d}t.\n$$\n\nWe now recall the following:\n\n- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r>0.$\n\n- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r<0.$\n\nWith that in mind, let's check each statement.\n\n- Statement I is true, while statement II is false. Since the force $F$ acts perpendicular to the motion of the particle as it moves around $C,$ it neither helps nor hinders its motion. \n\n![](images/63/6371bb04d33719ee18c65a92354e84be0e9077e780eac9559dcb7ec42deb8d99.png)\n\nSo, ${∮}_{C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r=0.$\n\n- Statement III is false. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $F$ remains unchanged.\n\n![](images/0b/0bd9476fa9b19f04b40fbb9cca2986ed90495aa134307606622ef91070af19a7.png)\n\nSo, ${∮}_{-C}F\\cdot \\text{d}r=0.$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I only.\""} :step/id "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by\n\n$$\n{\\int }_{C}f(x,y)\\,\\text{d}s={\\int }_{{\\theta }_{1}}^{{\\theta }_{2}}f(r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta )\\,\\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}\\theta \\,.\n$$\n\n \n\nThe connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}x & =r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  \\\\  & =2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\cdot \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  \\\\  & =2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta , \\\\ y & =r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  \\\\  & =2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\cdot \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  \\\\  & =2{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, along our curve, we have $x=2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta $ and $y=2{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta $, where $0\\le \\theta \\le \\pi .$\n\nNow, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ) & ={(2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta )}^{2}+{(2{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta )}^{2} \\\\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\\theta +4{sin}^{4}⁡\\theta  \\\\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta ) \\\\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta } & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}\\theta }(2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta )=2\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nand }_{2}}f(r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta )\\,\\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}\\theta \\,.\n$$\n\n \n\nThe connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}x & =2\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta =2\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta , \\\\ y & =r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta =2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, along our curve, we have $x=2\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta $ and $y=2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta $, where $0\\le \\theta \\le \\frac{\\pi }{2}.$\n\nNow, since $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y+1}$, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ) & =2\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta {e}^{2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta +1}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta } & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}\\theta }(2)=0,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nand therefore\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}\\theta  & =\\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\\\  & =2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe can now write the integral as\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{C}x{e}^{y+1}\\,\\text{d}s & ={\\int }_{0}^{\\pi /2}f(r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta )\\,\\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{\\pi /2}2\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta {e}^{2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta +1}\\cdot 2\\cdot \\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & =2{\\int }_{0}^{\\pi /2}2\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta {e}^{2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta +1}\\,\\text{d}\\theta .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe can solve this using the substitution $u=2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta +1,$ $\\text{d}u=2\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\,\\text{d}\\theta $ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}2{\\int }_{0}^{\\pi /2}2\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta {e}^{2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta +1}\\,\\text{d}\\theta  & =2{\\int }_{1}^{3}{e}^{u}\\,\\text{d}u \\\\  & =2{e}^{u}{|}_{1}^{3} \\\\  & =2{e}^{3}-2e \\\\  & =2e({e}^{2}-1)\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, along our curve, we have $x=2\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta $ and $y=2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta $, where $0\\le \\theta \\le \\frac{\\pi }{4}.$  \n\nNow, since )}^{2}\\cdot 1\\cdot \\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{\\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta \\,{(\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta +\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta )}^{2}\\text{d}\\theta .\\end{aligned}\n$$"} 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Given that the power series ${\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }{a}_{n}(x+7)^{n}$ converges at  $x=-3,$ which of the following **must** be true?\n- **I.** The series converges at $x=-11$\n- **II.** The series converges at $x=-8$\n- **III.** The series converges at $x=1$\n\nSelect all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "The center of the expansion is $x=-7,$ and since the series is convergent for $x=-3,$ this means that the radius of convergence $R$ is *at least* $4,$ i.e., $R\\ge 4.$ So, the series is convergent for every point in the interval $(-11,-3].$ However, we know nothing about the convergence of the series at any point outside the interval $(-11,-3].$\n\n![](images/47/4764256e5f00e7a11d688bd99d5fa1c22db819e7a188113f0ef4cd987a9b7595.png)\n\n \n\nWith this in mind, let's check each of our statements.\n\n- Statement I is false. Since $-11\\notin (-11,-3],$ we cannot guarantee that the series is convergent at $x=-11.$\n\n- Statement II is true. Since $-8\\in (-11,-3],$ the series is convergent at $x=-8.$\n\n- Statement III is false. Since $1\\notin (-11,-3],$ we cannot guarantee that the series is convergent at $x=1.$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"II only.\""} {:db/id 17592186332833 :question/id #uuid :step/math-academy-id 26731} {:db/id 17592186176692 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176978 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the following infinite power series.\n\n$$\n\\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty} \\dfrac{(x-2)^n}{n^2} = (x-2) + \\dfrac{(x-2)^2}{2^2} + \\dfrac{(x-2)^3}{3^2} + \\cdots\n$$\n\nHow do we determine the radius and interval of convergence for this series?\n\nFirst, note that the terms of the series are all powers of $(x-2).$ For this reason, we say that the series is **centered** at $x=2.$\n\nTo compute the radius of convergence, we use the ratio test for convergence. We define \n\n$$\na_n = \\dfrac{(x-2)^n}{n^2},\n$$\n\nand we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\\to \\infty,$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\\to \\infty }|\\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\\\  & ={lim}_{n\\to \\infty }|\\frac{(x-2)^{n+1}}{(n+1)^{2}}\\cdot \\frac{{n}^{2}}{(x-2)^{n}}| \\\\  & =|x-2|{lim}_{n\\to \\infty }(\\frac{{n}^{2}}{(n+1)^{2}}) \\\\  & =|x-2|{lim}_{n\\to \\infty }(\\frac{{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}+2n+1}) \\\\  & =|x-2|{lim}_{n\\to \\infty }(\\frac{1}{(1+\\frac{2}{n}+\\frac{1}{{n}^{2}})}) \\\\  & =|x-2|\\cdot 1 \\\\  & =|x-2|\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe series converges if \n\n$$\nL < {\\color{blue}1}\n\\qquad\\Longrightarrow\\qquad\n\\left| x-{\\color{red}2} \\right| < {\\color{blue}1}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, \n\n- the radius of convergence is ${\\color{blue}1},$ and\n\n- the interval of convergence is centered at the point $x={\\color{red}2}.$\n\nTo find the interval of convergence, we solve the inequality $\\left| x-2 \\right| < 1,$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}|x-2| & <1 \\\\ -1<x-2 & <1 \\\\ 1<x & <3\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, the series converges for any $x$ in the open interval $(1,3).$\n\nThe ratio test gives no conclusion about the convergence of the series at the endpoints of this interval. So, we need to investigate the endpoints $x=1$ and $x=3$ separately using another test for convergence.\n\n- We start with the left endpoint. When $x=1,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }\\frac{(x-2)^{n}}{{n}^{2}} & ={\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }\\frac{(1-2)^{n}}{{n}^{2}} \\\\  & ={\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }\\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}} \\\\  & =-1+\\frac{1}{4}-\\frac{1}{9}+\\frac{1}{16}+⋯,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhich is convergent by the alternating series test.\n\n- We then look at the right endpoint. When $x=3,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }\\frac{(x-2)^{n}}{{n}^{2}} & ={\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }\\frac{(3-2)^{n}}{{n}^{2}} \\\\  & ={\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }\\frac{{1}^{n}}{{n}^{2}} \\\\  & ={\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }\\frac{1}{{n}^{2}} \\\\  & =1+\\frac{1}{4}+\\frac{1}{9}+\\frac{1}{16}+⋯,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhich is convergent by the $p$-series test.\n\nFinally, we conclude that the interval of convergence is $I=[1,3].$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3711e5cb-ff53-5f13-a62a-da24f59e888b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5191 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "638d27e8-a48f-5883-adc8-de19b25a5a0e" :step/math-academy-id 32549 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176674}}] :activity/title "Radius of Convergence of Power Series" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186176111} {:db/id 17592186176692 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176978 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the following infinite power series.\n\n$$\n\\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty} \\dfrac{(x-2)^n}{n^2} = (x-2) + \\dfrac{(x-2)^2}{2^2} + \\dfrac{(x-2)^3}{3^2} + \\cdots\n$$\n\nHow do we determine the radius and interval of convergence for this series?\n\nFirst, note that the terms of the series are all powers of $(x-2).$ For this reason, we say that the series is **centered** at $x=2.$\n\nTo compute the radius of convergence, we use the ratio test for convergence. We can write this mathematically, as follows:\n\n$$\nf(x) \\rightarrow \\infty\\quad \\text{as}\\quad x \\rightarrow 1\n$$\n\nIn words, this reads \"the function $f(x)$ approaches infinity as $x$ approaches $1$\".\n\nNow, consider the function $y = g(x)$, shown below. {:db/id 17592186130336 :tutorial/content "We know that some functions approach infinity as $x$ approaches a certain value, like the function $y=f(x)$ plotted below.\n\n![](images/da/da7878b503b9dff8f04c0f2c42e021353dc8b5fa744476fa0227bb954472c5ed.png)\n\nHere, the function shoots upwards when $x$ approaches $2$ *from the right*, that is, from the positive direction of the $x$-axis.\n\nWe say that the function approaches positive infinity as $x$ approaches $2$ from the right, and we write\n\n$$\nf(x) \\rightarrow \\infty \\quad \\text{as} \\quad x \\rightarrow 2^+\n$$\n\nwhere the superscript $+$ next to the $2$ indicates that $x$ approaches $2$ from the right.\n\nSimilar to the case above, we can have a function that shoots upwards or downwards when $x$ approaches a finite value *from the left*, that is, from the negative direction of the $x$-axis. Consider the function $y=g(x)$, shown below.\n\n![](images/2c/2c3d79df60e6b0a5627f39e8397a1eb9dc6c5e48fb1e816f6adc5309545ffb29.png)\n\nWe say that the function approaches negative infinity as $x$ approaches $2$ from the left, and we write\n\n$$\ng(x) \\rightarrow -\\infty \\quad \\text{as} \\quad x \\rightarrow 2^-\n$$\n\nwhere the superscript $-$ indicates that $x$ approaches $2$ from the left." :tutorial/id #uuid "8d16be94-aa13-52a0-bb7a-333c0a9d03ba" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2790 :tutorial/title "One-Sided Infinite Behavior of Functions"} :step/id #uuid "f39e32c5-50b4-5125-8c49-cf5bb0d9a1c7" :step/math-academy-id 14367 :step/next {:db/id 17592186129924}} {:db/id 17592186129927 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129105 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128921 :question/id #uuid "b6212c1b-c1c8-5d0d-9984-1509b721e54d" :question/math-academy-id "e-4062"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d29ea673-5a84-5e48-b45d-85cade99566d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049573}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129729} {:db/id 17592186129731}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Points Where a Function Approaches Infinity"} :step/id #uuid "2e1906c7-3dc3-5800-8af2-7c02ee80bf1b" :step/math-academy-id 14434 :step/next {:db/id 17592186129919}} {:db/id 17592186129934 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130338 :tutorial/content "We know that some functions approach infinity as $x$ approaches a certain value from one side, like the functions $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ plotted below.\n\n![](images/1b/1b1633611a2ea867e44845a8ba484e253671b9d5c74629f4a153ea79cf9a62e0.png)\n\nWe call the line $x=2$ a **vertical asymptote** of the functions $y = f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$.\n\nAn asymptote is a line that a function gets very close to but never touches. Elements of a Covariance Matrix"}] :question/problem "$\\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 & 0 \\\\ a & 5 & b \\\\ c & 1 & 2\\end{bmatrix}$\n\nThe covariance matrix $\\Sigma$ for some random variables $X_1, X_2$, and $X_3$ is given above. Find $a + b + c$." :question/worked-solution "For random variables $X_1, \\ldots, X_n$, the covariance matrix $\\Sigma$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{bmatrix}Var[X_{1}] & Cov[X_{1}, X_{2}] & ⋯ & Cov[X_{1}, X_{n}] \\\\ Cov[X_{2}, X_{1}] & Var[X_{2}] & ⋯ & Cov[X_{2}, X_{n}] \\\\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\\\ Cov[X_{n}, X_{1}] & Cov[X_{n}, X_{2}] & ⋯ & Var[X_{n}]\\end{bmatrix}\n$$\n\nThat is,\n\n- the $i$th diagonal element is $\\Sigma_{ii} = \\textrm{Var}[X_i]$, and\n- the element in the $i$th row and $j$th column for $i \\neq j$ is $\\Sigma_{ij} = \\textrm{Cov}[X_i, X_j]$.\n\nNow, note that\n\n$$\n\\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = \\textrm{Cov}[Y,X]\n$$\n\nAs a result, the covariance matrix is always symmetric (moreover, it is a positive semi-definite matrix).\n\nSo, we can find the missing elements as follows:\n\n- $a = \\Sigma_{21} = \\textrm{Cov}[X_2,X_1] = \\textrm{Cov}[X_1,X_2] = \\Sigma_{12} = 2$\n- $b = \\Sigma_{23} = \\textrm{Cov}[X_2,X_3] = \\textrm{Cov}[X_3,X_2] = \\Sigma_{32} = 1$\n- $c = \\Sigma_{31} = \\textrm{Cov}[X_3,X_1] = \\textrm{Cov}[X_1,X_3] = \\Sigma_{13} = 0$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\na + b + c = 2 + 1 +0 = 3\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186050021} {:db/id 17592186188788 ---: | ---: |\n| $X=2$ | $0.3$ | $0.2$ |\n| $X=4$ | $0.1$ | $0.4$ |\n\nGiven that $\\textrm{E}[X] = 3$ and $\\textrm{E}[Y] = 2.2$, find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y$." :question/worked-solution "For two random variables $X$ and $Y$, the covariance matrix $\\Sigma$ is given by\n$\\begin{bmatrix}Var[X] & Cov[X, Y] \\\\ Cov[Y, X] & Var[Y]\\end{bmatrix}$\n\nRecall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula\n\n$$\n\\textrm{Var}[X] = \\textrm{E}[X^2] - \\textrm{E}[X]^2\n$$\n\nand the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula\n\n$$\n\\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = \\textrm{E}[XY] - \\textrm{E}[X] \\cdot \\textrm{E}[Y]\n$$\n\nFirst, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y$. These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.\n\n| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=3$ | $f_X$ |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| $X=2$ | $0.3$ | $0.2$ | $0.5$ |\n| $X=4$ | $0.1$ | $0.4$ | $0.5$ |\n| $f_Y$ | $0.4$ | $0.6$ | $1$ |\n\nNow, we can find $\\textrm{Var}[X]$. If $X$ is defined on a support $S_X$, then\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nE[X^{2}] &= ∑_(x ∈ S_{X})x^{2} \\cdot f_{X}(x) \\\\\n&= 2^{2} \\cdot 0.5 + 4^{2} \\cdot 0.5 \\\\\n&= 10\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nVar[X] &= E[X^{2}] - E[X]^{2} \\\\\n&= 10 - 3^{2} \\\\\n&= 1\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSimilarly, if $Y$ is defined on a support $S_Y$, then\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nE[Y^{2}] &= ∑_(y ∈ S_{y})y^{2} \\cdot f_{Y}(y) \\\\\n&= 1^{2} \\cdot 0.4 + 3^{2} \\cdot 0.6 \\\\\n&= 5.8\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nVar[Y] &= E[Y^{2}] - E[Y]^{2} \\\\\n&= 5.8 - 2.2^{2} \\\\\n&= 0.96\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, let's find $\\textrm{Cov}[X,Y]$. By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\\textrm{E}[XY]{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nE[XY] &= ∑_((x, y) ∈ S)xy \\cdot f(x, y) \\\\\n&= (2)(1)f(2, 1) + (4)(1)f(4, 1) + (2)(3)f(2, 3) + (4)(3)f(4, 3) \\\\\n&= 2 \\cdot 0.3 + 4 \\cdot 0.1 + 6 \\cdot 0.2 + 12 \\cdot 0.4 \\\\\n&= 7\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThen, using the covariance formula, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nCov[X, Y] &= E[XY] - E[X] \\cdot E[Y] \\\\\n&= 7 - 3 \\cdot 2.2 \\\\\n&= 0.4\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the covariance matrix is given by\n$\\begin{bmatrix}Var[X] & Cov[X, Y] \\\\ Cov[Y, X] & Var[Y]\\end{bmatrix}$"} {:db/id 17592186188789 :question/id #uuid "47ea81eb-7ed2-5d0e-8710-74aeecf151ff" :question/math-academy-id "q-148173"} {:db/id 17592186188846 :question/id #uuid "4e03221d-fcb6-5c03-bb5d-2324529a8410" :question/math-academy-id "q-159403"} {:db/id 17592186188363 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186188071 :question/id #uuid "33336c58-c83a-512f-8a79-9223d1442763" :question/math-academy-id "e-10453"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f2c2ed97-706b-565d-997e-39bd0c832726" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050327} {:db/id 17592186050351}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186188790 :question/id #uuid "29c433e1-ba8d-5d7e-b983-459746ebf86b" :question/math-academy-id "q-148179"} {:db/id 17592186188791 :question/id #uuid "62fb930e-2f28-571d-9c9f-e9c6e3be11c3" :question/math-academy-id "q-148182"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Covariance Matrix Given Some Moments"} {:db/id 17592186188071 :question/id #uuid "33336c58-c83a-512f-8a79-9223d1442763" :question/math-academy-id "e-10453" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186188363 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f2c2ed97-706b-565d-997e-39bd0c832726" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Covariance Matrix Given Some Moments"}] :question/problem "Consider two random variables $X$ and $Y$ with expectations $\\textrm{E}[X] = 4$, $\\textrm{E}[Y] = 3$, mixed moment $\\textrm{E}[XY] = 9$, and second raw moments $\\textrm{E}[X^2] = 18$ and $\\textrm{E}[Y^2] = 14$. Find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y$." :question/worked-solution "For two random variables $X$ and $Y$, the covariance matrix $\\Sigma$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{bmatrix}Var[X] & Cov[X, Y] \\\\ Cov[Y, X] & Var[Y]\\end{bmatrix}\n$$\n\nRecall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula\n\n$$\n\\textrm{Var}[X] = \\textrm{E}[X^2] - \\textrm{E}[X]^2\n$$\n\nand the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula\n\n$$\n\\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = \\textrm{E}[XY] - \\textrm{E}[X] \\cdot \\textrm{E}[Y]\n$$\n\nFirst, let's find $\\textrm{Var}[X]{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nVar[X] &= E[X^{2}] - E[X]^{2} \\\\\n&= 18 - 4^{2} \\\\\n&= 2\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSimilarly,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nVar[Y] &= E[Y^{2}] - E[Y]^{2} \\\\\n&= 14 - 3^{2} \\\\\n&= 5\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow lets find $\\textrm{Cov}[X,Y]{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nCov[X, Y] &= E[XY] - E[X] \\cdot E[Y] \\\\\n&= 9 - 4 \\cdot 3 \\\\\n&=-3\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the covariance matrix is given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{bmatrix}Var[X] & Cov[X, Y] \\\\ Cov[Y, X] & Var[Y]\\end{bmatrix}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186050351} {:db/id \\textrm{E}[X]^2\n$$\n\nand the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula\n\n$$\n\\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = \\textrm{E}[XY] - \\textrm{E}[X] \\cdot \\textrm{E}[Y]\n$$\n\nFirst, we find $\\textrm{Var}[X]$.\nWe compute $\\textrm{E}[X^2]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nE[X^{2}] &= \\int_{0}^{1}\\int_{0}^{1}x^{2} \\cdot f(x, y)dxdy \\\\\n&= \\int_{0}^{1}\\int_{0}^{1}x^{2}(x + \\frac{3}{2}y^{2})dxdy \\\\\n&= \\int_{0}^{1}\\int_{0}^{1}(x^{3} + \\frac{3}{2}x^{2}y^{2})dxdy \\\\\n&= \\int_{0}^{1}[\\frac{1}{4}x^{4} + \\frac{1}{2}x^{3}y^{2}]_{x = 0}^{x = 1}dy \\\\\n&= \\int_{0}^{1}(\\frac{1}{4} + \\frac{1}{2}y^{2})dy \\\\\n&= [\\frac{1}{4}y + \\frac{1}{6}y^{3}]_{0}^{1} \\\\\n&= \\frac{1}{4} + \\frac{1}{6} \\\\\n&= \\frac{5}{12}\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nVar[X] &= E[X^{2}] - E[X]^{2} \\\\\n&= \\frac{5}{12} - (\\frac{7}{12})^{2} \\\\\n&= \\frac{11}{144}\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSimilarly, we compute $\\textrm{E}[Y^2]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nE[Y^{2}] &= \\int_{0}^{1}\\int_{0}^{1}y^{2} \\cdot f(x, y)dxdy \\\\\n&= \\int_{0}^{1}\\int_{0}^{1}y^{2}(x + \\frac{3}{2}y^{2})dxdy \\\\\n&= \\int_{0}^{1}\\int_{0}^{1}(xy^{2} + \\frac{3}{2}y^{4})dxdy \\\\\n&= \\int_{0}^{1}[\\frac{1}{2}x^{2}y^{2} + \\frac{3}{2}xy^{4}]_{x = 0}^{x = 1}dy \\\\\n&= \\int_{0}^{1}(\\frac{1}{2}y^{2} + \\frac{3}{2}y^{4})dy \\\\\n&= [\\frac{1}{6}y^{3} + \\frac{3}{10}y^{5}]_{0}^{1} \\\\\n&= \\frac{1}{6} + \\frac{3}{10} \\\\\n&= \\frac{7}{15}\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nVar[Y] &= E[Y^{2}] - E[Y]^{2} \\\\\n&= \\frac{7}{15} - (\\frac{5}{8})^{2} \\\\\n&= \\frac{73}{960}\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, let's find $\\textrm{Cov}[X,Y]$. Using the given results, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nCov[X, Y] &= E[XY] - E[X] \\cdot E[Y] \\\\\n&= \\frac{17}{48} - (\\frac{7}{12}) \\cdot (\\frac{5}{8}) \\\\\n&=-\\frac{1}{96}\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the covariance matrix is given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{bmatrix}Var[X] & Cov[X, Y] \\\\ Cov[Y, X] & Var[Y]\\end{bmatrix}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186049786} below.\n\n![](images/9d/9d7ca10163c9b5096f90e19bdb50d98881bd55e92cbaea4aa5af6696e728f9f3.png)\n\nWe can see from the diagram that there are two points of intersection. So let's calculate the coordinates of these intersection points.\n\nAn intersection point is a common solution of the equations $y = x + 2$ and $y = x^2 + x + 1.$ In other words, to get the coordinates of the intersection points, we have to solve the following system of equations:\n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}y={x}^{2}+x+1 \\\\ y=x+2\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSetting the equations equal to one another and then solving for $x$ using our knowledge of quadratic equations, we get\n![](images/96/9618f0221da97c281424def31e5d2a8fb96422b800928ad4ec4a01ed4dbad3d7.svg)\n\nSo, the $x$-coordinates of the intersection points are $x=-1$ and $x=1.$ \n\nTo find the $y$-coordinates of the intersection points, we plug these values into either curve. Let's choose the line since it's simpler.\n\n- Substituting $x=−1,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}y & =x+2 \\\\  & =(-1)+2 \\\\  & =1,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nso one point of intersection is $(-1,1).$\n\n- Substituting $x=1,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}y & =x+2 \\\\  & =(1)+2 \\\\  & =3,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nso the other point of intersection is $(1,3).$\n\nTherefore, we conclude that the points of intersection are $\\left(-1,\\,1 \\right)$ and $\\left(1,\\,3 \\right).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b907a9fb-d730-5d33-b47d-e448e4bc64dd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13862 :tutorial/title :step/content {:db/id 17592186088851 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to calculate the Maclaurin expansion for $f(x) = e^{3x}.$ Computing this using the formula is a lot of work because we have to calculate many derivatives and then plug them into the formula. Is there any easier way?\n\nYes, there is! First, let's recall the Maclaurin expansion of $e^x{:}$\n\n$$\ne^x = 1 + x + \\dfrac{x^2}{2!} + \\dfrac{x^3}{3!} + \\cdots, \\qquad x \\in (-\\infty, \\infty)\n$$\n\nSimply replacing $x$ with $3x$ in the above gives\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{e}^{3x} & =1+(3x)+\\frac{(3x)^{2}}{2!}+\\frac{(3x)^{3}}{3!}+⋯ \\\\  & =1+3x+\\frac{9{x}^{2}}{2}+\\frac{27{x}^{3}}{6}+⋯ \\\\  & =1+3x+\\frac{9{x}^{2}}{2}+\\frac{9{x}^{3}}{2}+⋯\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo compute the new interval of convergence, we do the same:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}3x & \\in (-\\infty ,\\infty ) \\\\ -\\infty  & <3x<\\infty  \\\\ -\\infty  & <x<\\infty  \\\\ x & \\in (-\\infty ,\\infty )\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo the interval of convergence stays the same, and we have\n\n$$\ne^{3x} = 1 + 3x + \\dfrac{9x^2}{2} + \\dfrac{9x^3}{2}  + \\cdots, \\qquad x \\in (-\\infty, \\infty).\n$$\n\nAnd that's it! Notice how much quicker this was compared with calculating the expansion from scratch." :tutorial/id #uuid "96030fee-2ce6-5a54-86a7-0e9c64d26bc7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1307 :tutorial/title
