Expansions"} :step/id #uuid "24d27f91-863a-5781-8829-9273038dd369" :step/math-academy-id 2578} {:db/id 17592186088693 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088968 :tutorial/content "In order to quickly compute the Maclaurin expansions of a variety of functions, it's worth memorizing some of the most basic Maclaurin expansions so that you can use them as starting points. These are summarized below.\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned} & {e}^{x}=1+x+\\frac{1}{2!}{x}^{2}+\\frac{1}{3!}{x}^{3}+⋯\\, &  & x\\in (-\\infty ,\\infty ) \\\\  & \\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)=x-\\frac{1}{3!}{x}^{3}+\\frac{1}{5!}{x}^{5}-⋯\\, &  & x\\in (-\\infty ,\\infty ) \\\\  & \\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)=1-\\frac{1}{2!}{x}^{2}+\\frac{1}{4!}{x}^{4}-⋯\\, &  & x\\in (-\\infty ,\\infty ) \\\\  & \\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x)=x-\\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-⋯\\, &  & x\\in (-1,1] \\\\  & \\frac{1}{1-x}=1+x+{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}+⋯\\, &  & x\\in (-1,1) \\\\  & \\frac{1}{1+x}=1-x+{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}+⋯ &  & x\\in (-1,1)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Note:** To memorize the Maclaurin expansions above, it's helpful to notice the following:\n\n- The series for $\\dfrac{1}{1-x}$ consists a geometric series whose first term is $1$ and whose common ratio is $x.$ This makes sense, because the sum formula for a geometric series with first term $a_1$ and common ratio $r$ is $\\dfrac{a_1}{1-r}.$\n\n- The series for $\\sin (x)$ consists of the alternating sum of the odd-degree terms in the series for $e^x.$ This makes sense because $\\sin(x)$ is an odd function (its graph is symmetric across the origin).\n\n- The series for $\\cos (x)$ consists of the alternating sum of the even-degree terms in the series for $e^x.$ This makes sense because $\\cos(x)$ is an even function (its graph is symmetric across the $y$-axis).\n\n- The series for $e^x,$ $\\sin(x),$ and $\\cos(x)$ all have a factorial in the denominator and no factorial in the numerator. For all of our standard series, any term with a factorial in the denominator will converge for all $x,$ because the factorial grows much more quickly than the powers of $x.$ So, their intervals of convergence are $x \\in (-\\infty, \\infty).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1801e6eb-5326-5b15-a38c-b91f970d7a15" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4612 :tutorial/title "The Basic Maclaurin Expansions"} :step/id #uuid "5dc233c4-4b38-5913-8b2d-1f2421ba65d7" :step/math-academy-id 28401 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088669}} {:db/id 17592186088694 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088969 :tutorial/content "To find the Maclaurin expansion for a sum, difference, or product of functions, we can\n\n1\\. find the Maclaurin expansions of the individual functions, and then\n\n2\\. perform the corresponding operation on the expansions.\n\nThe only catch is that we must take the intersection of the intervals of convergence, since we want to find where *both* of the individual functions converge.\n\nFor example, recall the following two Maclaurin expansions:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned} & {e}^{x}=1+x+\\frac{1}{2!}{x}^{2}+\\frac{1}{3!}{x}^{3}+⋯\\, &  & x\\in (-\\infty ,\\infty ) \\\\  & \\frac{1}{1-x}=1+x+{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}+⋯\\, &  & x\\in (-1,1)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find the Maclaurin expansion of $e^x+\\dfrac{1}{1-x},$ we can simply add the two expansions:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}+\\frac{1}{1-x} & =(1+x+\\frac{1}{2!}{x}^{2}+\\frac{1}{3!}{x}^{3}+⋯)+(1+x+{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}+⋯) \\\\  & =(1+1)+(1+1)x+(\\frac{1}{2!}+1){x}^{2}+(\\frac{1}{3!}+1){x}^{3}+⋯ \\\\  & =2+2x+\\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+\\frac{7}{6}{x}^{3}+⋯\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find the interval of convergence, we take the intersection of the intervals of convergence of the individual functions:\n\n$$\n(-\\infty, \\infty) \\cap (-1, 1) = (-1, 1)\n$$\n\nTherefore, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}+\\frac{1}{1-x}=2+2x+\\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+\\frac{7}{6}{x}^{3}+⋯,\\, &  & x\\in (-1,1).\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "29e51064-92e4-53b6-870b-05fec1aa937f" :step/next {:db/id 17592186088694}} {:db/id 17592186088694 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088969 :tutorial/content "To find the Maclaurin expansion for a sum, difference, or product of functions, we can\n\n1\\. find the Maclaurin expansions of the individual functions, and then\n\n2\\. perform the corresponding operation on the expansions.\n\nThe only catch is that we must take the intersection of the intervals of convergence, since we want to find where *both* of the individual functions converge.\n\nFor example, recall the following two Maclaurin expansions:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned} & {e}^{x}=1+x+\\frac{1}{2!}{x}^{2}+\\frac{1}{3!}{x}^{3}+⋯\\, &  & x\\in (-\\infty ,\\infty ) \\\\  & \\frac{1}{1-x}=1+x+{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}+⋯\\, &  & x\\in (-1,1)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find the Maclaurin expansion of $e^x+\\dfrac{1}{1-x},$ we can simply add the two expansions:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}+\\frac{1}{1-x} & =(1+x+\\frac{1}{2!}{x}^{2}+\\frac{1}{3!}{x}^{3}+⋯)+(1+x+{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}+⋯) \\\\  & =(1+1)+(1+1)x+(\\frac{1}{2!}+1){x}^{2}+(\\frac{1}{3!}+1){x}^{3}+⋯ \\\\  & =2+2x+\\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+\\frac{7}{6}{x}^{3}+⋯\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find the interval of convergence, we take the intersection of the intervals of convergence of the individual functions:\n\n$$\n(-\\infty, \\infty) \\cap (-1, 1) = (-1, 1)\n$$\n\nTherefore, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}+\\frac{1}{1-x}=2+2x+\\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+\\frac{7}{6}{x}^{3}+⋯,\\, &  & x\\in (-1,1).\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "29e51064-92e4-53b6-870b-05fec1aa937f" that $P$ is a stationary point. to approximate $y(1)$ *and* $y(2)$ using Euler's method. \n\n![](images/88/88b9a68dd2f5982b14a1d16588320a4770612eacdd2f1915a5e659c4a89b9760.png)\n\nWe will proceed using two steps of equal size. The step size $\\Delta x$ is\n\n$$\n\\Delta x = \\dfrac{{\\color{blue}{2}}-{\\color{red}{0}}}{2} = 1.\n$$\n\nWe will use a table to keep track of all the numbers. Let's start by adding the initial condition data $y(0) = 2.$\n\n| $\\,x\\,$ | $\\,y\\,$ | $\\, y'\\,$ | $\\, \\Delta y \\,$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| $0$ | $2$ |  |  |\n\nWe now proceed in two steps.\n\n**Step 1**: We compute $y'$ using the values of $x$ and $y$ in the first row of the table, and we calculate $\\Delta y$ using Euler's method.\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} & =x+y+1 \\\\  & =0+2+1 \\\\  & =3 \\\\ Δy & ={y}^{'}\\cdot Δx \\\\  & =3\\cdot 1 \\\\  & =3\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThen, we find the values of $x_{\\text{new}}$ and $y_{\\text{new}}\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{\\text{new}} & =x+Δx \\\\  & =0+1 \\\\  & =1 \\\\ {y}_{\\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\\\  & =2+3 \\\\  & =5\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFilling in our table, we get the following:\n\n| $\\,x\\,$ | $\\,y\\,$ | $\\, y'\\,$ | $\\, \\Delta y \\,$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| $0$ | $2$ | $3$ | $3$ |\n| $1$ | $5$ |  |  |\n\n**Step 2**: We now repeat the process. We compute $y'$ using the values of $x$ and $y$ in the *second* row of the table, and we calculate $\\Delta y$ using Euler's method.\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} & =x+y+1 \\\\  & =1+5+1 \\\\  & =7 \\\\ Δy & ={y}^{'}\\cdot Δx \\\\  & =7\\cdot 1 \\\\  & =7\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThen, we find new values for $x_{\\text{new}}$ and $y_{\\text{new}}\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{\\text{new}} & =x+Δx \\\\  & =1+1 \\\\  & =2 \\\\ {y}_{\\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\\\  & =5+7 \\\\  & =12\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFilling in our table, we get the following:\n\n| $\\,x\\,$ | $\\,y\\,$ | $\\, y'\\,$ | $\\, \\Delta y \\,$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| $0$ | $2$ | $3$ | $3$ |\n| $1$ | $5$ | $7$ | $7$ |\n| $2$ | $12$ |  |  |\n\nLooking at the two leftmost columns, we conclude that $y(1)\\approx 5$ and :step/content {:db/id 17592186055932 :tutorial/content "Suppose the Taylor (Maclaurin) series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by \n\n$$\nf(x) = \\sum_{n=0}^\\infty \\dfrac{(-1)^n}{2n+1} How can we calculate the first three non-zero terms of Taylor series for the derivative, $f'(x),$ about $x=0?$\n\nAll we need to do is differentiate the Taylor series of $f(x).$ Writing out the first three terms, we get\n\n$$\nf(x) = \\sum_{n=0}^\\infty \\dfrac{(-1)^n}{2n+1} x^{2n+1} = x - \\dfrac{x^3}{3} + \\dfrac{x^5}{5} - \\cdots.\n$$\n\nNow, to find $f'(x),$ we differentiate term-by-term and get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}x}(x)-\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}x}(\\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})+\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}x}(\\frac{{x}^{5}}{5})-⋯ \\\\  & =1-{x}^{2}+{x}^{4}-⋯.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nAnd that's it! [{:db/id 17592186093128 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093372 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we are given the **infinite power series**\n\n$$\n\\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty} \\frac{x^n}{n^2}=x +\\frac{x^2}{2^2}+\\frac{x^3}{3^2}+\\frac{x^4}{4^2} +\\cdots \\,.\n$$\n\nThis series is a function of $x,$ and it may converge for some values of $x$ and diverge for other values. How can we determine the values of $x$ for which the series is convergent?\n\nOne method that often works is the ratio test for convergence. We define $a_n=\\dfrac{x^n}{n^2},$ and we calculate the limit of the ratio of two successive terms, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\\to \\infty }|\\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\\\  & ={lim}_{n\\to \\infty }|\\frac{{x}^{n+1}}{(n+1)^{2}}\\cdot \\frac{{n}^{2}}{{x}^{n}}| \\\\  & ={lim}_{n\\to \\infty }\\frac{{n}^{2}}{(n+1)^{2}}\\,|x| \\\\  & =|x|{lim}_{n\\to \\infty }\\frac{{n}^{2}}{(n+1)^{2}} \\\\  & =|x|{lim}_{n\\to \\infty }\\frac{{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}+2n+1} \\\\  & =|x|{lim}_{n\\to \\infty }\\frac{1}{1+\\frac{2}{n}+\\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}} \\\\  & =|x|\\cdot 1 \\\\  & =|x|\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe ratio test says that the series converges if $L<1,$ diverges if $L>1,$ and is inconclusive if $L=1.$ So, the series converges if $|x|<1.$ Therefore, the series converges for any $x$ that lies in the open interval $(-1,1).$\n\nUnfortunately, the ratio test gives no conclusion about the convergence when $|x|=1,$ so the endpoints $x=1$ and $x=-1$ need to be investigated separately using another test for convergence.\n\n- When $x=1,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty} \\frac{x^n}{n^2}= \\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty} \\frac{1}{n^2} = 1 +\\frac{1}{2^2}+\\frac{1}{3^2}+\\frac{1}{4^2} +\\cdots \\,,\n$$\n\nwhich is convergent by the $p$-series test.\n\n- When $x=-1,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty} \\frac{x^n}{n^2}= \\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty} \\frac{(-1)^n}{n^2} = -1 +\\frac{1}{2^2}-\\frac{1}{3^2}+\\frac{1}{4^2} +\\cdots\n$$\n\nwhich is convergent by the alternating series test.\n\nTherefore, the series is convergent provided that $x \\in [-1,1].$ We call the interval $[-1,1]$ the **interval of convergence**.\n\nThe **radius of convergence** $R$ is half of the length of the interval (in the same way that the radius of a circle is equal to half the diameter of the circle). In our case, we have\n\n$$\nR = \\dfrac{1-(-1)}{2} = 1.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f42b2bfc-490f-56a9-876e-52951e6626f8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1296 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid :topic/math-academy-id 1179} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186101715 :step/content {:db/id 17592186102032 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find a solution to the differential equation\n\n$$\ny' = (1-2x)y^2 \\,,\n$$\n\nsatisfying the additional condition $y(0)=1.$ This additional condition $y(0)=1$ is called an **initial condition** or sometimes a **boundary condition** of the differential equation. \n\nFirst of all, we note that the given differential equation is separable, so we can separate variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{\\text{d}y}{\\text{d}x} & =(1-2x){y}^{2} \\\\ \\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\\cdot \\frac{\\text{d}y}{\\text{d}x} & =1-2x \\\\ \\int \\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\\cdot \\frac{\\text{d}y}{\\text{d}x}\\,\\text{d}x & =\\int (1-2x)\\,\\text{d}x \\\\ \\int \\frac{\\text{d}y}{{y}^{2}}\\, & =\\int (1-2x)\\,\\text{d}x \\\\ -\\frac{1}{y} & =x-{x}^{2}+C \\\\ \\frac{1}{y} & ={x}^{2}-x-C \\\\ y & =\\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-x-C}\\,.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe conclude that the general solution is\n\n$$\ny    =   \\dfrac {1} {x^2 - x - C} \\,,\n$$\n\nwhere $C$ is an arbitrary constant. \n\nNow we choose the constant $C$ such that the condition $y(0)=1$ is satisfied. Substituting $x=0$ and $y=1$ into the general solution and solving for $C,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}y(0)=\\frac{1}{0-0-C}=1\\,\\Rightarrow \\,C=-1\\,.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the particular solution of $y' = (1-2x)y^2$ that satisfies the condition $y(0)=1$ is\n\n$$\ny    =   \\dfrac {1} {x^2 - x - (-1)} = \\dfrac {1} {x^2 - x + 1}\\,.\n$$\n\nTo recap: the solution of a first-order separable ordinary differential equation (ODE) with an initial condition is obtained by \n\n- separating the variables,\n\n- integrating the equation, and then\n\n- substituting the condition into the solution to solve for the constant of integration." :tutorial/id #uuid "e2c4c33d-a1bd-537e-9daa-1960f765953d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 974 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id &=2t-8,\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nwhere $t\\in (-\\infty ,\\infty ).$\n\nSubstituting the above expressions for $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ into the equation of the elliptic cone, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2} & ={z}^{2} \\\\ 2{t}^{2}+2{t}^{2} & =(2t-8)^{2} \\\\ 4{t}^{2} & =4{t}^{2}-32t+64 \\\\ 32t & =64 \\\\ t & =2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we substitute our solution back into the equations of the line. For $t=2,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}x &=2 \\\\ y &=2 \\\\ z &=2(2)-8=-4.\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the point of intersection is $(2,2,-4).$"} {:db/id 17592186360497 :question/worked-solution "First, we write the equation of our line in parametric form:\n\n$$\n\\frac{x}{1}=\\frac{y+1}{1}=\\frac{z-2}{2}=t\\,⟹\\,\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}x &=t \\\\ y &=t-1 \\\\ z &=2t+2,\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nwhere $t\\in (-\\infty ,\\infty ).$\n\nSubstituting the above expressions for $x$, $y$, and $z$ into the equation of the sphere, we obtain:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y+4)^{2}+(z-2)^{2} & =9 \\\\ (t)^{2}+((t-1)+4)^{2}+((2t+2)-2)^{2} & =9 \\\\ (t)^{2}+(t+3)^{2}+(2t)^{2} & =9 \\\\ {t}^{2}+({t}^{2}+6t+9)+4{t}^{2} & =9 \\\\ 6{t}^{2}+6t+9 & =9 \\\\ 6{t}^{2}+6t & =0 \\\\ t(t+1) & =0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nHence, we get the solutions $t=0$ and $t=-1.$ \n\nNow, we substitute our solutions back into the equations of the line.\n\n- For $t=0$, we have\n\n$$\n\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}x &=(0)=0 \\\\ y &=(0)-1=-1 \\\\ z &=2(0)+2=2,\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nso the first point is $(0,-1,2).$\n\n- For $t=-1$, we have\n\n$$\n\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}x &=(-1)=-1 \\\\ y &=(-1)-1=-2 \\\\ z &=2(-1)+2=0,\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nso the second point is $(-1,-2,0).$\n\nTherefore, the points of intersection are \\\\ z &=t-2,\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nwhere $t\\in (-\\infty ,\\infty ).$\n\nSubstituting the above expressions for $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ into the equation of the elliptic cone, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2} & =4{z}^{2} \\\\ (2t-1)^{2}+3{t}^{2} & =4(t-2)^{2} \\\\ 4{t}^{2}-4t+1+3{t}^{2} & =4({t}^{2}-4t+4) \\\\ 4{t}^{2}-4t+1+3{t}^{2} & =4{t}^{2}-16t+16 \\\\ 3{t}^{2}+12t-15 & =0 \\\\ 3({t}^{2}+4t-5) & =0 \\\\ 3(t+5)(t-1) & =0 \\\\ t & =-5,1.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we substitute our solutions back into the equations of the line.\n\n- For $t=-5,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}x &=2(-5)-1=-11 \\\\ y &=-5 \\\\ z &=-5-2=-7,\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nso the first point is $(-11,-5,-7).$\n\n- For $t=1,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}x &=2(1)-1=1 \\\\ y &=1 \\\\ z &=1-2=-1,\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nso the second point is $(1,1,-1).$\n\nTherefore, the points of intersection are $(-11,-5,-7)$ {:db/id 17592186199369 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199499 :tutorial/content "Now, let's consider the intersection of the elliptic paraboloid \n$z=x^2+y^2$\nand the plane \n$z = x+y-\\dfrac{1}{4},$\nas shown below.\n\n![](images/1d/1d4b8db0985d437807f6e580bc6c2c16cacca1ea7c8e49ed4653717cdb3c9e27.png)\n\n \n\nNote that the intersection of the paraboloid and plane is given by the solution to the system\n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\\\ z=x+y-\\frac{1}{4}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\n- To find the projection of the intersection onto the $xy$-plane, we need to eliminate the variable $z$ from the system. The resulting projection curve will be an ellipse, as depicted below.\n\n![](images/52/520b57cf872ede31d4397d59a833c565147d82a45be1d6b2634f82e1effdff8c.png)\n\n \n\n- To find the projection of the intersection onto the $xz$-plane, we need to eliminate the variable $y$ from the system. The resulting projection curve will be an ellipse, as depicted below.\n\n![](images/05/059acf1ec5dadaa98b2cd4d4b6c79884e4facc96dd49664abbc247cfba86aaeb.png)\n\n \n\n- To find the projection of the intersection onto the $yz$-plane, we need to eliminate the variable $x$ from the system. The resulting projection curve will be an ellipse, as depicted below.\n\n![](images/80/80d3042d21d2e7265a40739ae1531ac30b03fea16fa67609a4e1b0eac8559411.png)\n\n \n\nLet's see some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "1d0d1b4d-a008-573c-b368-9ab2bfc7f41c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7833 :tutorial/title "Intersections of Surfaces With Planes"} :step/id #uuid "d692d6c4-d307-5093-8885-932a55dd02f4" :step/math-academy-id 45271 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199240}} {:db/id 17592186199370 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199500 :tutorial/content "Suppose we wish to find the points of intersection of the elliptic paraboloid \n$z=x^2+y^2$\nand the line with the equation\n$x = -y = -z+1.$\nThe line, paraboloid, and their points of intersection are shown below.\n\n![](images/51/5159ac99a1bc9f73c01df3c2cc2e6fb2093a3d68e00731609d7b62a6fa55149d.png)\n\n \n\nThe trick is to express the equation of the line in parametric form, substitute the parametric equations into the equation of the surface, and solve for the parameter.\n\nSo, first, we write the equation of our line in the parametric form:\n\n![](images/01/01357a5c6b72d7c976765aeed04db8afa3e3a80e13095d9be1ea2f2594ae5bf5.svg)\n\nwhere $t \\in (-\\infty,\\infty).$\n\nOur intersection points must belong to the line and the surface simultaneously. So, substituting the expressions for $x$, $y$, and $z$ from the parametric equation of the line into the equation of the paraboloid, we obtain the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}z & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\\\ (-t+1) & =(t)^{2}+(-t)^{2}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSimplifying this equation, we get\n\n$$\n2t^2+t - 1=0.\n$$\n\nThe solutions to this equation are\n$t=\\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $t=-1.$ 17592186045485} :question/problem "Find the $25$th term of the following arithmetic sequence. \n\n$$\n4,\\,8,\\,12,\\,16,\\,…\n$$" :question/worked-solution "The formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is\n\n$$\n{a}_{n}={a}_{1}+(n-1)d.\n$$\n\nFirst, we will write the formula for the $n$th term of this sequence. From the first few terms\n\n$$\n4,\\,8,\\,12,\\,16,\\,…,\n$$\n\nwe see that the first term is ${a}_{1}=4$ and the common difference is \n\n$$\nd=8-4=4.\n$$\n\nSo, we substitute into the formula and simplify:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\\\  & =4+(n-1)(4) \\\\  & =4+4n-4 \\\\  & =4n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we can use our formula to find the $25$th term. All we have to do is substitute $n=25:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =4n \\\\ {a}_{25} & =4(25) \\\\  & =100\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the $25$th term of the sequence is ${a}_{25}=100.$"} for $x\\in\\mathbb R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $\\pi$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x \\in [0,\\pi)$ to $x \\in \\mathbb{R}.$ Which of the following statements are true?\n\nI. $f(x+\\pi) = f(x)$ for all $x \\in \\mathbb{R}$\n\nII. $f(x) = F(x)$ for all $x \\in \\mathbb{R}$\n\nIII. $f\\left(x+\\dfrac{\\pi}{2}\\right) = f(x)$ for all $x \\in \\mathbb{R}$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f$ is the $\\pi$-periodic extension of $F,$ we have  \n\n- $f(x+\\pi)=f(x)$ for all $x\\in\\mathbb{R},$ and\n\n- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\\in[0,\\pi).$\n\nWith that in mind, we examine each statement in turn.\n\n- Statement I is true. This is exactly the definition of $\\pi$-periodicity:\n\n$$\nf(x+\\pi)=f(x)\n$$\n\nfor all $x\\in\\mathbb{R}.$\n\n- Statement II is true. Notice that $F$ itself is $\\pi$-periodic, because for any $x\\in\\mathbb{R},$ we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(x+\\pi )=\\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(x+\\pi ))=\\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+2\\pi )=\\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)=F(x).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince $F$ already satisfies the periodicity rule, the $\\pi$-periodic extension agrees with $F$ everywhere, so $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\\in\\mathbb{R}.$\n\n- Statement III is false. For example, take $x=0.$ Then,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x+\\frac{\\pi }{2})=f(\\frac{\\pi }{2})=F(\\frac{\\pi }{2})=\\operatorname{cos}⁡(\\pi )=-1,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhile\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x)=f(0)=F(0)\\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=1.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nHence, $f\\left(x+\\dfrac{\\pi}{2}\\right) \\neq f(x)$ for $x=0.$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I and II only\"."} {:db/id 17592186049353} {:db/id 17592186050172} {:db/id 17592186167264 :question/id #uuid "a8290119-5783-5de1-8f8a-4d7cbbad292c" :question/math-academy-id "q-338488" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186166962 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "544f5154-5213-5898-a45d-4546bc8004c8" :knowledge-point/title "Understanding the Periodic Extension of a Function"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8f77c573-2e4c-536e-af1e-09bf69080857" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186164763} {:answer/id #uuid "def9c8ed-19ee-58e5-969f-de9782068ef0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186164764} {:answer/id #uuid "37f67a97-5731-525d-8eea-9e2adde19ccb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186164765} {:answer/id #uuid "7a4cd2e6-0da4-5d24-b3e3-7bda7e4d5751" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186164766} {:answer/id #uuid "7ceba1a1-ec81-5071-86b8-40131cdb7eed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186164767}] :answer-field/id #uuid "757753c4-07c4-5df7-886c-f4e557b69cad" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186164762}] :question/problem "Let $F(x) = 2x$ for $x ∈ R$. **II.** $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\\in R$\n- **III.** $f(x+\\frac{\\pi }{2})=f(x-\\frac{\\pi }{2})$ for all $x\\in R$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f$ is the $\\pi /2$-periodic extension of $F,$ we have  \n\n- $f(x+\\frac{\\pi }{2})=f(x)$ for all $x\\in R,$ and\n\n- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\\in [0,\\frac{\\pi }{2}).$\n\nWith that in mind, we examine each statement in turn.\n\n- Statement I is For example, take $x=\\frac{3\\pi }{4}.$ Using the periodicity of $f(x):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(\\frac{3\\pi }{4})=f(\\frac{\\pi }{4}+\\frac{\\pi }{2})=f(\\frac{\\pi }{4})=F(\\frac{\\pi }{4})=\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\\cdot \\frac{\\pi }{4})=1,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhile\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(\\frac{3\\pi }{4})=\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\\cdot \\frac{3\\pi }{4})=\\operatorname{sin}⁡(\\frac{3\\pi }{2})=-1.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nHence, $f(x)\\ne F(x)$ for $x=\\frac{3\\pi }{4}.$\n\n- Statement III is true. }{2})=f((x-\\frac{\\pi }{2})+\\frac{\\pi }{2})=f(x).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince both sides equal $f(x),$ the statement is true for all $x\\in R.$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I and III \\int_{0}^{2\\pi} f(x)g(x)\\,\\textrm{d}x.\n$$\n\nFor a $2\\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous over $x\\in [0,2\\pi),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by \n\n$$\nf(x) \\sim \\dfrac{a_0}{2}+\\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty}\\left( a_n\\cos(nx)+b_n\\sin(nx)\\right),\n$$\n\nwhere $a_0,$ $a_n,$ and $b_n$ are constants to be determined. \n\nNow, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with }({a}_{n}\\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)⟩ & = \\\\ ⟨\\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},\\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)⟩+{\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)⟩+{\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)⟩ & = \\\\ }{b}_{n}⟨\\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince the functions\n$1, \\sin(x), \\cos(x), \\sin(2x), \\cos(2x), \\ldots$\nare orthogonal with respect to the defined }\\frac{1}{2}+\\frac{1}{2}\\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={[\\frac{1}{2}x+\\frac{1}{16}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)]}_{0}^{2\\pi } \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}(2\\pi -0)-\\frac{1}{16}(\\operatorname{sin}⁡(16\\pi )-\\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\\\  & =\\pi .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we obtain that\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)⟩ & infinite sum of simple sine and cosine waves. This representation is called the **Fourier series** for $f(x)$:\n\n$$\nf(x)\\sim \\frac{a_0}{2}+\\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty}\\big(a_n\\cos(nx)+b_n\\sin(nx)\\big)\n$$\n\nThe key idea is that we can \"build\" a complicated periodic graph by adding together basic waves. For example, below we have a discontinuous periodic function approximated by the first few terms of its Fourier series.\n\n![](images/39/392a8df0fab00010e76036aa0fec2c60f25b5766b3cacc7983b7443d909866eb.png)\n\nThis gives us a powerful way to analyze periodic behavior by breaking it down into simple oscillations. Fourier series play a central role in modeling vibrations, signals, and other repeating patterns.\n\nTo work with Fourier series, we typically start with a function defined on a single base interval, such as $[-\\pi,\\pi),$ and then extend it to be periodic over all real numbers. This process creates what is called a **periodic extension**.\n\nIn the next slide, we will define this concept formally and look at some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid by\n\n$$\n\\langle f(x), g(x)\\rangle=\\int_{-\\pi}^{\\pi} f(x)g(x)\\,\\textrm{d}x.\n$$\n\nAlso recall that functions $f$ and $g$ are called *orthogonal* (with respect to this inner product) if $\\langle f(x), g(x)\\rangle=0.$\n\nThe key fact we will use throughout this lesson is that the functions\n\n$$\n1,\\ \\cos(x),\\ \\sin(x),\\ \\cos(2x),\\ \\sin(2x),\\ \\ldots\n$$\n\nare orthogonal with respect to the inner product defined above.\n\nMore precisely, for integers $m,n\\ge 1,$ we have the following orthogonality relations on $[-\\pi,\\pi)$:\n\n- $\\langle \\cos(mx),\\cos(nx)\\rangle=0$ if $m\\ne n,$\n\n- $\\langle \\sin(mx),\\sin(nx)\\rangle=0$ if $m\\ne n,$ and\n\n- $\\langle \\sin(mx),\\cos(nx)\\rangle=0$ for all $m,n.$\n\nAlso, the constant function $1$ is orthogonal to every sine and cosine:\n\n- $\\langle 1,\\cos(nx)\\rangle=0,$ and\n\n- $\\langle 1,\\sin(nx)\\rangle=0$ for all $n\\ge 1.$\n\nFinally, we will also use the squared norms of these functions:\n\n$$\n\\langle 1,1\\rangle=2\\pi,\n\\quad\n\\langle \\cos(nx),\\cos(nx)\\rangle=\\langle \\sin(nx),\\sin(nx)\\rangle=\\pi\n\\quad\n\\text{for all } n\\ge 1.\n$$\n\nLet's see how this works in concrete examples.\n\n**Note:** Both intervals $[-\\pi,\\pi)$ and $[0,2\\pi)$ are considered standard in this context. {:db/id 17592186167949 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168043 :tutorial/content "Once again, recall that we are considering a $2\\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous on $[-\\pi,\\pi).$ We represent $f$ by its Fourier series\n\n$$\nf(x)\\sim \\dfrac{a_0}{2}+\\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty}\\big(a_n\\cos(nx)+b_n\\sin(nx)\\big).\n$$\n\nTo determine the coefficients, we use the inner product on $[-\\pi,\\pi)$:\n\n$$\n\\langle f(x), g(x)\\rangle=\\int_{-\\pi}^{\\pi} f(x)g(x)\\,\\textrm{d}x.\n$$\n\nWe have already seen the derivation for the coefficient $a_0$ early in the lesson.\n\nNow, we derive the formula for $a_n$ for $n\\ge 1{:}$\n\n- First, we take the inner product of both sides with $\\cos(nx){:}$\n\n$$\n\\langle f(x),\\cos(nx)\\rangle\n=\n\\left\\langle \\dfrac{a_0}{2}+\\sum_{k=1}^{\\infty}\\big(a_k\\cos(kx)+b_k\\sin(kx)\\big),\\,\\cos(nx)\\right\\rangle.\n$$\n\n- Using linearity, we get\n\n$$\n\\langle f(x),\\cos(nx)\\rangle\n=\n\\dfrac{a_0}{2}\\langle 1,\\cos(nx)\\rangle\n\\!+\\! \\sum_{k=1}^{\\infty} a_k\\langle \\cos(kx),\\cos(nx)\\rangle\n\\!+\\! \\sum_{k=1}^{\\infty} b_k\\langle \\sin(kx),\\cos(nx)\\rangle.\n$$\n\n- By orthogonality, $\\langle 1,\\cos(nx)\\rangle=0,$ $\\langle \\sin(kx),\\cos(nx)\\rangle=0$ for all $k,$ and $\\langle \\cos(kx),\\cos(nx)\\rangle=0$ whenever $k\\ne n,$ so\n\n$$\n\\langle f(x),\\cos(nx)\\rangle=a_n\\langle \\cos(nx),\\cos(nx)\\rangle.\n$$\n\nSince $\\displaystyle \\langle \\cos(nx),\\cos(nx)\\rangle=\\int_{-\\pi}^{\\pi} \\cos^2(nx)\\,\\textrm{d}x=\\pi,$ we obtain\n\n$$\na_n=\\dfrac{\\langle f(x),\\cos(nx)\\rangle}{\\langle \\cos(nx),\\cos(nx)\\rangle}\n=\\dfrac{1}{\\pi}\\int_{-\\pi}^{\\pi} f(x)\\cos(nx)\\,\\textrm{d}x.\n$$\n\nFinally, we derive the formula for $b_n$ for $n\\ge 1{:}$\n\n- First, we take the inner product of both sides with $\\sin(nx){:}$\n\n$$\n\\langle f(x),\\sin(nx)\\rangle\n=\n\\left\\langle \\dfrac{a_0}{2}+\\sum_{k=1}^{\\infty}\\big(a_k\\cos(kx)+b_k\\sin(kx)\\big),\\,\\sin(nx)\\right\\rangle.\n$$\n\n- Using linearity, we get\n\n$$\n\\langle f(x),\\sin(nx)\\rangle\n=\n\\dfrac{a_0}{2}\\langle 1,\\sin(nx)\\rangle\n\\!+\\! \\sum_{k=1}^{\\infty} a_k\\langle \\cos(kx),\\sin(nx)\\rangle\n\\!+\\! \\sum_{k=1}^{\\infty} b_k\\langle \\sin(kx),\\sin(nx)\\rangle.\n$$\n\n- By orthogonality, $\\langle 1,\\sin(nx)\\rangle=0,$ $\\langle \\cos(kx),\\sin(nx)\\rangle=0$ for all $k,$ and $\\langle \\sin(kx),\\sin(nx)\\rangle=0$ whenever $k\\ne n,$ so\n\n$$\n\\langle f(x),\\sin(nx)\\rangle=b_n\\langle \\sin(nx),\\sin(nx)\\rangle.\n$$\n\nSince $\\displaystyle \\langle \\sin(nx),\\sin(nx)\\rangle=\\int_{-\\pi}^{\\pi} \\sin^2(nx)\\,\\textrm{d}x=\\pi,$ we obtain\n\n$$\nb_n=\\dfrac{\\langle f(x),\\sin(nx)\\rangle}{\\langle \\sin(nx),\\sin(nx)\\rangle}\n=\\dfrac{1}{\\pi}\\int_{-\\pi}^{\\pi} f(x)\\sin(nx)\\,\\textrm{d}x.\n$$\n\nPutting these together, the Fourier coefficients are the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\\frac{1}{\\pi }{\\int }_{-\\pi }^{\\pi }f(x)\\,\\text{d}x \\\\ {a}_{n} & =\\frac{1}{\\pi }{\\int }_{-\\pi }^{\\pi }f(x)\\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\\,\\text{d}x,\\,n\\ge 1 \\\\ {b}_{n} & =\\frac{1}{\\pi }{\\int }_{-\\pi }^{\\pi }f(x)\\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\\,\\text{d}x,\\,n\\ge 1\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "dc7b8526-b305-5026-8e7d-5e426bbe1a15" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14668 :tutorial/title "Deriving the **$p$-periodic extension** $f$ is defined by the two properties:  \n\n- $f(x+p)=f(x)$ for all $x \\in \\mathbb{R}$\n\n- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x \\in [a,b).$\n\nFor example, let $F(x) = -x$ be defined on $x\\in [0,2).$ Now, suppose $f(x)$ is the $2$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\\in [0,2)$ to $x \\in \\mathbb{R}.$ The graphs of $y=F(x)$ and $y=f(x)$ are shown instance, consider the function $F(x)=2\\sin(x)$ defined on $x \\in [0,\\pi)$ and its $\\pi$-periodic extension $f(x).$ The graphs of $y=F(x)$ and $y=f(x)$ are shown below.\n\n![](images/b1/b1299bb593554a930a12870d39c74aa8d23ea97027b9e9e253e8fda6b592e42a.png)\n\nNotice that $f(x)$ is not just $2\\sin(x)!$ But it would coincide with $2\\sin(x)$ if we were to consider the $2\\pi$-periodic extension of $F(x)=2\\sin(x)$ from, say, $x \\in [0,2\\pi]$ to $x \\in \\mathbb{R}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bbf1ed42-199b-56dd-ba70-e35c3597339a" :tutorial/math-academy-id {:db/id 17592186168053 :tutorial/content "Let's derive the formula for the coefficient $a_0$ by taking the inner product of the entire Fourier series \n\n$$\nf(x)\\sim \\dfrac{a_0}{2}+\\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty}\\big(a_n\\cos(nx)+b_n\\sin(nx)\\big)\n$$\n\nwith the constant function $1.$\n\n- **Step 1.** Start with the Fourier series and take the inner product of both sides with $1{:}$\n\n$$\n\\langle f(x),1\\rangle\n=\n\\left\\langle \\dfrac{a_0}{2}+\\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty}\\big(a_n\\cos(nx)+b_n\\sin(nx)\\big),\\,1\\right\\rangle\n$$\n\n- **Step 2.** Use the linearity of the inner product to distribute it across the sum:\n\n$$\n\\langle f(x),1\\rangle\n=\n\\dfrac{a_0}{2}\\langle 1,1\\rangle\n+\\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty} a_n\\langle \\cos(nx),1\\rangle\n+\\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty} b_n\\langle \\sin(nx),1\\rangle\n$$\n\n- **Step 3.** Apply the orthogonality property. For any $n\\ge 1,$ we have $\\langle \\cos(nx),1\\rangle=0$ and $\\langle \\sin(nx),1\\rangle=0.$ This makes all the terms in the sums equal to zero:\n\n$$\n\\langle f(x),1\\rangle=\\dfrac{a_0}{2}\\langle 1,1\\rangle\n$$\n\n- **Step 4.** Solve for $a_0.$ We just need to calculate $\\langle 1,1\\rangle=\\displaystyle\\int_{-\\pi}^{\\pi} 1\\cdot 1\\,\\textrm{d}x=2\\pi.$\n\n$$\na_0=\\dfrac{2\\langle f(x),1\\rangle}{\\langle 1,1\\rangle}\n=\\dfrac{2\\int_{-\\pi}^{\\pi} f(x)\\cdot 1\\,\\textrm{d}x}{2\\pi}\n=\\dfrac{1}{\\pi}\\int_{-\\pi}^{\\pi} f(x)\\,\\textrm{d}x\n$$\n\nWe find the formulas for $a_n$ and $b_n$ (for $n\\ge 1$) in a similar way.\n\n- To find $a_n,$ we take the inner product of the Fourier series with $\\cos(nx).$ By orthogonality, the only term that is not zero on the right-hand side is the one involving $\\langle \\cos(nx),\\cos(nx)\\rangle.$\n\n$$\n\\langle f(x),\\cos(nx)\\rangle = a_n \\langle \\cos(nx), \\cos(nx)\\rangle\n$$\n\nSince $\\langle \\cos(nx),\\cos(nx)\\rangle = \\displaystyle\\int_{-\\pi}^{\\pi}\\cos^2(nx)\\,\\textrm{d}x = \\pi,$ we can solve for $a_n{:}$\n\n$$\na_n = \\dfrac{\\langle f(x),\\cos(nx)\\rangle}{\\langle \\cos(nx),\\cos(nx)\\rangle}\n=\\dfrac{1}{\\pi}\\int_{-\\pi}^{\\pi} f(x)\\cos(nx)\\,\\textrm{d}x\n$$\n\n- Similarly, to find $b_n,$ we take the inner product with $\\sin(nx){:}$\n\n$$\nb_n = \\dfrac{\\langle f(x),\\sin(nx)\\rangle}{\\langle \\sin(nx),\\sin(nx)\\rangle}\n=\\dfrac{1}{\\pi}\\int_{-\\pi}^{\\pi} f(x)\\sin(nx)\\,\\textrm{d}x\n$$\n\n**Note:** If $f$ is the $2\\pi$-periodic extension of a function $F$ defined on $[-\\pi,\\pi),$ then we can replace $f(x)$ with $F(x)$ inside the integrals.\n\nNow that we have the formulas for all the coefficients, let's work through a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "c5d2770f-53de-5939-9ec7-4155aef67173" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14854 :tutorial/title "The Formula For the Constant Term"} :step/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186167945 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168036 :tutorial/content "Recall that we can define an inner product on functions over $[-\\pi,\\pi)$ given by\n\n$$\n\\langle f(x), g(x)\\rangle=\\int_{-\\pi}^{\\pi} f(x)g(x)\\,\\textrm{d}x.\n$$\n\nAlso recall that functions $f$ and $g$ are called *orthogonal* (with respect to this inner product) if $\\langle f(x), g(x)\\rangle=0.$\n\nThe key fact we will use throughout this lesson is that the functions\n\n$$\n1,\\ \\cos(x),\\ \\sin(x),\\ \\cos(2x),\\ \\sin(2x),\\ \\ldots\n$$\n\nare orthogonal with respect to the inner product defined above.\n\nMore precisely, for integers $m,n\\ge 1,$ we have the following orthogonality relations on $[-\\pi,\\pi)$:\n\n- $\\langle \\cos(mx),\\cos(nx)\\rangle=0$ if $m\\ne n,$\n\n- $\\langle \\sin(mx),\\sin(nx)\\rangle=0$ if $m\\ne n,$ and\n\n- $\\langle \\sin(mx),\\cos(nx)\\rangle=0$ for all $m,n.$\n\nAlso, the constant function $1$ is orthogonal to every sine and cosine:\n\n- $\\langle 1,\\cos(nx)\\rangle=0,$ and\n\n- $\\langle 1,\\sin(nx)\\rangle=0$ for all $n\\ge 1.$\n\nFinally, we will also use the squared norms of these functions:\n\n$$\n\\langle inner product on $[-\\pi,\\pi)$:\n\n$$\n\\langle f(x), g(x)\\rangle=\\int_{-\\pi}^{\\pi} f(x)g(x)\\,\\textrm{d}x.\n$$\n\nWe have already seen the derivation for the coefficient $a_0$ early in the \\sin(kx),\\sin(nx)\\rangle.\n$$\n\n- By orthogonality, $\\langle 1,\\sin(nx)\\rangle=0,$ $\\langle \\cos(kx),\\sin(nx)\\rangle=0$ for all $k,$ and $\\langle \\sin(kx),\\sin(nx)\\rangle=0$ whenever f(x)\\sin(nx)\\,\\textrm{d}x.\n$$\n\nPutting these together, the Fourier coefficients are the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\\frac{1}{\\pi }{\\int }_{-\\pi }^{\\pi }f(x)\\,\\text{d}x piecewise continuous over $x\\in [-\\pi ,\\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by \n\n$$\nf(x)∼\\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }({a}_{n}\\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\n$$\n\nwhere ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. \n\nNow, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with \\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince the }({a}_{n}\\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),1⟩ & = \\\\ ⟨\\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},1⟩+{\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),1⟩+{\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty piecewise continuous over $x\\in [-\\pi ,\\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by \n\n$$\nf(x)∼\\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }({a}_{n}\\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\n$$\n\nwhere ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. \n\nNow, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with \\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince the }\\frac{1}{2}-\\frac{1}{2}\\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={[\\frac{1}{2}x-\\frac{1}{8}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)]}_{-\\pi }^{\\pi } \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}(\\pi -(-\\pi ))-\\frac{1}{8}(\\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\\pi )-(\\operatorname{sin}⁡(-4\\pi ))) \\\\  & =\\pi .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we obtain that\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & ={b}_{2}⟨\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ \\\\ {b}_{2} & =\\frac{⟨f(x),\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩}{⟨\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩} \\\\ {b}_{2} & =\\frac{1}{\\pi Fourier series of $f$ is given by\n\n$$\nf(x)∼\\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }({a}_{n}\\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)).\n$$\n\nSelect the correct options in the expression for the coefficient ${a}_{0}$ below, where $⟨\\,,⟩$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[0,2\\pi ).$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & ={{field-1}} \\\\  & ={{field-2}}\\,\\cdot \\,{{field-3}}\\end{aligned}\n$$" :question/worked-solution "The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\\in [0,2\\pi )$ is given by\n\n$$\n⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\\int }_{0}^{2\\pi }f(x)g(x)\\,\\text{d}x.\n$$\n\nFor a $2\\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that's piecewise continuous over $x\\in [0,2\\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by \n\n$$\nf(x)∼\\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }({a}_{n}\\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\n$$\n\nwhere ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. \n\nNow, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $1:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),1⟩ & = \\\\ ⟨\\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }({a}_{n}\\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),1⟩ & = \\\\ ⟨\\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},1⟩+{\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),1⟩+{\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),1⟩ & = \\\\ \\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,1⟩+{\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),1⟩+{\\sum }_{n=1}^{\\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),1⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince the functions\n$1,\\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$\nare orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is\n\n$$\n\\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,1⟩.\n$$\n\nComputing the inner product, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}⟨1,1⟩ & ={\\int }_{0}^{2\\pi }1\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={[x]}_{0}^{2\\pi } \\\\  & =2\\pi .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we obtain that\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),1⟩ & =\\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,1⟩ \\\\ {a}_{0} & =\\frac{2⟨f(x),1⟩}{⟨1,1⟩} \\\\ {a}_{0} & =\\frac{1}{\\pi }{\\int }_{0}^{2\\pi }f(x)\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\pi }\\cdot {\\int }_{0}^{2\\pi }({x}^{3}-2{x}^{2})\\,\\text{d}x.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "e117ceb3-8a58-58f9-8d3a-2b451769283b"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "067f1f01-946a-508e-8cd3-212922a30cb6" pattern\n\n$$\n{a}^{5}{b}^{0},\\,{a}^{4}{b}^{1},\\,{a}^{3}{b}^{2},\\,{a}^{2}{b}^{3},\\,{a}^{1}{b}^{4},\\,{a}^{0}{b}^{5}.\n$$\n\nThe $5$th row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,5,10,10,5,1).$ Therefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{(10y+\\frac{1}{2})}^{5} & =1{a}^{5}+5{a}^{4}b+10{a}^{3}{b}^{2}+10{a}^{2}{b}^{3}+5a{b}^{4}+1{b}^{5} \\\\  & =1(10y)^{5}{(\\frac{1}{2})}^{0}+5(10y)^{4}{(\\frac{1}{2})}^{1}+10(10y)^{3}{(\\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\\\  & \\,+10(10y)^{2}{(\\frac{1}{2})}^{3}+5(10y)^{1}{(\\frac{1}{2})}^{4}+1(10y)^{0}{(\\frac{1}{2})}^{5} \\\\  & =1(100\\,000{y}^{5})(1)+5(10\\,000{y}^{4})(\\frac{1}{2})+10(1\\,000{y}^{3})(\\frac{1}{4}) \\\\  & \\,+10(100{y}^{2})(\\frac{1}{8})+5(10y)(\\frac{1}{16})+1(1)(\\frac{1}{32}) \\\\  & =100\\,000{y}^{5}+\\frac{50\\,000{y}^{4}}{2}+\\frac{10\\,000{y}^{3}}{4}+\\frac{1\\,000{y}^{2}}{8}+\\frac{50y}{16}+\\frac{1}{32} \\\\  & =100\\,000{y}^{5}+25\\,000{y}^{4}+2\\,500{y}^{3}+125{y}^{2}+\\frac{25y}{8}+\\frac{1}{32}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, in ascending powers of $y$, the first three terms are\n\n$$\n\\frac{1}{32}+\\frac{25y}{8}+125{y}^{2}.\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186100807 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186100719 :question/id #uuid "bc866f37-17b6-59e0-9088-fd71a46c5b9a" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial\n\n$$\n(a+b)^{n}.\n$$\n\nHere we have that $n=3,$ $a=y,$ and $b=-x.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern\n\n$$\n{a}^{3}{b}^{0},\\,{a}^{2}{b}^{1},\\,{a}^{1}{b}^{2},\\,{a}^{0}{b}^{3}.\n$$\n\nThe $3$rd row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,3,3,1).$ Therefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{(y-x)}^{3} {:db/id 17592186101975 :tutorial/content "Multiplying a binomial by itself $n$ times is known as a **binomial expansion**.\nFor instance, multiplying the binomial $(a + b)$ by itself gives\n\n$$\n(a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2.\n$$\n\nLet's consider the binomial expansion of \n\n$$\n(a+b)^n,\n$$\n\nwhere $n$ is a positive integer.\n\nTo write out the expansion, we use two patterns to simplify most of the hard work: the **exponent pattern** and the **coefficient pattern**.\n\n- The **exponent pattern** is\n \n\n$$\na^{\\color{red}n}b^{\\color{blue}0},\\quad  a^{\\color{red}{n-1}}b^{{\\color{blue}1}}, \\quad   a^{{\\color{red}n-2}}b^{\\color{blue}2}, \\quad  \\dots\\quad   a^{\\color{red}2}b^{{\\color{blue}n-2}},\\quad    a^{\\color{red}1}b^{{\\color{blue}n - 1}}, \\quad   a^{\\color{red}0}b^{{\\color{blue}n}}.\n$$\n\nThe exponents of $a$ start at $n$ and go down ($n, n-1, \\cdots, 1, 0$) while the exponents of $b$ increase from $0$ to $n.$ In every term, the two exponents always add up to $n.$\n\n- The **coefficient pattern** can be found using Pascal's Triangle:\n \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned} &  &  &  &  &  & 1 \\\\  &  &  &  &  & 1 &  & 1 \\\\  &  &  &  & 1 &  & 2 &  & 1 \\\\  &  &  & 1 &  & 3 &  & 3 &  & 1 \\\\  &  & 1 &  & 4 &  & 6 &  & 4 &  & 1 \\\\  & 1 &  & 5 &  & 10 &  & 10 &  & 5 &  & 1 \\\\ ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe take the top row to be the $0$th row. Then, the $n$th row of Pascal's Triangle are the coefficients of $(a+b)^n.$\n\nLet's use this to expand the binomial \n\n$$\n(a+b)^3.\n$$\n\nThe exponent pattern is\n\n$$\na^{\\color{red}3}b^{\\color{blue}0},\\quad  a^{\\color{red}2}b^{\\color{blue}1}, \\quad a^{\\color{red}1}b^{\\color{blue}2}, \\quad  a^{\\color{red}0}b^{\\color{blue}3}.\n$$\n\nSince $n=3,$ the coefficient pattern is found using the $3$rd row in Pascal's Triangle: $(1,3,3,1).$ \n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n(a + b)^3  \n= \\mathbf{1}a^{\\color{red}3}b^{\\color{blue}0} + \\mathbf{3}a^{\\color{red}2}b^{\\color{blue}1} + \\mathbf{3}a^{\\color{red}1}b^{\\color{blue}2} + \\mathbf{1}a^{\\color{red}0}b^{\\color{blue}3}.\n$$\n\nFinally, simplifying the above gives\n\n$$\n(a + b)^3= a^{3} + 3a^{2}b + 3ab^{2} + b^{3} ,\n$$\n\nand we're done!" :tutorial/id #uuid "5a75ca66-5c0a-578d-ad4a-170fe5297413" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3385 :tutorial/title "Expanding Binomials Using :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to evaluate $\\displaystyle \\int x^3e^{x/2} \\textrm{d}x$. We can do it by applying integration by parts three times, but the calculation is pretty long. How can we speed it up?\n\nMultiple applications of integration by parts becomes quick and easy if we use the **tabular method**.\n\nLet's start by picking our $u$ and\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\textrm{d}v}{\\textrm{d}x}\n$$\n\nas normal:\n\n$$\nu = x^3\\,,\\quad \\dfrac{\\textrm{d}v}{\\textrm{d}x} = e^{x/2}\\,\n$$\n\nWe put this in a table, as shown below:\n\n| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same Color Products** |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3$ | $e^{x/2}$ |  |  |\n\nTo fill in the second row of the table, we differentiate the function in the first column and integrate the function in the second column. Doing this, we find\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\textrm{d}}{\\textrm{d}x}\\left(x^3\\right) = 3x^2\\,,\\quad \\int e^{x/2} \\textrm{d}x = 2e^{x/2}\\,\n$$\n\nFilling in our table, we get the following:\n\n| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same Color Products** |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3$ | $e^{x/2}$ |  |  |\n| $\\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 3x^2$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2e^{x/2}$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0} +$ |  |\n\nAt this step, we begin filling the third column. It always starts with a \"$+$\" and then the signs alternate at each subsequent step.\n\nWe continue by differentiating the expression in the first column and integrating the expression in the second column until we get zero in the first column.\n\n| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same Color Products** |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3$ | $e^{x/2}$ |  |  |\n| $\\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 3x^2$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2e^{x/2}$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0} +$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0}$ |\n| $\\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 6x$ | $\\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 4e^{x/2}$ | $\\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -$ | $\\color[rgb]{0,0.5,0}$ |\n| $\\color[rgb]{1,0,1} 6$ | $\\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 8e^{x/2}$ | $\\color[rgb]{0,0,1} +$ | $\\color[rgb]{0,0,1}$ |\n| $0$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,1}16e^{x/2}$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,1} -$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,1}$ |\n\nNow we multiply the same colored terms along with the same colored sign. Specifically we multiply $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3$ with ${\\color[rgb]{1,0,0} 2e^{x/2}}$, $\\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}3x^2$ with $\\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}4e^{x/2}$, and so on. We get\n\n| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same Color Products** |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3$ | $e^{x/2}$ |  |  |\n| $\\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}3x^2$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2e^{x/2}$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0} +$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0} 2x^3e^{x/2}$ |\n| $\\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 6x$ | $\\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 4e^{x/2}$ | $\\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -$ | $\\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -12x^2e^{x/2}$ |\n| $\\color[rgb]{1,0,1} 6$ | $\\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 8e^{x/2}$ | $\\color[rgb]{0,0,1} +$ | $\\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 48xe^{x/2}$ |\n| $0$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,1}16e^{x/2}$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,1} -$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,1} -96e^{x/2}$ |\n\nFinally, we add up all the terms of the last column to get the answer for our integral. We get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\intx^{3}e^{x/2}dx &= 2x^{3}e^{x/2} - 12x^{2}e^{x/2} + 48xe^{x/2} - 96e^{x/2} + C \\\\\n&= e^{x/2}(2x^{3} - 12x^{2} + 48x - 96) + C\n\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ce8fcadc-c0d9-53c8-93f1-7c7946d0ec31" :tutorial/math-academy-id 907 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "a907607b-33d6-5787-9f76-4ba49a6d4daf" :step/math-academy-id 1760 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097531}} {:db/id 17592186097531 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096680 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096479 :question/id #uuid "f4bca758-9903-505c-9828-0e1788b25d9f" :question/math-academy-id "e-499"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7ffce8b3-cc12-5a4d-88fd-77889b6bdd3f" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049069} {:db/id 17592186050489}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186097061} {:db/id 17592186097062}] :knowledge-point/title "Integrating a Trigonometric Expression Using the Tabular Method of Integration by Parts"} :step/id #uuid "2713bc66-d154-57b0-a43a-a25388531743" :step/math-academy-id 1761 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097532}} {:db/id 17592186097532 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096681 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096482 :question/id #uuid "96f1c791-f1cd-5a20-a6ee-004475bbd482" :question/math-academy-id "e-500"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "708faaf1-be43-502c-88dc-94270e8783b6" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186097127} {:db/id 17592186097168}] :knowledge-point/title "Integrating Algebraic and Exponential Expressions Using the Tabular Method of Integration by Parts"} :step/id #uuid "ba6ae8dc-2771-5af3-981d-bd894fac5705" :step/math-academy-id 1765}] :activity/title "The Tabular Method of Integration by Parts" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186096911} {:db/id 17592186097530 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097928 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to evaluate $\\displaystyle \\int x^3e^{x/2} \\textrm{d}x$. $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\\,Q,\\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by\n\n$$\n{∬}_{S}F\\cdot \\text{d}S={∬}_{D}(-P\\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\\text{d}A.\n$$\n\nWe first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+y)=2 \\\\ \\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+y)=1\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $F(x,y,z):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨-x,\\,-y,\\,xyz⟩{|}_{z=2x+y} \\\\  & =⟨-x,\\,-y,\\,xy(2x+y)⟩ \\\\  & =⟨{{-x}_{⏟}}_{P},\\,{{-y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\\,{{xy(2x+y)}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨-x,\\,-y,\\,xyz⟩\\cdot \\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-x)\\cdot 2-(-y)\\cdot (1)+xy(2x+y))\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y+2{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}{\\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+y+2{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\\,\\text{d}y\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}{[2xy+\\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\\frac{x{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+\\frac{1}{2}+{x}^{2}+\\frac{x}{3})\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+\\frac{7x}{3}+\\frac{1}{2})\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={[\\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\\frac{7{x}^{2}}{6}+\\frac{x}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{3}+\\frac{7}{6}+\\frac{1}{2} \\\\  & =2.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186278509 :question/id #uuid parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by\n\n$$\n{∬}_{S}F\\cdot \\text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\\cdot n\\,\\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\\times {r}_{v}^{′})\\,\\text{d}A.\n$$\n\nUsing the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as\n\n$$\nr(u,v)=⟨u,\\,v,\\,u+v⟩\n$$\n\nover the domain \n\n$$\nD=\\{(u,v)\\,:\\,0\\le u\\le 4,\\,-2\\le v\\le 3\\}.\n$$\n\nWe now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\\frac{∂x}{∂u},\\,\\frac{∂y}{∂u},\\,\\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\\\  & =⟨\\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\\,\\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\\,\\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v)⟩ \\\\  & =⟨1,\\,0,\\,1⟩ \\\\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\\frac{∂x}{∂v},\\,\\frac{∂y}{∂v},\\,\\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\\\  & =⟨\\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\\,\\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\\,\\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v)⟩ \\\\  & =⟨0,\\,1,\\,1⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, the fundamental vector product is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\\\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\\\ 0 & 1 & 1\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =⟨|\\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}|,\\,-|\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}|,\\,|\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}|⟩ \\\\  & =⟨-1,\\,-1,\\,1⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨z-y,\\,2y-z,\\,xy⟩{|}_{x=u,\\,\\,y=v,\\,\\,z=u+v} \\\\  & =⟨u+v-v,\\,2v-(u+v),\\,uv⟩ \\\\  & =⟨u,\\,v-u,\\,uv⟩\\cdot ⟨-1,\\,-1,\\,1⟩ \\\\  & =u\\cdot (-1)+(v-u)\\cdot (-1)+uv\\cdot 1 \\\\  & =-u-v+u+uv \\\\  & =uv-v.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the surface integral can be written as\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z-y,\\,2y-z,\\,xy⟩\\cdot \\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\\times {r}_{v}^{′})\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(uv-v)\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{4}{\\int }_{-2}^{3}uv-v\\,\\text{d}v\\,\\text{d}u.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186198610 :question/id #uuid "a3bcb9d3-050c-5ab9-bd2a-436465223147" :question/math-academy-id "q-161360" general formula for the flux through an *upward-oriented* Cartesian surface.\n\nFor a surface $S$ with parametrization $\\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\iint\\limits_S \\mathbf{F} \\cdot \\textrm{d}\\mathbf{S}\n=\n\\iint\\limits_S \\mathbf{F} \\cdot \\mathbf{n} \\,\\textrm{d}S\n=\n\\iint\\limits_D \\mathbf{F}(\\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \\cdot (\\mathbf{r}'_u \\times \\mathbf{r}'_v) \\,\\textrm{d}A.\n$$\n\nConsider a surface $S$ given by the equation $z=g(x,y).$ The canonical parameterization of the surface is\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{r}(x,y) = \\left\\langle x,\\: y,\\: g(x,y) \\right\\rangle.\n$$\n\nComputing the tangent vectors to the grid curves, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨1,\\,0,\\,\\frac{∂g}{∂x}⟩ \\\\ {r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨0,\\,1,\\,\\frac{∂g}{∂y}⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, the fundamental vector product is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\\times {r}_{y}^{′} & =|\\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\\\ 1 & 0 & \\frac{∂g}{∂x} \\\\ 0 & 1 & \\frac{∂g}{∂y}\\end{aligned}|=⟨-\\frac{∂g}{∂x},\\,-\\frac{∂g}{∂y},\\,1⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNotice that the $\\mathbf k$-component is positive, which indicates that our surface is upward-oriented.\n\nTherefore, the surface integral can be written as\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\\cdot \\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(x,y))\\cdot ({r}_{x}^{′}\\times {r}_{y}^{′})\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\\,Q,\\,R⟩\\cdot ⟨-\\frac{∂g}{∂x},\\,-\\frac{∂g}{∂y},\\,1⟩\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(-P\\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\\,\\text{d}A.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe summarize as follows:\n\n- *For a surface $S$ given by $z = g(x,y)$ for $(x,y) \\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \\left\\langle P,\\: Q,\\: R \\right\\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*\n\n$$\n\\iint\\limits_S \\mathbf{F} \\cdot \\textrm{d}\\mathbf{S}\n=\n\\iint\\limits_D \\left( -P\\dfrac{\\partial g}{\\partial x} - Q\\dfrac{\\partial g}{\\partial y} + R \\right) \\textrm{d}A.\n$$\n\nWe have analogous results for surfaces of the form $y = h(x,z)$ and $x=k(y,z){:}$\n\n- *For a surface $S$ given by $y = h(x,z)$ for $(x,z) \\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \\left\\langle P,\\: Q,\\: R \\right\\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*\n\n$$\n\\iint\\limits_S \\mathbf{F} \\cdot \\textrm{d}\\mathbf{S}\n=\n\\iint\\limits_D \\left( -P\\dfrac{\\partial h}{\\partial x} + Q - R\\dfrac{\\partial h}{\\partial z} \\right) \\textrm{d}A,\n$$\n\n*where the unit normal to the surface is chosen such that the $\\mathbf j$-component is positive.*\n\n- *For a surface $S$ given $x = k(y,z)$ for $(y,z) \\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \\left\\langle P,\\: Q,\\: R \\right\\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*\n\n$$\n\\iint\\limits_S \\mathbf{F} \\cdot \\textrm{d}\\mathbf{S}\n=\n\\iint\\limits_D \\left( P - Q\\dfrac{\\partial k}{\\partial y} - R\\dfrac{\\partial k}{\\partial z} \\right) \\textrm{d}A,\n$$\n\n*where the unit normal to the surface is chosen such that the $\\mathbf i$-component is positive.*" :tutorial/id #uuid \\leq 1$ and $0 \\leq y \\leq 1.$ \n\nFor surfaces like this, substituting $x=u$ and $y=v,$ we obtain a parametrization \n\n$$\n\\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \\left\\langle u,\\: v,\\: 2v-2u \\right\\rangle\n$$\n\nover the domain \n\n$$\nD = \\big\\{ (u,v) \\: : \\: 0 \\leq u \\leq 1, \\: 0 \\leq v \\leq 1 \\big\\}.\n$$\n\n \n\nRecall that for a surface $S$ with parametrization $\\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\iint\\limits_S \\mathbf{F} \\cdot \\textrm{d}\\mathbf{S}\n=\n\\iint\\limits_S \\mathbf{F} \\cdot \\mathbf{n} \\,\\textrm{d}S\n=\n\\iint\\limits_D \\mathbf{F}(\\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \\cdot (\\mathbf{r}'_u \\times \\mathbf{r}'_v) \\,\\textrm{d}A.\n$$\n\nWe now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\\frac{∂x}{∂u},\\,\\frac{∂y}{∂u},\\,\\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\\\  & =⟨\\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\\,\\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\\,\\frac{∂}{∂u}(2v-2u)⟩ \\\\  & =⟨1,\\,0,\\,-2⟩ \\mathbf{F}(\\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \\cdot (\\mathbf{r}'_u \\times \\mathbf{r}'_v) \\,\\textrm{d}A.\n$$\n\nConsider a surface $S$ given by the equation $z=g(x,y).$ The canonical parameterization of the surface is\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{r}(x,y) = \\left\\langle x,\\: y,\\: g(x,y) \\right\\rangle.\n$$\n\nComputing the tangent vectors to the grid curves, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨1,\\,0,\\,\\frac{∂g}{∂x}⟩ \\\\ {r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨0,\\,1,\\,\\frac{∂g}{∂y}⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, the fundamental vector product is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\\times {r}_{y}^{′} & =|\\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\\\ 1 & 0 & \\frac{∂g}{∂x} \\\\ 0 & 1 & \\frac{∂g}{∂y}\\end{aligned}|=⟨-\\frac{∂g}{∂x},\\,-\\frac{∂g}{∂y},\\,1⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNotice that the $\\mathbf k$-component is positive, which indicates that our surface is upward-oriented.\n\nTherefore, the surface integral can be written as\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\\cdot \\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(x,y))\\cdot ({r}_{x}^{′}\\times {r}_{y}^{′})\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\\,Q,\\,R⟩\\cdot ⟨-\\frac{∂g}{∂x},\\,-\\frac{∂g}{∂y},\\,1⟩\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(-P\\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\\,\\text{d}A.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe summarize as follows:\n\n- *For a surface $S$ given by $z = g(x,y)$ for $(x,y) \\in D,$ the flux of a vector field \\mathbf{F} \\cdot \\textrm{d}\\mathbf{S}\n=\n\\iint\\limits_D \\left( -P\\dfrac{\\partial h}{\\partial x} + Q - R\\dfrac{\\partial h}{\\partial z} \\right) \\textrm{d}A,\n$$\n\n*where the unit normal to the surface is chosen such that the $\\mathbf j$-component is positive.*\n\n- *For a surface $S$ given $x = k(y,z)$ for $(y,z) \\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = $S$ is defined by $z=2x+y$ for $0\\le x\\le 1$ and $0\\le y\\le 1.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\\,Q,\\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by\n\n$$\n{∬}_{S}F\\cdot \\text{d}S={∬}_{D}(-P\\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\\text{d}A.\n$$\n\nWe first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+y)=2 \\\\ \\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+y)=1\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $F(x,y,z):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨-x,\\,-y,\\,xyz⟩{|}_{z=2x+y} \\\\  & =⟨-x,\\,-y,\\,xy(2x+y)⟩ \\\\  & =⟨{{-x}_{⏟}}_{P},\\,{{-y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\\,{{xy(2x+y)}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨-x,\\,-y,\\,xyz⟩\\cdot \\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-x)\\cdot 2-(-y)\\cdot (1)+xy(2x+y))\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y+2{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}{\\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+y+2{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\\,\\text{d}y\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}{[2xy+\\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\\frac{x{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+\\frac{1}{2}+{x}^{2}+\\frac{x}{3})\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+\\frac{7x}{3}+\\frac{1}{2})\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={[\\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\\frac{7{x}^{2}}{6}+\\frac{x}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{3}+\\frac{7}{6}+\\frac{1}{2} \\\\  & =2.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "d9521b99-85a2-58ce-8fc3-398a930f1cb4" n\\,\\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\\times {r}_{v}^{′})\\,\\text{d}A.\n$$\n\nUsing the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as\n\n$$\nr(u,v)=⟨u,\\,v,\\,u-3v⟩\n$$\n\nover the domain \n\n$$\nD=\\{(u,v)\\,:\\,-1\\le u\\le 2,\\,-1\\le v\\le 3\\}.\n$$\n\nWe now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\\frac{∂x}{∂u},\\,\\frac{∂y}{∂u},\\,\\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\\\  & =⟨\\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\\,\\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\\,\\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-3v)⟩ \\\\  & =⟨1,\\,0,\\,1⟩ \\\\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\\frac{∂x}{∂v},\\,\\frac{∂y}{∂v},\\,\\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\\\  & =⟨\\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\\,\\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\\,\\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-3v)⟩ \\\\  & =⟨0,\\,1,\\,-3⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, the fundamental vector product is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\\\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\\\ 0 & 1 & -3\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =⟨|\\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\\\ 1 & -3\\end{aligned}|,\\,-|\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ 0 & -3\\end{aligned}|,\\,|\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}|⟩ \\\\  & =⟨-1,\\,3,\\,1⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨x+z,\\,2z,\\,y+z⟩{|}_{x=u,\\,\\,y=v,\\,\\,z=u-3v} \\\\  & =⟨u+u-3v,\\,2(u-3v),\\,v+u-3v⟩ \\\\  & =⟨2u-3v,\\,2u-6v,\\,u-2v⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThen, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨2u-3v,\\,2u-6v,\\,u-2v⟩\\cdot ⟨-1,\\,3,\\,1⟩ \\\\  & =(2u-3v)\\cdot (-1)+(2u-6v)\\cdot (3)+(u-2v)\\cdot 1 \\\\  & =-2u+3v+6u-18v+u-2v \\\\  & =5u-17v.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the surface integral can be written as\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z-y,\\,2y-z,\\,xy⟩\\cdot \\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\\times {r}_{v}^{′})\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(5u-17v)\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={\\int }_{-1}^{2}{\\int }_{-1}^{3}(5u-17v)\\,\\text{d}v\\,\\text{d}u.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "89beea92-c19b-5b20-850a-a15dc788a7e6" :step/next =⟨\\frac{∂x}{∂v},\\,\\frac{∂y}{∂v},\\,\\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\\\  & =⟨\\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\\,\\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\\,\\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-3v)⟩ \\\\  & =⟨0,\\,1,\\,-3⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, the fundamental vector product is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\\\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\\\ 0 & 1 & -3\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =⟨|\\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\\\ 1 & -3\\end{aligned}|,\\,-|\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ 0 & -3\\end{aligned}|,\\,|\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}|⟩ \\\\  & =⟨-1,\\,3,\\,1⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we substitute the 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "acc5680d-481f-574e-9c37-7723114fd2f1" :question/math-academy-id "q-161381" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z+x,\\,y+2z,\\,x-4y⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=2x-4y$ for $-2\\le x\\le 0$ and $-1\\le y\\le 5.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as\n\n$$\n{∬}_{S}F\\cdot \\text{d}S={\\int }_{-2}^{0}{\\int }_{-1}^{5}\\boxed{}\\,\\text{d}v\\,\\text{d}u.\n$$\n\nWhat is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by\n\n$$\n{∬}_{S}F\\cdot \\text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\\cdot n\\,\\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\\times {r}_{v}^{′})\\,\\text{d}A.\n$$\n\nUsing the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as\n\n$$\nr(u,v)=⟨u,\\,v,\\,2u-4v⟩\n$$\n\nover the domain \n\n$$\nD=\\{(u,v)\\,:\\,-2\\le u\\le 0,\\,-1\\le v\\le 5\\}.\n$$\n\nWe now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\\frac{∂x}{∂u},\\,\\frac{∂y}{∂u},\\,\\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\\\  & =⟨\\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\\,\\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\\,\\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u-4v)⟩ \\\\  & =⟨1,\\,0,\\,2⟩ \\\\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\\frac{∂x}{∂v},\\,\\frac{∂y}{∂v},\\,\\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\\\  & =⟨\\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\\,\\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\\,\\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u-4v)⟩ \\\\  & =⟨0,\\,1,\\,-4⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, the fundamental vector product is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\\\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\\\ 0 & 1 & -4\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =⟨|\\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\\\ 1 & -4\\end{aligned}|,\\,-|\\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\\\ 0 & -4\\end{aligned}|,\\,|\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}|⟩ \\\\  & =⟨-2,\\,4,\\,1⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨z+x,\\,y+2z,\\,x-4y⟩{|}_{x=u,\\,\\,y=v,\\,\\,z=2u-4v} \\\\  & =⟨2u-4v+u,\\,v+2(2u-4v),\\,u-4v⟩ \\\\  & =⟨3u-4v,\\,4u-7v,\\,u-4v⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThen, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨3u-4v,\\,4u-7v,\\,u-4v⟩\\cdot ⟨-2,\\,4,\\,1⟩ \\\\  & =(3u-4v)\\cdot (-2)+(4u-7v)\\cdot 4+(u-4v)\\cdot 1 \\\\  & =-6u+8v+16u-28v+u-4v \\\\  & =11u-24v.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the surface integral can be written as\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z+x,\\,y+2z,\\,x-4y⟩\\cdot \\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\\times {r}_{v}^{′})\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(11u-24v)\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={\\int }_{-2}^{0}{\\int }_{-1}^{5}(11u-24v)\\,\\text{d}v\\,\\text{d}u.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "bfcd2b83-a5f2-52eb-abff-126d7bb1b47b" :step/next So we have\n\n$$\n\\lim_\\limits{x\\to -4^-} f(x)=\\text{DNE}\n$$\n\nand therefore\n\n$$\n\\lim_\\limits{x\\to -4} f(x)=\\text{DNE}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186120390 :question/id #uuid "65ff03b7-53b4-5f67-b1ce-746099c419cd" :question/math-academy-id "q-35501"} {:db/id 17592186120392 :question/id #uuid "b5b2ae47-ab2b-5ac5-8edd-d55265a307ac" :question/math-academy-id "q-35510"} {:db/id 17592186119871 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119535 :question/id #uuid "a9e611ae-68f1-5618-a53b-2c9b3606d468" :question/math-academy-id "e-15"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e021f949-0f55-50b8-8681-0b1ce71b21d9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048943} {:db/id 17592186049078}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120389 :question/id #uuid "7805d540-3137-5d89-bd04-cc371720703d" :question/math-academy-id "q-35499"} {:db/id 17592186120393 :question/id #uuid "906b500e-f169-5aed-8d52-1c7e1c9c3bbf" :question/math-academy-id "q-35511"}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Infinite Limits when the Left and Right Limits are the Same"} {:db/id 17592186119535 :question/id #uuid "a9e611ae-68f1-5618-a53b-2c9b3606d468" :question/math-academy-id "e-15" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186119871 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e021f949-0f55-50b8-8681-0b1ce71b21d9" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Infinite Limits when the Left and Right Limits are the Same"}] :question/problem "The figure below shows the graph of $f(x)$. Evaluate $\\lim_\\limits{x \\to \\,4} f(x)$.\n\n![](images/16/168433761f6629ad555a70acf5764f93246484c253f3c7ecba8fdfdfd87c2adf.png)" :question/worked-solution "We see from the graph that as $x$ approaches $4$ from the left, the function $f(x)$ approaches $-\\infty$. So, the left-hand limit is\n\n$$\n\\lim_\\limits{x\\rightarrow 4^-} f(x) = -\\infty \\,\n$$\n\nLikewise, as $x$ approaches $4$ from the right, the function $f(x)$ again approaches $-\\infty$. So, the right-hand limit is\n\n$$\n\\lim_\\limits{x\\rightarrow 4^+} f(x) = -\\infty \\,\n$$\n\nConsequently,\n\n$$\n\\lim_\\limits{x\\rightarrow 4} f(x)=-\\infty \\,\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186048943} {:db/id 17592186120389 :question/id #uuid "7805d540-3137-5d89-bd04-cc371720703d" :question/math-academy-id "q-35499"} {:db/id 17592186120393 :question/id #uuid "906b500e-f169-5aed-8d52-1c7e1c9c3bbf" :question/math-academy-id "q-35511"} {:db/id 17592186048515} {:db/id 17592186049614} {:db/id 17592186050490} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186120776} :activity/id #uuid "e4df6ef2-6323-5da7-9712-42a8b0ec2db6" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186051049 :topic/id #uuid "7d21c9de-358a-52ec-b910-f6117a085d7f" :topic/math-academy-id 1814} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186120776 :step/content {:db/id 17592186120993 :tutorial/content "Until now, all limits of the form $\\lim\\limits_{x \\to a} f(x)$ that we have encountered have evaluated to either a finite number or $\\text{DNE}$. However, there is another possibility: the limit could be *infinite*!\n\nFor example, consider the function $f(x)$ whose graph is shown below. This function has a vertical asymptote at $x=1$, and the function value $f(x)$ grows without bound as $x$ approaches the asymptote $x=1$. What is the limit $\\lim_\\limits{x\\to 1} f(x)$?\n\n![](images/ab/ab9d57d3952fe0221616f9e64e1295fd0511703bdd5ed3a5fe91113cc7c8bf1b.png)\n\nRemember that in order for computing any limit, in this case, $\\lim_\\limits{x\\to 1} f(x)$, we have to compute the left and right-sided limits separately and ensure that they match up.\n\n- **Left-sided limit:** As we approach $x=1$ (the vertical asymptote) from the left side of the graph, the function $f(x)$ increases without bound, approaching $\\infty$. We conclude that\n$\\lim_\\limits{x\\to 1^-} f(x) = \\infty$.\n- **Right-sided limit:** Likewise, as we approach the vertical asymptote $x=1$ from the right side of the graph, $f(x)$ still approaches $\\infty$. Consequently,\n$\\lim_\\limits{x\\to 1^+} f(x) = \\infty$.\n\nWe see that both the left and right limits exist and are equal to $\\infty$:\n\n$$\n\\lim_\\limits{x\\to 1^-} f(x) = \\lim_\\limits{x\\to 1^+} f(x) = \\infty\n$$\n\nAs a result, the overall limit is also equal to $\\infty$:\n\n$$\n\\lim_\\limits{x\\to 1} f(x) = \\infty\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6db8e507-0d4f-555c-b39b-e6a52ace2cd9" Which of the following is a basis of the eigenspace corresponding to the eigenvalue $\\lambda =3?$" :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation \n\n$$\n(A-\\lambda I)\\text{x}=0.\n$$\n\n \n\nIn our case, we have $\\lambda =3.$ So, we get \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}A-\\lambda I & =\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 4 \\\\ 2 & 1 & -4 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 3\\end{bmatrix}-3\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 1\\end{bmatrix}=\\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & 4 \\\\ 2 & -2 & -4 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 0\\end{bmatrix}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find the eigenvectors, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:\n\n$$\n\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3} &=0 \\\\ 2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3} &=0 \\\\ 0 &=0\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nSo, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}M & =\\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & 4 & 0 \\\\ 2 & -2 & -4 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\\\  & ∼\\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & 4 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\\end{bmatrix}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nIn the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}.$ So, the general solution is\n\n$$\n\\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\\\ {x}_{2} \\\\ {x}_{3}\\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}\\begin{bmatrix}1 \\\\ 1 \\\\ 0\\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\\begin{bmatrix}2 \\\\ 0 \\\\ 1\\end{bmatrix},\\,{x}_{2},{x}_{3}\\in R.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the required basis is\n\n$$\nB=\\{\\begin{bmatrix}1 \\\\ 1 \\\\ 0\\end{bmatrix},\\begin{bmatrix}2 \\\\ 0 \\\\ 1\\end{bmatrix}\\}.\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186125091 :question/id #uuid "02557e97-c0e8-5b1b-bde6-e5dfd458ddff" :question/math-academy-id "q-37622"} {:db/id expected value of a discrete random variable $X$ given a joint mass function $f(x,y),$ we must first find its marginal mass function $f_X.$ Once the marginal mass function is known, we can then compute $\\textrm{E}[X]$ using the formula\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[X]\n= \\sum\\limits_{i=1}^n x_i \\, f_X(x_i).\n$$\n\nFor example, consider the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y,$ shown below.\n\n| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| $X=1$ | $0.05$ | $0.15$ |\n| $X=2$ | $0.7$ | $0.1$ |\n\nRecall that the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals. Since we're only interested in the expected value of $X,$ let's compute the row totals only.\n\n| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | $f_X$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| $X=1$ | $0.05$ | $0.15$ | $\\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\\color{blue}0.20}$ |\n| $X=2$ | $0.7$ | $0.1$ | $\\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\\color{blue}0.80}$ |\n\nTherefore, the marginal mass function of $X$ is as follows:\n\n| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| $f_X(x)$ | $0.20$ | $0.80$ |\n|  |  |  |\n\nWe can now compute the expected value of $X\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\text{E}[X] & ={\\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\\,{f}_{X}({x}_{i}) \\\\  & =1\\cdot 0.2+2\\cdot 0.8 \\\\  & =0.2+1.6 \\\\  & =1.8\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we conclude that $\\textrm{E}[X] = 1.8.$" :tutorial/id #uuid structure $\\mathbb{R}^n$ is called a **vector space**. However, many other structures possess properties similar to $\\mathbb{R}^n.$ These other structures can be called vector spaces too. \n\nIn this lesson, we'll learn about some important properties used to construct vector spaces. We begin by discussing what it means for a set to be **closed** under addition and scalar multiplication.\n\nAs an example, consider the set $\\mathrm{M}_2(\\mathbb{R})$ of all $2 \\times 2$ matrices with real entries:\n\n![](images/a5/a53ec7e9416ae5eee4a1408df358302567a5aa98a393d6ddcb19e861645d2317.svg)\n\nFor this set of matrices, we can define two operations:\n\n- the addition of two matrices, and\n\n- the multiplication of a matrix by a real number (called a scalar).\n\nNow, notice the following:\n\n- $\\mathrm{M}_2(\\mathbb{R})$ is **closed under addition**. This means that the sum of *any* two matrices from $\\mathrm{M}_2(\\mathbb{R})$ is also a matrix in $\\mathrm{M}_2(\\mathbb{R}).$\n\n- $\\mathrm{M}_2(\\mathbb{R})$ is **closed under scalar multiplication**. This means that the product of *any* scalar and *any* matrix from $\\mathrm{M}_2(\\mathbb{R})$ is also a matrix in $\\mathrm{M}_2(\\mathbb{R}).$\n\nIdentifying that a set is closed under addition and scalar multiplication is an essential first step in determining whether a set can form a vector space." :tutorial/id #uuid "18653f19-b4cf-5f0f-ab39-b1ae33ecdc6b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4935 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "befa8020-1248-59aa-b092-5fd7f5b45c2e" :step/math-academy-id 30790 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125600}} {:db/id 17592186125590 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124628 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124432 :question/id #uuid "ff4fdeaf-bdb3-54d7-b5e9-2f3ad88b55a1" :question/math-academy-id "e-9960"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cb02b67c-90d9-5baf-b00e-590e9271d89e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049304} {:db/id 17592186049755} {:db/id 17592186050782} {:db/id 17592186050979}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125240} {:db/id 17592186125241} {:db/id 17592186278339} {:db/id 17592186278340} {:db/id 17592186278341} {:db/id 17592186278342} {:db/id 17592186281458} {:db/id 17592186323707} {:db/id 17592186329743} {:db/id 17592186440653} {:db/id 17592186440654} {:db/id 17592186440655} {:db/id 17592186445223}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Sets Closed Under Addition and Scalar Multiplication"} :step/id #uuid "78f1d4af-7528-5705-8b7b-224b627efd47" :step/math-academy-id 37506 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125341}} {:db/id 17592186125600 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125860 :tutorial/content "It's important to realize that not all sets are closed under addition and scalar multiplication. Sets not closed under addition and scalar multiplication *cannot* be vector spaces. \n\nFor instance, let $S$ be the set of all polynomials with real coefficients whose degree is greater than or equal to $5.$  \n\nWe note that $S$ is not closed under addition. To see why this is the case, let's define the polynomials $p(x),q(x)\\in S$ as \n\n$$\np(x) = x^5, \\qquad q(x) = 1-x^5.\n$$\n\nAdding the two polynomials using regular polynomial addition, we get\n\n$$\np(x) + q(x) = x^5 + (1-x^5) = 1\\notin S\n$$\n\nThe sum $p(x) + q(x)$ is not in $S$ because it is a polynomial of degree zero, which is less than $5.$\n\nTherefore, we conclude that our set $S$ is *not* closed under addition." :tutorial/id #uuid "b014039e-61b6-58d7-8f35-a72e6153c126" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6230 :tutorial/title "Sets That Are Not Closed"} :step/id #uuid
