17592186125833 :tutorial/content "The structure $\\mathbb{R}^n$ is called a **vector space**. However, many other structures possess properties similar to $\\mathbb{R}^n.$ These other structures can be called vector spaces too. \n\nIn this lesson, we'll learn about some important properties used to construct vector spaces. We begin by discussing what it means for a set to be **closed** under addition and scalar multiplication.\n\nAs an example, consider the set $\\mathrm{M}_2(\\mathbb{R})$ of all $2 \\times 2$ matrices with real entries:\n\n![](images/a5/a53ec7e9416ae5eee4a1408df358302567a5aa98a393d6ddcb19e861645d2317.svg)\n\nFor this set of matrices, we can define two operations:\n\n- the addition of two matrices, and\n\n- the multiplication of a matrix by a real number (called a scalar).\n\nNow, notice the following:\n\n- $\\mathrm{M}_2(\\mathbb{R})$ is **closed under addition**. This means that the sum of *any* two matrices from $\\mathrm{M}_2(\\mathbb{R})$ is also a matrix in $\\mathrm{M}_2(\\mathbb{R}).$\n\n- $\\mathrm{M}_2(\\mathbb{R})$ is **closed under scalar multiplication**. This means that the product of *any* scalar and *any* matrix from $\\mathrm{M}_2(\\mathbb{R})$ is also a matrix in $\\mathrm{M}_2(\\mathbb{R}).$\n\nIdentifying that a set is closed under addition and scalar multiplication is an essential first step in determining whether a set can form a vector space." :tutorial/id #uuid "18653f19-b4cf-5f0f-ab39-b1ae33ecdc6b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4935 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186125600 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125860 :tutorial/content "It's important to realize that not all sets are closed under addition and scalar multiplication. Sets not closed under addition and scalar multiplication *cannot* be vector spaces. \n\nFor instance, let $S$ be the set of all polynomials with real coefficients whose degree is greater than or equal to $5.$  \n\nWe note that $S$ is not closed under addition. To see why this is the case, let's define the polynomials $p(x),q(x)\\in S$ as \n\n$$\np(x) = x^5, \\qquad q(x) = 1-x^5.\n$$\n\nAdding the two polynomials using regular polynomial addition, we get\n\n$$\np(x) + q(x) = x^5 + (1-x^5) = 1\\notin S\n$$\n\nThe sum $p(x) + q(x)$ is not in $S$ because it is a polynomial of degree zero, which is less than $5.$\n\nTherefore, we conclude that our set $S$ is *not* closed under addition." :tutorial/id #uuid "b014039e-61b6-58d7-8f35-a72e6153c126" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6230 :tutorial/title "Sets That Are Not Closed"} :step/id #uuid "1402186a-b64d-5406-9767-99815ff7ecc1" :step/math-academy-id 37838 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125590}} {:db/id 17592186125590 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124628 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124432 :question/id #uuid "ff4fdeaf-bdb3-54d7-b5e9-2f3ad88b55a1" :question/math-academy-id "e-9960"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cb02b67c-90d9-5baf-b00e-590e9271d89e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049304} {:db/id 17592186049755} {:db/id 17592186050782} {:db/id 17592186050979}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125240} {:db/id 17592186125241} {:db/id 17592186278339} {:db/id 17592186278340} {:db/id 17592186278341} {:db/id 17592186278342} {:db/id 17592186281458} {:db/id 17592186323707} {:db/id 17592186329743} {:db/id 17592186440653} {:db/id 17592186440654} {:db/id 17592186440655} {:db/id 17592186445223}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Sets Closed Under Addition and Scalar Multiplication"} :step/id #uuid "78f1d4af-7528-5705-8b7b-224b627efd47" :step/math-academy-id 37506 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125341}} {:db/id 17592186125860 :tutorial/content "It's important to realize that not all sets are closed under addition and scalar multiplication. real matrices $A=({a}_{ij})$ such that ${a}_{22}=0.$ Which of the following statements are true?\n\nI. For any $A,B\\in P$ and any $\\alpha \\in R,$ we have $\\alpha (A+B)=\\alpha A+\\alpha B.$\n\nII. The scalar multiplication of matrices in $P$ is associative.\n\nIII. For any $A\\in P,$ we have $1\\cdot A={I}_{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's verify the statements one by one.\n\n- Statement I is true. Indeed, for any $2\\times 2$ matrices $A=({a}_{ij})$ and $B=({b}_{ij})$ from $P,$ the entries are just real numbers. Thus, for any $\\alpha \\in R,$ we obtain that\n\n$$\n\\alpha ({a}_{ij}+{b}_{ij})=\\alpha {a}_{ij}+\\alpha {b}_{ij},\n$$\n\nand hence,\n\n$$\n\\alpha (A+B)=\\alpha A+\\alpha B.\n$$\n\n- Statement II is true. Indeed, for any $2\\times 2$ matric $A=({a}_{ij})$ from $P,$ the entries are just real numbers. Thus, for any $\\alpha ,\\beta \\in R,$ we obtain that\n\n$$\n\\alpha (\\beta {a}_{ij})=(\\alpha \\beta ){a}_{ij},\n$$\n\nand hence,\n\n$$\n\\alpha (\\beta A)=(\\alpha \\beta )A.\n$$\n\n- Statement III is false. For example, consider the matrix $A=[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 1 & 0\\end{aligned}]$ from $P.$ Then,\n\n$$\n1\\cdot A=1\\cdot [\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 1 & 0\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}1\\cdot 1 & 1\\cdot 0 \\\\ 1\\cdot 1 & 1\\cdot 0\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 1 & 0\\end{aligned}]\\ne {I}_{2}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I and II only.\""} :step/id #uuid 17592186134674 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135049 :tutorial/content "We've already seen how to find the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace in the case when the subspace is defined using an orthogonal basis. In this lesson, we'll learn how to do the same thing in the case of non-orthogonal bases.\n\nFor example, consider the following vectors:\n![](images/28/28ce7470231775d8889555d0dd9f37ee9215044762a40335bd43578b121486a3.svg)\nHow can we find the orthogonal projection $\\mathbf{x}_S$ of the vector $\\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S = \\textrm{Span}\\{ \\mathbf{a}_1, \\mathbf{a}_2 \\}?$ Notice that since $\\mathbf a_1\\cdot \\mathbf a_2 \\neq 0,$ the vectors $\\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\\mathbf{a}_2$ are not orthogonal.\n\nAs usual, we would like to write $\\mathbf{x}$ as \n\n$$\n\\mathbf{x} = \\mathbf{x}_S + \\mathbf{x}_{S^\\perp},\n$$\n\nwhere $\\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \\mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \\mathbf{a}_2 \\in S$ and $\\mathbf{x}_{S^\\perp} \\!\\in S^\\perp.$\n\n![](images/3a/3a5576fcaf9e0be6fc14978eb91dcbaceee75cbfddaa537fdb05d34b8e31e2e0.png)\n\nSo, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}} & =x-{x}_{S} \\\\  & =x-({k}_{1}{a}_{1}+{k}_{2}{a}_{2}) \\\\  & =x-{k}_{1}{a}_{1}-{k}_{2}{a}_{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince $\\mathbf{x}_{S^\\perp} \\in S^\\perp,$ that is, $\\mathbf{x}_{S^\\perp} \\perp S,$ we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\{\\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{1} \\\\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{2}\\end{aligned}\\,⟹\\,\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\\cdot {a}_{1} &=0 \\\\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\\cdot {a}_{2} &=0.\\end{aligned}\\right.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we substitute the expression for $\\mathbf{x}_{S^\\perp}$ into the system to get\n![](images/f1/f1e3c7ae9e966ebcab88901c9e44a5449cb98716f43fc526d306e0af5186923b.svg)\n\nWe can write this system in an equivalent matrix form as follows:\n![](images/47/472c41e1e509d2db9c41dfa95127382eeba7ab5fbaa4172d680c39335694ef2e.svg)\n\nIf we denote \n![](images/26/2650c1020d413a7c988279cc698ab4b7c4caff427615d49b35ef4e9a42651ff0.svg)\nand ![](images/9b/9b50884bd0af404e71f9d7734e9bc054fc9439aba02780cf2beb5fa0a6ac1f32.svg) then we obtain\n\n$$\nA^TA\\mathbf{k} = A^T\\mathbf{x}\n\t\\qquad\\Longrightarrow\\qquad\n\t\\mathbf{k}=(A^TA)^{-1}A^T\\mathbf{x}.\n$$\n\nAlso, we note that  $\\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \\mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \\mathbf{a}_2$ can be expressed as $\\textrm{proj}_{S}\\,\\mathbf{x}\t= A\\mathbf{k}.$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\text{proj}}_{S}\\,x & =Ak \\\\  & =A({A}^{T}A)^{-1}{A}^{T}x.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis is a formula for the orthogonal projection!\n\nNow, we return to our example. Using the formula, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\text{proj}}_{S}\\,x & =\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\\\ 2 & 3 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{bmatrix}\\cdot {(\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 3 & 1\\end{bmatrix}\\cdot \\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\\\ 2 & 3 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\\cdot \\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 3 & 1\\end{bmatrix}\\cdot \\begin{bmatrix}2 \\\\ 4 \\\\ 0\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\\\ 2 & 3 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{bmatrix}\\cdot {(\\begin{bmatrix}6 & 8 \\\\ 8 & 11\\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\\cdot \\begin{bmatrix}10 \\\\ 14\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\\\ 2 & 3 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{bmatrix}\\cdot \\frac{1}{2}\\begin{bmatrix}11 & -8 \\\\ -8 & 6\\end{bmatrix}\\cdot \\begin{bmatrix}10 \\\\ 14\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\\\ 2 & 3 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{bmatrix}\\cdot \\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\\\ 2\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}1 \\\\ 4 \\\\ 1\\end{bmatrix}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Note**: Pay attention to the order in which we carried out the multiplication. Carrying out the operations in the order shown above can save us a lot of work!" :tutorial/id #uuid "0a9a954f-9338-5c3f-a9db-9b39a1a60c0b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3626 :tutorial/title are the vectors of $\\mathbf{a}_1, \\mathbf{a}_2 , \\ldots, \\mathbf{a}_n,$ that is,\n![](images/25/25a85721a3721ace1a32f6ed457749091452df93053d2eba7dbfaa48f6f74189.svg)\n\n**Watch out!** The fact that $\\{ \\mathbf{a}_1, \\mathbf{a}_2 , \\ldots, \\mathbf{a}_n \\}$ must be linearly independent is important. using an orthogonal basis. In this lesson, we'll learn how to do the same thing in the case of non-orthogonal bases.\n\nFor example, consider the following vectors:\n![](images/28/28ce7470231775d8889555d0dd9f37ee9215044762a40335bd43578b121486a3.svg)\nHow can we find the orthogonal projection $\\mathbf{x}_S$ of the vector $\\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S = \\textrm{Span}\\{ \\mathbf{a}_1, \\mathbf{a}_2 \\}?$ Notice that since $\\mathbf a_1\\cdot \\mathbf a_2 \\neq 0,$ the vectors $\\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\\mathbf{a}_2$ are not orthogonal.\n\nAs usual, we would like to write $\\mathbf{x}$ as \n\n$$\n\\mathbf{x} = \\mathbf{x}_S + \\mathbf{x}_{S^\\perp},\n$$\n\nwhere $\\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \\mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \\mathbf{a}_2 \\in S$ and $\\mathbf{x}_{S^\\perp} \\!\\in S^\\perp.$\n\n![](images/3a/3a5576fcaf9e0be6fc14978eb91dcbaceee75cbfddaa537fdb05d34b8e31e2e0.png)\n\nSo, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}} & =x-{x}_{S} \\\\  & =x-({k}_{1}{a}_{1}+{k}_{2}{a}_{2}) \\\\  & =x-{k}_{1}{a}_{1}-{k}_{2}{a}_{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince $\\mathbf{x}_{S^\\perp} \\in S^\\perp,$ that is, $\\mathbf{x}_{S^\\perp} \\perp S,$ we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\{\\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{1} \\\\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{2}\\end{aligned}\\,⟹\\,\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\\cdot {a}_{1} &=0 \\\\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\\cdot {a}_{2} &=0.\\end{aligned}\\right.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we substitute the expression for $\\mathbf{x}_{S^\\perp}$ into the system to get\n![](images/f1/f1e3c7ae9e966ebcab88901c9e44a5449cb98716f43fc526d306e0af5186923b.svg)\n\nWe can write this system in an equivalent matrix form as follows:\n![](images/47/472c41e1e509d2db9c41dfa95127382eeba7ab5fbaa4172d680c39335694ef2e.svg)\n\nIf we denote \n![](images/26/2650c1020d413a7c988279cc698ab4b7c4caff427615d49b35ef4e9a42651ff0.svg)\nand ![](images/9b/9b50884bd0af404e71f9d7734e9bc054fc9439aba02780cf2beb5fa0a6ac1f32.svg) then we obtain\n\n$$\nA^TA\\mathbf{k} = A^T\\mathbf{x}\n\t\\qquad\\Longrightarrow\\qquad\n\t\\mathbf{k}=(A^TA)^{-1}A^T\\mathbf{x}.\n$$\n\nAlso, we note that  $\\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \\mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \\mathbf{a}_2$ can be expressed as $\\textrm{proj}_{S}\\,\\mathbf{x}\t= A\\mathbf{k}.$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\text{proj}}_{S}\\,x & =Ak \\\\  & =A({A}^{T}A)^{-1}{A}^{T}x.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis is a formula for the orthogonal projection!\n\nNow, we return to our example. Using the formula, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\text{proj}}_{S}\\,x & =\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\\\ 2 & 3 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{bmatrix}\\cdot {(\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 3 & 1\\end{bmatrix}\\cdot \\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\\\ 2 & 3 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\\cdot \\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 3 & 1\\end{bmatrix}\\cdot \\begin{bmatrix}2 \\\\ 4 \\\\ 0\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\\\ 2 & 3 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{bmatrix}\\cdot {(\\begin{bmatrix}6 & 8 \\\\ 8 & 11\\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\\cdot \\begin{bmatrix}10 \\\\ 14\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\\\ 2 & 3 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{bmatrix}\\cdot \\frac{1}{2}\\begin{bmatrix}11 & -8 \\\\ -8 & 6\\end{bmatrix}\\cdot \\begin{bmatrix}10 \\\\ 14\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\\\ 2 & 3 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{bmatrix}\\cdot \\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\\\ 2\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}1 \\\\ 4 \\\\ 1\\end{bmatrix}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Note**: Pay attention to the order in which we carried out the multiplication. On the other hand, the vectors from the general solution form a basis $\\mathcal B$ of our eigenspace:\n\n![](images/06/060bba6a9639bb7658256cea78cf6cb362a3a15a435b3391e806ca43742509ed.svg)\n\nIn particular, we have $\\dim(V_{-3}) =2.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5d00ddf6-6fe9-56f2-98f7-dd367ce7b91d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3567 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid #uuid "56638735-6442-509a-9127-6494dc299da9" :step/math-academy-id 20105 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125415}} {:db/id 17592186125413 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125788 :tutorial/content "In general, given an eigenvalue $\\lambda$ of a matrix $A,$ we can have the following two situations:\n\n- If $\\lambda$ is a simple root of the characteristic equation, then the eigenspace $V_{\\lambda}$ has dimension $1\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\text{dim}(V_{\\lambda}) = 1\n$$\n\n- If $\\lambda$ is *not* a simple root of the characteristic equation (it's a double, triple, quadruple root, etc.), the dimension of the eigenspace $V_{\\lambda}$ equals the number of free variables in the system of linear equations corresponding to \n\n$$\n(A-\\lambda I)\\mathbf{x} = \\mathbf{0}.\n$$\n\n**Watch out!** The second rule does *not* claim that if an eigenvalue is, say, a double root, then $\\text{dim}(V_{\\lambda}) = 2.$ It says that we have to examine the corresponding linear system and only then make the conclusion depending on the number of free variables.\n\nHowever, there is one thing we can determine about the dimension of the eigenspace, and it is given by the following theorem.\n\n*If an eigenvalue $\\lambda$ is a root of multiplicity $k$ in the corresponding characteristic equation, then the eigenspace $V_{\\lambda}$ has dimension not greater than $k \\mathbin{:}$ \n\n$$\n\\text{dim}(V_{\\lambda}) \\leq k\n$$\n\n*\n\nRecall that the multiplicity of an eigenvalue as a root of the characteristic equation is called *algebraic multiplicity*. On the other hand, the dimension of the corresponding eigenspace is called the **geometric multiplicity** of the eigenvalue. Our theorem above states the following: \n\n*The geometric multiplicity of an eigenvalue is always less than or equal to the algebraic multiplicity.*" :tutorial/id #uuid robotic rover moves in a straight line with velocity \n$v(t)=3{t}^{2}-t,$ where $t$ is measured in seconds and $v$ is measured in meters per second. \n\nFind the average acceleration ${a}_{\\text{avg}}$ of the rover over the time interval $t\\in [0,2].$ Do not round your answer.\n\n${a}_{\\text{avg}}=$ \n{{field-1}}\n${\\text{m/s}}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "The average :question/worked-solution "To determine whether $f$ is even or odd, we compare $f(-x)$ and $f(x){:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)\\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(-x)) \\\\  & cosine coefficients are given by\n\n$$\na_n=\\frac{1}{\\pi}\\int_{-\\pi}^{\\pi} f(x)\\cos(nx)\\,\\text{d}x,\n$$\n\nand the constant coefficient is\n\n$$\na_0=\\frac{1}{\\pi}\\int_{-\\pi}^{\\pi} f(x)\\,\\text{d}x.\n$$\n\nHere, $f(x)$ is odd and $\\cos(nx)$ is even, so $f(x)\\cos(nx)$ is odd. Also, $f(x)$ itself is odd.\n\nNow, the integral of an odd function over $[-\\pi,\\pi]$ is $0.$ Thus, $a_n=0$ for all $n\\ge1,$ and $a_0=0.$\n\nTherefore, the function $f(x)$ is $\\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\\text{odd}}$ and the $\\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\\text{cosine}}$ terms  in its Fourier series must be zero."} {:db/id 17592186048495} {:db/id 17592186050762} Setting up the equation $y'(t) = 0$ gives\n\n$$\n5y(10-y) = 0.\n$$\n\nSo, there are two equilibrium solutions, $y=0,$ and $y=10.$ Let's create a diagram and plot these two solutions.\n\n![](images/98/98d52420673e65eedf5679e57b9c562f8a8eeabde24d0d2ed4fff827a6447fc2.png)\n\nWe will now sketch a solution curve that lies between these two equilibrium solutions. \n\nNotice the following:\n\n- Since $0 < y < 10$ for all $t,$ we have that $5y(10-y)$ is positive for all $t.$\n\n- Therefore, $y'(t)$ is positive for all $t.$\n\n- Hence, $y(t)$ is increasing for all $t.$\n\nUsing this information, we can start to sketch a solution curve.\n\n![](images/ce/ce6f493f4c2830acf42e189ace04027f8452ec3df92d24b9d223f92848832996.png)\n\nNext, we note the following regarding the end-behavior of our solution:\n\n- The expression $5y(10-y)\\to 0$ as $y\\to10.$\n\n- Therefore, $y'\\to 0$ as $y\\to 10.$\n\nIn other words, the curve flattens as $y$ approaches $10.$ Adding this behavior to our diagram, we get a complete sketch of the solution curve.\n\n![](images/f3/f329f3cd49d61c3a1e2838397521cdd6d3bbefc7dadd09d1dd25b00767a0cd37.png)\n\nGathering information about the solutions to a differential equation without solving it is called **qualitative analysis.**" 17592186045417] [17592186177033 1065 5718 17592186045417] [17592186177033 1066 #uuid "05ebc248-7295-5381-964a-30c7e3b638e5" 17592186045417] [17592186177033 1067 "Introduction" 17592186045417] [17592186177034 1064 "Let's go back to the following logistic growth equation:\n\n$$\ny' = 5y(10-y), \\qquad y(0) = y_0.\n$$\n\nThe logistic growth curve for this problem is sketched below.\n\n![](images/0a/0a225fd04f81bd65e1bad3ff14097563d112a16e3847aac26cc86591533ea5d0.png)\n\nThe curve contains an inflection point, that is, a point where $y(t)$ is growing at its fastest possible rate. [17592186222331 1063 17592186222512 17592186045417] [17592186222498 1064 "Each step of a numerical method produces a local truncation error $\\tau,$ which, over multiple steps, accumulates into a global truncation error $e.$ Both LTE and GTE depend on step size $\\Delta x.$\n\nThe **order** of a numerical method describes how fast these errors shrink as $\\Delta x$ decreases.\nA numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the *largest positive* integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies\n\n$$\ne(\\Delta x) = \\mathcal O\\!\\left((\\Delta x)^p\\right)\\quad\\textrm{as}\\quad \\Delta x \\to 0.\n$$\n\nIn other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately $k^p{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}e(\\frac{Δx}{k}) & ≈K{(\\frac{Δx}{k})}^{p}=\\frac{K(Δx)^{p}}{{k}^{p}}≈\\frac{e(Δx)}{{k}^{p}}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nLet's demonstrate with an example. Suppose a numerical method is used to approximate the solution to an initial value problem.\n\n- With step size $\\Delta x = 0.21,$ the observed global truncation error is $e(0.21) = 0.785.$\n\n- With step size $\\Delta x = 0.07,$ the observed global truncation error is $e(0.07) = 0.010.$\n\nUsing this data, we can estimate the order of the numerical method.\n\nThe step size decreases from $0.21$ to $0.07.$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\nk = \\dfrac{0.21}{0.07} = 3.\n$$\n\nAs a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the GTE should decrease by a factor of approximately\n\n$$\nk^p = 3^p.\n$$\n\nOn the other hand, the GTE actually decreases from $0.785$ to $0.010.$ So, it reduces by a factor of\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{0.785}{0.010} = 78.5.\n$$\n\nComparing the two scale factors for the GTE, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{3}^{p} & ≈78.5 \\\\ p & ≈{log}_{3}⁡(78.5) \\\\ p & ≈3.97….\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the approximate order of the method is $4.$\n\nBut why is order important? Well, a higher order means that the error decreases faster as $\\Delta x$ decreases. As a result, higher-order methods can achieve a target accuracy *with fewer steps*. "Suppose we want to evaluate $\\displaystyle \\int x^3e^{x/2} \\textrm{d}x$. We can do it by applying integration by parts three times, but the calculation is pretty long. How can we speed it up?\n\nMultiple applications of integration by parts becomes quick and easy if we use the **tabular method**.\n\nLet's start by picking our $u$ and\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\textrm{d}v}{\\textrm{d}x}\n$$\n\nas normal:\n\n$$\nu = x^3\\,,\\quad \\dfrac{\\textrm{d}v}{\\textrm{d}x} = e^{x/2}\\,\n$$\n\nWe put this in a table, as shown below:\n\n| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same Color Products** |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3$ | $e^{x/2}$ |  |  |\n\nTo fill in the second row of the table, we differentiate the function in the first column and integrate the function in the second column. Doing this, we find\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\textrm{d}}{\\textrm{d}x}\\left(x^3\\right) = 3x^2\\,,\\quad \\int e^{x/2} \\textrm{d}x = 2e^{x/2}\\,\n$$\n\nFilling in our table, we get the following:\n\n| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same Color Products** |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3$ | $e^{x/2}$ |  |  |\n| $\\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 3x^2$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2e^{x/2}$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0} +$ |  |\n\nAt this step, we begin filling the third column. It always starts with a \"$+$\" and then the signs alternate at each subsequent step.\n\nWe continue by differentiating the expression in the first column and integrating the expression in the second column until we get zero in the first column.\n\n| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same Color Products** |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3$ | $e^{x/2}$ |  |  |\n| $\\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 3x^2$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2e^{x/2}$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0} +$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0}$ |\n| $\\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 6x$ | $\\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 4e^{x/2}$ | $\\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -$ | $\\color[rgb]{0,0.5,0}$ |\n| $\\color[rgb]{1,0,1} 6$ | $\\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 8e^{x/2}$ | $\\color[rgb]{0,0,1} +$ | $\\color[rgb]{0,0,1}$ |\n| $0$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,1}16e^{x/2}$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,1} -$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,1}$ |\n\nNow we multiply the same colored terms along with the same colored sign. Specifically we multiply $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3$ with ${\\color[rgb]{1,0,0} 2e^{x/2}}$, $\\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}3x^2$ with $\\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}4e^{x/2}$, and so on. We get\n\n| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same Color Products** |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3$ | $e^{x/2}$ |  |  |\n| $\\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}3x^2$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2e^{x/2}$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0} +$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,0} 2x^3e^{x/2}$ |\n| $\\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 6x$ | $\\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 4e^{x/2}$ | $\\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -$ | $\\color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -12x^2e^{x/2}$ |\n| $\\color[rgb]{1,0,1} 6$ | $\\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 8e^{x/2}$ | $\\color[rgb]{0,0,1} +$ | $\\color[rgb]{0,0,1} 48xe^{x/2}$ |\n| $0$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,1}16e^{x/2}$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,1} -$ | $\\color[rgb]{1,0,1} -96e^{x/2}$ |\n\nFinally, we add up all the terms of the last column to get the answer for our integral. We get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\intx^{3}e^{x/2}dx &= 2x^{3}e^{x/2} - 12x^{2}e^{x/2} + 48xe^{x/2} - 96e^{x/2} + C \\\\\n&= e^{x/2}(2x^{3} - 12x^{2} + 48x - 96) + C\n\\end{aligned}\n$$" Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.\nStudents learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.\nStudents then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.\nThe course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.\nThe course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.\nStudents then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.\nThe final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating But what can we say about the eigenspace $V_{-3}$ for this particular matrix?\n\nRecall that given a matrix with eigenvalue $\\lambda,$ the eigenspace $V_{\\lambda}$ is\n\n![](images/dc/dc954c4b48b2ea3bed7a1ab8370d6a2be9a1e22298e9a838acfe47b5b5d0c47d.svg)\n\nTo compute the eigenvectors of the matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation \n\n$$\n(A - \\lambda I) \\textbf{x}=\\mathbf{0}.\n$$\n\n \n\nIn our case, we have $\\lambda =-3.$ So, we get \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}A-\\lambda I & =\\begin{bmatrix}5 & 8 & 16 \\\\ 4 & 1 & 8 \\\\ -4 & -4 & -11\\end{bmatrix}-(-3)\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 1\\end{bmatrix}=\\begin{bmatrix}8 & 8 & 16 \\\\ 4 & 4 & 8 \\\\ -4 & -4 & -8\\end{bmatrix}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:\n\n$$\n\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}8{x}_{1}+8{x}_{2}+16{x}_{3} &=0 \\\\ 4{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}+8{x}_{3} &=0 \\\\ -4{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3} &=0\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nSolving the system, we obtain the general solution \n\n![](images/a5/a552b978409debb7cf783cd683eceda220ba5eb0f37a82b08add9a66106d75fc.svg)\n\nTherefore, our eigenspace is\n\n![](images/87/8767b25332906b9b6149be3a007cbb89e07d791ed58625e9df369880524f2fdb.svg)\n\nNotice that $s=t=0$ gives the zero vector.
